blocks.title: What ICAI's published papers tell us
bullets: ICAI has published no examiners' comments for Paper 6; the guidance below comes from its suggested answers, RTPs and MTPs.

**This is the largest chapter in Paper 6A and the most heavily examined.** Sixty-eight register headings over six units, and **fifty-one official question parts** between May 2024 and September 2026 — more than Chapters 7 and 8 together.

**Two topics take almost half the marks.** **Credit policy evaluation** (eight official questions) and **factoring** (eight official questions) account for sixteen of the fifty-one parts. Learn ICAI's two printed formats cold — the Total Approach / Incremental Approach statement and the Statement showing the Evaluation of Factoring Proposal — and those sixteen questions become fill-in-the-blanks.

**The operating cycle and the cash-cost statement take most of the rest.** Six questions on the operating cycle and nine on estimating working capital, five of them specifically on the cash-cost basis.

**The Part I case scenario lands here more often than anywhere else in the paper.** Five of the fourteen papers reviewed put a ten-mark working-capital case in Division A: SA May 2025 (XYZ Ltd), SA September 2025 (RG Limited), RTP January 2025 (Samvar Ltd), RTP January 2026 (PPW Ltd) and MTP March 2024 Series I (NV Industries). September 2025's RG Limited runs the operating cycle **backwards** from the working-capital figure — the hardest single question in the chapter.

**The theory slots are short and they repeat.** Liquidity versus profitability (three times), the factors in planning working capital (three times), virtual banking (twice), trade credit versus bank overdraft, the costs of availing trade credit, factoring versus forfaiting, the treasury department's tasks and the forms of bank credit. Each is a four-mark answer that needs no arithmetic at all.

blocks.title: How ICAI marks this chapter (study guidance)
bullets: **Decide cost basis or sales basis in the first line, and write it down.** Debtors and finished goods go in at **cash cost** unless the question says otherwise, and depreciation always comes out. Getting this wrong costs every subsequent figure.
**Write the operating cycle as R + W + F + D − C**, name each letter, then compute each period as a labelled fraction. The marks are in the five fractions, not in the total.

**Read the safety-margin wording twice.** 'A margin of 15%' on net working capital is not the same as 'a margin of 15% of the net working capital inclusive of the margin'. The second means the computed excess is 85% of the answer, so the margin is excess × 15/85, which is how ICAI applies it in RTP September 2024 (₹4,49,792 × 1/9).

**Use ICAI's own layout for credit-policy questions** — Expected Profit (a to g), then Opportunity Cost of Investment in Receivables, then Net Benefits — and close with the one-sentence recommendation. The recommendation is a mark.

**In every factoring question, state the decision rule before the arithmetic:** accept if the effective cost of factoring is below the existing cost of borrowing. Several official answers carry that sentence as a separate mark.
**Assume 360 days unless told otherwise, and say which you used.** ICAI prints both; September 2025's Wint Limited and May 2026's Puja Limited both use 365.

**Six units means six question styles.** Do not revise this chapter as one block; revise it as Unit I (estimation), Unit II (cash), Unit IV (receivables) and Unit VI (financing), which is where the questions actually come from.

blocks.title: The five errors that cost the most marks here
bullets: **Valuing debtors at sales value instead of cash cost.** SM §6.3 is explicit: debtors worth ₹1 lakh on a cost of sales of ₹75,000 of which ₹5,000 is depreciation tie up only **₹70,000** of funds.

**Forgetting that work-in-progress carries full material but only part of the conversion cost.** MTP January 2026 Series I gives 50% conversion with materials issued at the start; MTP January 2025 Series II gives 90% material and 60% conversion.

**Applying the lending percentage and the reserve in the wrong order** in a receivables-collateral question. RTP January 2025's Nirmoh Limited deducts the reserve first and then lends 90% of the balance.
**Using sales rather than cost of sales in the opportunity cost of receivables.** ICAI's own formula is Total Cost of Credit Sales × collection period ÷ 365 × required return.

**Confusing the two cost-of-payables formulae.** The nominal annual cost is d ÷ (100 − d) × 365 ÷ t; the compounded cost is [100 ÷ (100 − d)]^(365/t) − 1. SM Illustration 17 gives 23.5% on 2/10 net 45 using the second.

key_provisions: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities

Number of operating cycles in a year = 360 (or 365) ÷ Operating cycle period

trend: Every attempt from May 2024 to May 2026 carried at least two working-capital parts, and January 2025, September 2025 and May 2026 carried three each.

**Three of the last five papers put this chapter in Division A as a ten-mark case scenario** — May 2025 (XYZ Ltd), September 2025 (RG Limited) and, counting the RTPs, January 2025 and January 2026 as well. No other chapter is used that way so consistently.

**Factoring has been asked in eight of the fourteen paper sets reviewed**, and five of those eight run the same 2/40 net 120 data with only the bad-debt percentage or the comparison rate changed: MTP March 2024 Series I (1%, bank at 14%), RTP September 2025 (1.5%, bank at 12%) and RTP September 2026 (1%, bank at 14%) are the same question three times.
**Credit policy has been asked eight times** and ICAI uses the Total Approach in every published answer except MTP May 2025 Series II, which uses the Incremental Approach.

The reverse workings are getting harder: September 2025's RG Limited inverts the whole operating cycle, and January 2026's MCQ 7 inverts Baumol's formula. Expect at least one inverted formula in Division A.

The theory marks cluster on four questions — liquidity versus profitability, the factors in planning working capital, virtual banking, and trade credit against bank overdraft — which between them appeared nine times in fourteen paper sets.

concepts.title: 1–2.2 Meaning and Concept of Working Capital, its Significance, Adequate Working Capital and Optimum Working Capital
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 direct (but every numerical in the chapter rests on these definitions) · RTP 0 direct · MTP 0 direct
understand: ==**The one definition everything else hangs on** (SM §1): **Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities.**==

**When is an asset current?** SM §1: when **(i) it is expected to be realised or intends to be sold or consumed in the normal operating cycle of the entity or within twelve months after the reporting period, whichever is longer; and (ii) the asset is held primarily for the purpose of trading in the ordinary course of business.**

**The four groups of current assets** for working-capital purposes: **(a) Inventory** (raw material, work in process and finished goods), **(b) Receivables** (trade receivables and bills receivables), **(c) Cash or cash equivalents** (including short-term marketable securities) and **(d) Prepaid expenses.** Other current assets may include short-term loans or advances and accrued revenue.

**When is a liability current?** When **(i) it is expected to be settled in the normal operating cycle or within twelve months, whichever is longer; and (ii) it is settled either by the use of current assets or by the creation of a new current liability.** The two groups are **(a) Payables** (trade and bills payables) and **(b) Outstanding payments** (wages and salary, overheads and other expenses).

==**Two ways of cutting the concept, and ICAI draws both as a tree** (SM §1):
**On the basis of value** → **Gross** working capital = the firm's **investment in current assets**; **Net** working capital = **current assets less current liabilities**.
**On the basis of time** → **Permanent** and **Fluctuating (temporary)**.==

**Permanent working capital** is the **base working capital — the minimum level of investment in current assets carried by the entity at all times** to carry on its day-to-day activities. It stays invested unless operations are scaled up or down permanently, and **it is generally financed by long-term sources of finance.**

**Temporary (variable, fluctuating) working capital** is what is needed **in addition to** the permanent amount, to finance short-term requirements **arising from fluctuation in sales volume** — the extra inventory held for a seasonal peak, for instance. ==**Both kinds are necessary to facilitate production and sales through the operating cycle.**==
**A positive working capital indicates the company's ability to pay its short-term liabilities; a negative working capital shows inability to meet short-term obligations.**

==**Why too much is as bad as too little** (SM §2.1). **Too large:** the company has **idle funds**; since funds have a cost it pays interest on funds invested in surplus working capital, and there is an **opportunity cost** — the return it could have earned on long-term investment. ==**ICAI cites the Bureau of Public Enterprises studies: one reason for the poor performance of public sector undertakings in India has been the large amount of funds locked up in working capital, which results in over capitalization — too large funds for requirements, a low rate of return, a less than optimal use of resources.**==

==**Too small:** the firm **runs the risk of insolvency**; paucity of working capital may mean it cannot meet its liabilities, and it may not hold enough inventory to meet customers' demand, **losing sales and eventually some reputation as well.**==

**The long-term point ICAI makes twice.** Maintaining adequate working capital matters in the long term too: when a business makes an investment decision it must consider not only the outlay on the machine or building but **the additional current assets usually required with any expansion of activity** — increased production means **additional stocks of raw materials and work-in-progress**; increased sales mean **higher debtors and finished goods**; and a general increase in scale **tends to imply a need for greater levels of working capital.**

==**What 'optimum' means** (SM §2.2). **Current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) has traditionally been considered the best indicator of the working capital situation**, supplemented by the **acid test ratio**. ==**A current ratio of 2 for a manufacturing firm implies an optimum amount of working capital**; a higher ratio may indicate inefficient use of funds and a lower ratio liquidity problems. The quick ratio should be **at least 1**, where quick assets are **current assets less inventory and prepaid expenses.**==

**But ICAI immediately qualifies the thumb rule, and this is the examinable sentence:** **'optimum working capital can be determined only with reference to the particular circumstances of a specific situation.'** Where inventories are easily saleable and debtors are as good as liquid cash the current ratio **may be lower than 2 and yet the firm may be sound**; a **restaurant**, whose finished goods are perishable, cannot afford to hold a large amount of working capital; a company whose **products take a longer production time** may need more. ==**In a nutshell, both excessive and inadequate working capital positions are dangerous.**==
concepts.example: January 2026's BEE Ltd question in the past paper opens 'BEE Ltd. has a current ratio of 2:1, showing enough short-term liquidity in the company' and then asks whether a series of transactions improves, worsens or leaves the ratio unchanged. The question is marked in Chapter 3 as ratio analysis, but the premise is this section's: a current ratio of 2 is the conventional benchmark, not a proof of health, and ICAI's own text says so.

mcqs.question: A firm's current assets are ₹18,00,000 and its current liabilities ₹12,00,000. Its gross working capital and net working capital are respectively:
mcqs.explanation: SM §1: gross working capital is the firm's investment in current assets, so ₹18,00,000; net working capital is current assets less current liabilities, so ₹6,00,000. Option B reverses the two, which is the standard distractor.

mcqs.question: A restaurant chain reports a current ratio of 1.1 : 1. According to the study material this:

options.A: Proves the business is heading for insolvency, since the benchmark is 2 : 1
options.B: Need not indicate weakness, because optimum working capital can be determined only with reference to the particular circumstances of a specific situation
options.C: Is irrelevant, because the current ratio does not measure the working capital situation
options.D: Means the business is over-capitalised

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.2 gives the 2 : 1 thumb rule and then qualifies it in the same breath, using a restaurant as its own example: where finished goods are perishable the organisation cannot afford to hold a large amount of working capital. Option C contradicts the section, which calls the current ratio the traditional best indicator.

recap: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities.
Value splits it into gross (investment in current assets) and net (the difference); time splits it into permanent and fluctuating.
Permanent working capital is financed by long-term sources; temporary by short-term sources.
Excess working capital means idle funds and over capitalization; inadequate working capital means the risk of insolvency.
Current ratio 2 and quick ratio 1 are thumb rules only — optimum depends on the particular circumstances of the specific situation.

concepts.title: 3 Determinants of Working Capital
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 2 (Sep 2026 Q10(c); the same list underlies Sep 2025 Q10(c)) · MTP 0 direct
understand: **What working capital management is concerned with** (SM §3): **(a) maintaining adequate working capital** — managing the level of individual current assets and current liabilities — **and (b) financing of the working capital.** The finance manager plans and computes the requirement, then ensures it is financed properly; **this whole exercise is known as Working Capital Management.**
**ICAI's instruction on how to forecast:** **sound financial and statistical techniques, supported by judgment, should be used to predict the quantum of working capital required at different times.**
==**The nine factors, which ICAI prints as a labelled diagram and which is the answer to 'factors to be considered while planning for working capital requirement'** (SM §3):==

==**1. Need for Cash** — identify the cash balance that allows the business to meet day-to-day expenses **but reduces cash holding costs**, for example the loss of interest on long-term investment had the surplus cash been invested there.==

==**2. Desired level of Inventory** — the level that allows **uninterrupted production** but reduces the investment in raw materials and so increases cash flow. **The techniques used are Just in Time (JIT) and Economic Order Quantity (EOQ).**==

==**3. Receivables** — identify the appropriate credit policy, that is **credit terms which will attract customers such that any impact on cash flows and the cash conversion cycle will be offset by increased revenue and hence Return on Capital** (or vice versa). **The tools are Early Payment Discounts and allowances.**==

==**4. Short-term Financing Options** — **inventory is ideally financed by credit granted by the supplier**; depending on the cash conversion cycle it may be necessary to use a bank loan or overdraft, or to 'convert debtors to cash' through factoring.==
==**5. Nature of Business** — in a **restaurant** most sales are in cash, so the need for working capital is very low; a **pharmacy or a bookstore** carries higher inventory.==

==**6. Market and Demand Conditions** — if an item's demand far exceeds its production the working capital requirement is **less**, because investment in finished goods inventory is very small with continuous sales.==

==**7. Technology and Manufacturing Policies** — where demand is **seasonal**, a business may follow a policy of **steady production throughout the year** or of **production only during the demand season**; the two choices need very different working capital.==
==**8. Operating Efficiency** — a company can reduce the requirement by **eliminating waste, improving coordination and process improvements**.==

==**9. Price Level Changes and Exchange Rate Fluctuations** — **rising prices necessitate the use of more funds for maintaining an existing level of activity**; for the same level of current assets, higher cash outlays are required, so **the effect of rising prices is that a higher amount of working capital is required**. An unfavourable exchange rate movement on imported raw materials has the same effect.==

**How to turn the list into a case answer, which is what both RTPs actually ask.** September 2026's Sunrise Healthcare faces rising raw material costs (factor 9), exchange-rate swings on imported medicines (factor 9 again), rising inventory from uncertain demand (factor 2), a credit policy under review (factor 3) and short-term financing options (factor 4). ==**Name the factor, then tie it to the fact in the case in one clause.** A bare list of nine headings scores much less than five headings each with a sentence drawn from the scenario.==
concepts.example: RTP September 2026 Q10(c) gives Sunrise Healthcare Pvt. Ltd., a pharmacy chain, and asks for 'the factors that should be considered while planning its working capital requirements'. ICAI's answer is this section verbatim. The marks are free if the nine headings are memorised, and the difference between a pass and a good answer is whether the candidate attaches the case's own facts — imported medicines, uncertain demand, the credit policy review — to the headings.

mistakes: Saying inflation reduces the working capital requirement. ICAI says the opposite: higher cash outlays are needed for the same level of current assets.
Saying a business whose demand exceeds production needs more working capital. It needs less, because finished goods do not accumulate.
Listing the nine headings with no reference to the case in a case-based question. Both RTP askings are case-based.

Confusing these nine planning factors with the five factors in §4.2 that govern the **level of investment** in working capital (nature of industry, type of product, manufacturing versus trading versus service, volume of sales, credit policy). Different list, different section, and MTP September 2024 Series II Q2(b) asks for the second one.
Omitting short-term financing options, which is the only one of the nine that points forward to Unit VI.

official_questions.question: Sunrise Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. operates a chain of pharmacies across India. The company has recently experienced rising raw material costs, fluctuations in exchange rates affecting imported medicines, and increasing inventory levels due to uncertain demand. Management is also reviewing its credit policy to improve cash flows and is considering various short-term financing options to meet working capital needs. In the context of the above case, discuss the factors that should be considered by Sunrise Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. while planning its working capital requirements.
answer_points: **Open with the frame.** Working capital management is concerned with maintaining adequate working capital and with financing it; **sound financial and statistical techniques, supported by judgment, should be used to predict the quantum required at different times.**

**Price Level Changes and Exchange Rate Fluctuations** — the factor the case leads with. **Rising prices necessitate the use of more funds for maintaining an existing level of activity**: for the same level of current assets, higher cash outlays are required, so **the effect of rising prices is that a higher amount of working capital is required.** For Sunrise, **unfavourable exchange rate movement on imported medicines warrants an additional cost of the same**, compounding the effect.

**Desired level of Inventory** — identify the level that allows uninterrupted supply to the pharmacies but reduces investment in stock and so increases cash flow. **JIT and EOQ** are the techniques; with demand uncertain, the safety stock element of that calculation is what is actually rising.

**Receivables** — the credit policy under review. The test is whether **credit terms which attract customers** produce increased revenue, and hence return on capital, sufficient to offset the impact on cash flows and the cash conversion cycle. **Early payment discounts and allowances** are the tools.

**Short-term Financing Options** — **inventory is ideally financed by credit granted by the supplier**; beyond that, and depending on the cash conversion cycle, a bank loan or overdraft, or converting debtors to cash through factoring.
**Need for Cash** — the balance that meets day-to-day expenses while reducing cash holding costs, such as the interest forgone on long-term investment.
**Nature of Business** — a pharmacy carries **higher inventory** by its nature, which is ICAI's own example in this very list.

**Market and Demand Conditions** — where demand far exceeds production the requirement falls because finished goods do not accumulate; Sunrise's problem is the reverse, uncertain demand building inventory.

**Technology and Manufacturing Policies** and **Operating Efficiency** — complete the list: the production or procurement pattern chosen, and the scope to cut the requirement by eliminating waste and improving coordination.
keywords: rising prices require more working capital

concepts.title: 4–4.2 Management of Working Capital, Liquidity and Profitability, and the Investment and Financing Decision
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 1 (Sep 2025 Q10(c)) · MTP 4 (Mar 2024 Series II, Sep 2024 Series II, Sep 2025 Series I, Sep 2026 Series II)
understand: ==**ICAI's image, worth quoting in any theory answer** (SM §4): **'The importance of working capital for an entity can be compared to importance of life blood for a living body or of a lubricant/fuel for an engine.'** Working capital is required for the smooth functioning of the business, as lack of it **may interrupt the ordinary course of activities.**==

==**The three Es.** Management involves **3 Es — Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness — and all three are required for working capital management.** They map onto the chapter: **economy in financing, efficiency in utilisation and effectiveness in achieving the intended objectives.**==
==**The scope of working capital management is grouped into two broad areas** (SM §4): **(i) Liquidity and Profitability** and **(ii) Investment and Financing Decision.**==

**§4.1 Liquidity and Profitability — why there must be a trade-off.** For uninterrupted day-to-day functioning it is important to maintain liquidity of funds evenly, but **each rupee of capital bears some cost**, so the cost aspect must be borne in mind. A higher working capital may be intended to increase revenue and hence profitability, **but unnecessary tying up of funds in idle assets not only reduces liquidity but also reduces the opportunity to earn a better return from a productive asset.** ==**Hence a trade-off is required between liquidity and profitability which increases profitability without disturbing day-to-day functioning.**==
==**ICAI's five-row trade-off table is the answer to the 'trade-offs between components' question** (SM §4.1), and it has a counter-intuitive final row:==

==**Inventory** — higher side: **fewer stock-outs increase profitability**. Trade-off: **use EOQ, JIT to carry the optimum level**. Lower side: **less capital required but endangered stock-out and loss of goodwill.**==

==**Receivables** — higher side: **a higher credit period attracts customers and increases revenue, but can result in more bad debts.** Trade-off: **evaluate the credit policy; use the services of debt management (factoring) agencies.** Lower side: **cash sales provide liquidity but fail to boost sales and revenue** because of the lower credit period.==

==**Pre-payment of expenses** — higher side: **reduces uncertainty and is profitable in an inflationary environment.** Trade-off: **cost-benefit analysis required.** Lower side: **improves or maintains liquidity.**==

==**Cash and cash equivalents** — higher side: **payables are honoured in time, which improves goodwill and helps in getting future discounts.** Trade-off: **cash budgets and other cash management techniques.** Lower side: **cash can be invested in some other investment avenues.**==

==**Payables and expenses** — higher side: **capital can be used in some other investment avenues.** Trade-off: **evaluate the credit policy and related cost.** Lower side: **payables are honoured in time, improving goodwill and helping to get future discounts.** ==**Note the inversion: for payables the 'liquidity' column carries the goodwill argument, because holding more payables releases cash but delays settlement.**==

**§4.2 Investment and Financing.** ==**Working capital policy is a function of two decisions.** **Investment** in working capital is concerned with the level of investment in current assets and answers **'How much'** fund is to be tied up to achieve the organisation's objectives — that is **effectiveness** of fund. **Financing** is concerned with the arrangement of funds and answers **'Where from'** funds are to be sourced at the lowest cost possible — that is **economy**.==
==**The five factors governing the level of investment** (SM §4.2) — a different list from §3's nine, and MTP September 2024 Series II asks for this one:==
==**(a) Nature of Industry** — construction companies, breweries and the like require large investment **due to a long gestation period**.==
==**(b) Types of products** — **consumer durables have large inventory as compared to perishable products.**==

==**(c) Manufacturing vs Trading vs Service** — a manufacturing entity maintains **three levels of inventory** (raw material, work-in-process, finished goods); a trading entity only **trading stock**; a service entity only **consumables**.==
==**(d) Volume of sales** — where sales are high there is a possibility of **high receivables** as well.==

==**(e) Credit policy** — a liberal policy means not only a high level of receivables but **may require more capital to fund raw material purchases**, depending on the credit period allowed by suppliers.==

**ICAI's own framing of 'there are no rules':** **'There are not set or fixed rules for deciding the level of investment in working capital.'** An infrastructure development company requires more because of huge work-in-process; a fast-food business requires less because inventory is perishable and most sales are cash.
concepts.example: MTP September 2025 Series I Q4(a) quotes a finance executive claiming that 'increasing the firm's current ratio by accumulating more inventory is a sound strategy for improving working capital efficiency' and asks whether you agree. The answer is this section: the current ratio rises, but the extra inventory is idle assets which reduce liquidity in substance while appearing to improve it, carry a capital cost, risk obsolescence, and reduce the opportunity to earn a better return from a productive asset. The ratio improves and the position worsens — which is exactly the liquidity-profitability trade-off stated backwards.

official_questions.question: DISCUSS the liquidity vs. profitability issue in management of working capital. (4 Marks)
answer_points: **The setting.** Working capital management means **maintaining the balance between a firm's short-term assets and short-term liabilities**, and involves the **3 Es — Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness.**

**Why liquidity is needed.** For **uninterrupted and smooth functioning of day-to-day business it is important to maintain liquidity of funds evenly.** A shortage interrupts the ordinary course of activities; working capital is to the business what **life blood is to a living body, or a lubricant to an engine.**
**Why liquidity has a cost.** **Each rupee of capital bears some cost**, so while maintaining liquidity the cost aspect must be borne in mind.

**The conflict in ICAI's own words.** A higher working capital may be intended to increase revenue and hence profitability, **'but at the same time unnecessary tying up of funds in idle assets not only reduces the liquidity but also reduces the opportunity to earn better return from a productive asset.'**

==**The resolution.** **'Hence, a trade-off is required between the liquidity and profitability which increases the profitability without disturbing the day-to-day functioning.'** This requires **economy in financing, efficiency in utilisation and effectiveness in achieving the intended objectives.**==

**Illustrate with two rows of the trade-off table** if marks allow: on **inventory**, fewer stock-outs raise profitability while a lower level needs less capital but risks stock-outs and loss of goodwill, with EOQ and JIT as the balancing tools; on **receivables**, a longer credit period attracts customers and raises revenue but brings more bad debts, against cash sales which give liquidity but fail to boost sales.

**Close on the policy consequence.** **A conservative policy implies greater liquidity and lower risk; an aggressive policy indicates higher risk and poor liquidity**, and most firms adopt a moderate policy in the middle.

answer_points: **The identical question to MTP March 2024 Series II Q4(b), reproduced unchanged** — which is itself the point worth noting: ICAI's mock papers recycle this four-marker, so it should be written out once and learnt.
**Liquidity must be maintained evenly** for uninterrupted day-to-day functioning, but **each rupee of capital bears a cost**, so the cost aspect cannot be ignored.

**Higher working capital may raise revenue and profitability**, but **unnecessary tying up of funds in idle assets reduces liquidity and reduces the opportunity to earn a better return from a productive asset.**

**A trade-off is therefore required** which **increases profitability without disturbing day-to-day functioning**, achieved through **economy in financing, efficiency in utilisation and effectiveness in achieving the intended objectives.**

**Name the five components across which the trade-off runs** — inventory, receivables, pre-payment of expenses, cash and cash equivalents, and payables and expenses — and give the two sides for at least two of them.
**End with the policy label.** Conservative means greater liquidity and lower return; aggressive means higher return and poor liquidity; moderate strikes the balance that most firms adopt.

official_questions.question: A finance executive of XYZ company claims that "Increasing the firm's current ratio by accumulating more inventory is a sound strategy for improving working capital efficiency." As a financial analyst, do you agree with the statement? Justify your answer using relevant working capital concepts, and explain the potential risks associated with the strategy mentioned. (4 Marks)
answer_points: ==**The verdict first: no, the statement is not sound.** The **current ratio does rise** — inventory is a current asset and the denominator is untouched — **but the ratio improves while the underlying position worsens.** A ratio is a symptom, not the thing itself.==

**Reason 1 — the quick ratio does not move, and may be the more telling measure.** SM §2.2 defines quick assets as **current assets less inventory and prepaid expenses**. Building inventory therefore leaves the **acid test ratio unchanged** while flattering the current ratio, which is precisely why ICAI says the current ratio must be **'supplemented by'** the quick ratio.

**Reason 2 — the cost of the funds.** SM §4.1: **each rupee of capital bears some cost.** Inventory financed by borrowing carries interest; inventory financed internally carries an opportunity cost. **Unnecessary tying up of funds in idle assets not only reduces the liquidity but also reduces the opportunity to earn better return from a productive asset.**

**Reason 3 — this is a move along the wrong axis.** On ICAI's trade-off table the advantage of a **higher** inventory level is **fewer stock-outs**, and the tool for getting there is **EOQ or JIT**, not accumulation for its own sake. Holding stock the business does not need buys none of the profitability benefit and all of the liquidity cost.

**Reason 4 — over capitalisation.** SM §2.1: large idle funds locked in working capital **'results in over capitalization … too large funds for its requirements, resulting in a low rate of return, a situation which implies a less than optimal use of resources.'** ICAI attributes the poor performance of several public sector undertakings to exactly this.

==**The risks to name explicitly:** **inventory obsolescence** (ICAI lists it as a disadvantage of the conservative approach); **a longer operating cycle**, since R rises and so does the working capital requirement; **shortage of liquidity in the long run** despite the better-looking ratio; **carrying and storage costs**; and **price risk** if the stock has to be marked down.==

**What a sound strategy would look like instead.** Shorten the cycle rather than lengthen it: **collect receivables faster, shift inventory faster, negotiate better credit from suppliers** — ICAI's own 'If you … Then …' table in §6. **'If you can get money to move faster around the cycle … the business will generate more cash or it will need to borrow less money to fund working capital.'**

**Close on the principle.** The objective is to **minimise total costs — the cost of liquidity and the cost of illiquidity** (SM §4.4); accumulating inventory raises the first without reducing the second.
keywords: current ratio rises but position worsens
each rupee of capital bears a cost

official_questions.question: Determining the amount to be invested in current assets as working capital is a crucial policy decision for any entity. What FACTORS should a company consider when deciding the level of investment in working capital? (3 Marks)
answer_points: **Open with ICAI's caveat, because it is the framing mark.** **'How much to be invested in current assets as working capital is a matter of policy decision by an entity. It has to be decided in the light of organisational objectives, trade policies and financial (cost-benefit) considerations.'** And bluntly: **'There are not set or fixed rules for deciding the level of investment in working capital.'**
==**(a) Nature of Industry.** **Construction companies, breweries etc. require large investment in working capital due to a long gestation period.**==
==**(b) Types of products.** **Consumer durables carry large inventory as compared to perishable products.**==

==**(c) Manufacturing versus Trading versus Service.** A manufacturing entity has to maintain **three levels of inventory — raw material, work-in-process and finished goods**; a trading entity only **trading stock**; a service entity only **consumables.**==
==**(d) Volume of sales.** **Where the sales are high, there is a possibility of high receivables as well.**==

==**(e) Credit policy.** An entity whose credit policy is liberal **has not only a high level of receivables but may require more capital to fund raw material purchases**, since that depends on the credit period allowed by suppliers.==

**Illustrate with ICAI's own pair.** An **infrastructure development company** requires more investment because of huge work-in-process; a **fast food business** requires comparatively less because inventory is perishable and most sales are cash sales.

**One caution for three marks.** This is the §4.2 list, not the §3 list of nine planning factors. If a question asks about **planning the requirement**, the nine apply; if it asks about the **level of investment**, these five do.
keywords: liberal credit policy funds raw material too

official_questions.question: ABC Ltd. is a manufacturing company experiencing rapid sales growth. To meet the increased demand, the company has started maintaining higher inventory levels and offering more generous credit terms to customers. However, its cash reserves are depleting, and it is facing difficulties in paying suppliers on time. As a financial analyst, apply your understanding of the scope of working capital management to ANALYZE the trade-offs the company is making between different components of working capital (inventory, receivables, advances, payables, and cash).
answer_points: **Name the scope first, since the question asks you to apply it.** The scope of working capital management is grouped into two broad areas: **(i) liquidity and profitability** and **(ii) investment and financing decision.** ABC Ltd has moved decisively towards profitability on three components and is now paying for it in liquidity on the other two.

==**Inventory.** The **higher side** gives **fewer stock-outs and so higher profitability** — which is the benefit ABC is buying as sales grow. The **lower side** needs **less capital but endangers stock-out and loss of goodwill.** The **trade-off tool is EOQ or JIT, to carry the optimum level** rather than simply more. ABC has taken the profitability side without applying the tool.==

==**Receivables.** The **higher side** — **a higher credit period attracts customers and increases revenue, but can result in more bad debts.** The **lower side** — **cash sales provide liquidity but fail to boost sales and revenue.** The **tool is to evaluate the credit policy and to use the services of debt management (factoring) agencies.** More generous terms are exactly the higher side; the missing step is the evaluation.==

==**Advances (pre-payment of expenses).** The **higher side** **reduces uncertainty and is profitable in an inflationary environment**; the **lower side improves or maintains liquidity**; the tool is a **cost-benefit analysis.** With cash short, ABC should be moving to the lower side here.==

==**Payables and expenses.** The **higher side** means **capital can be used in some other investment avenues**; the **lower side** means **payables are honoured in time, which improves goodwill and helps in getting future discounts.** The tool is to **evaluate the credit policy and related cost.** ABC's inability to pay suppliers on time is the higher side imposed by circumstance rather than chosen — and the cost is precisely the goodwill and the future discounts.==

==**Cash and cash equivalents.** The **higher side** lets **payables be honoured in time, improving goodwill and helping to get future discounts**; the **lower side** lets **cash be invested in other avenues**; the tool is **cash budgets and other cash management techniques.** Depleting reserves is the binding constraint, and the cash budget is the instrument ABC has not used.==

==**The diagnosis in one sentence.** ABC has pushed **inventory, receivables and (in effect) payables all to their profitability extremes at the same time**, which has **lengthened the operating cycle at both ends while shortening the credit it can rely on** — so the extra sales are being funded out of cash that was never budgeted for them. **'The faster a business expands the more cash it will need for working capital and investment'** (SM §6).==

**The remedy, in ICAI's own 'If you … Then …' terms** (SM §6): **collect receivables faster and you release cash from the cycle; shift inventory faster and you free up cash; get better credit from suppliers, in duration or amount, and you increase your cash resources.** And the structural point: **a trade-off is required between liquidity and profitability which increases profitability without disturbing day-to-day functioning** — ABC's growth has disturbed exactly that.

concepts.title: 4.3–4.4 Approaches of Working Capital Investment, and the Current Assets to Fixed Assets Ratio
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 2 (Jan 2025 Series I Q4(a); the ratio appears in SM Illustration 1)
understand: ==**Three approaches, decided by organisational policy and the risk-return trade off** (SM §4.3): **aggressive, conservative and moderate.**==

==**(a) Aggressive.** Investment in working capital is kept at **minimal investment in current assets** — the entity **holds a lower level of inventory, follows a strict credit policy and keeps less cash balance.** **Advantage:** a **lower level of funds is tied up, which results in lower financial costs.** **Flip side:** **risk of stock-outs**, and that the organisation **could not grow, which leads to lower utilisation of fixed assets and long-term debts**; in the long run the firm **may stay behind the competitors.** ==**This approach would better suit a highly integrated organisation with efficient processes.**==

==**(b) Conservative.** The organisation **invests high capital in current assets** — **inventory level higher, liberal credit policies, and cash balance as high as to meet any current liabilities immediately.** **Advantages:** **higher sales volume, increased demand due to liberal credit policy, and increased goodwill among suppliers due to payment in short time.** **Disadvantages:** **increased cost of capital, inventory obsolescence, higher risk of bad debts, and shortage of liquidity in the long run due to longer operating cycles.**==
==**(c) Moderate.** In between the other two: **a balance between risk and return is maintained to gain more by using the funds in a very efficient manner.**==

==**The summary sentence ICAI gives, which is the answer to any 'compare the approaches' question:** **'A conservative policy implies greater liquidity and lower risk whereas an aggressive policy indicates higher risk and poor liquidity. Moderate current assets policy will fall in the middle of conservative and aggressive policies which most of the firms follow to strike an appropriate balance as per the requirements of their trade or industry.'** And a firm **may follow a different policy at different times** depending on the determinants discussed earlier.==

**§4.4 The measuring stick.** The finance manager must determine the **optimum level of current assets so that the shareholders' value is maximized.** A firm needs **both fixed and current assets to support a particular level of output**, and as output and sales increase the need for current assets also increases — ==**but 'generally, current assets do not increase in direct proportion to output; current assets may increase at a decreasing rate with output. As the output increases, the firm starts using its current asset more efficiently.'**==

==**The ratio.** **Dividing current assets by fixed assets gives the current assets / fixed assets ratio.** **Assuming a constant level of fixed assets, a higher CA/FA ratio indicates a conservative current assets policy and a lower CA/FA ratio an aggressive current assets policy**, all other factors constant.==

==**SM Illustration 1, the arithmetic of the whole section.** Sales ₹20,00,000 (1,00,000 units at ₹20), EBIT ₹2,00,000, fixed assets ₹5,00,000, and three possible current asset holdings of ₹5,00,000, ₹4,00,000 and ₹3,00,000:==

==**Conservative:** total assets ₹10,00,000 → **Return on Total Assets 20%**, CA/FA **1.00**.
**Moderate:** total assets ₹9,00,000 → **22.22%**, CA/FA **0.80**.
**Aggressive:** total assets ₹8,00,000 → **25%**, CA/FA **0.60**.==

**ICAI's reading of its own table:** the conservative policy **provides greater liquidity (solvency) but a lower return on total assets**; the aggressive policy **gives a higher return but low liquidity and thus is very risky**; the moderate policy generates a return **higher than conservative but lower than aggressive**, and is **less risky than aggressive but riskier than conservative.** ==**'It also reflects inverse relationship between Current Assets / Fixed Assets ratio and Return on Total Assets.'**==

==**The closing principle, which is the single most quotable line in Unit I:** **'In determining the optimum level of current assets, the firm should balance the profitability – solvency tangle by minimizing total costs – Cost of liquidity and cost of illiquidity.'**==

**The financing side of the same choice, which MTP January 2025 Series I asks about.** Financing current assets with **short-term** loans is cheaper — short rates are normally below long rates — but carries **refinancing risk and interest-rate risk**, since the loan must be renewed repeatedly and may not be renewed when it is most needed. Financing them with **long-term** loans is dearer but secure. ==**The reconciling principle is the hedging or matching approach named in SM §26: 'Financing of assets with the same maturity as of assets' — permanent working capital from long-term sources, temporary working capital from short-term sources.**==

The answer is this section plus §26: price the two sources, then split the requirement into permanent and temporary and match each to a source of the same maturity, with the approach — aggressive, moderate or conservative — deciding how much of the temporary layer is pushed onto short-term funds.

official_questions.question: A company is evaluating two options for financing its current assets: using short-term loans or long-term loans. HOW should the company balance risk and return in making this decision, and WHAT factors should it consider to ensure optimal financing? (4 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Start with the split, because it decides everything else.** SM §26: **'it is advisable that the finance manager bifurcate the working capital requirements between the permanent working capital and temporary working capital.'** **Permanent working capital is always needed irrespective of sales fluctuation; hence it should be financed by long-term sources such as debt and equity. Temporary working capital may be financed by short-term sources of finance.**==

**The return side of the trade-off.** Short-term funds are normally **cheaper** — trade credit and accruals cost nothing explicitly, and bank short-term rates sit below long-term rates — so financing more of the requirement short term **raises the return on total assets**, exactly as the aggressive policy does in SM Illustration 1 (25% against 20%).

**The risk side.** Short-term funds must be **renewed repeatedly**, which exposes the company to **refinancing risk** (the facility may not be renewed, and least of all when the company most needs it) and to **interest-rate risk** (the rate resets on every renewal). Long-term funds are dearer but **secure for the term**, which is why the permanent layer belongs to them.

==**The reconciling principle to name.** SM §26 lists **'Hedging approach or matching approach i.e., Financing of assets with the same maturity as of assets'** among the parameters guiding the choice. Match the maturity of the source to the maturity of the asset and the refinancing risk is contained without paying long-term rates on a seasonal peak.==

**Then the policy choice on top of it.** SM §4.3: an **aggressive** stance pushes more of the requirement onto short-term funds — **lower financial costs** but **higher risk and poor liquidity**; a **conservative** stance funds even part of the temporary layer long term — **greater liquidity and lower risk** but **increased cost of capital**; a **moderate** stance, which **most firms follow**, strikes the balance appropriate to the trade or industry.

==**The six factors SM §26 lists as guiding the selection of a source:** **(i) Cost factor, (ii) Impact on credit rating, (iii) Feasibility, (iv) Reliability, (v) Restrictions, and (vi) the hedging or matching approach.** These are the 'factors to consider' the question asks for.==

**Two more that the figures will usually decide.** The **nature of the business and the seasonality of its sales** — the sharper the seasonal peak, the larger the temporary layer and so the larger the legitimate role for short-term funds; and the **existing capital structure and interest coverage**, since long-term debt raised for working capital carries a fixed charge that raises financial leverage.

**Close on the objective.** SM §4.4: the firm should **'balance the profitability – solvency tangle by minimizing total costs – Cost of liquidity and cost of illiquidity.'** Cheap short-term money reduces the cost of liquidity and raises the cost of illiquidity; the optimum is where the sum of the two is least, not where either alone is.

refinancing risk and interest rate risk

concepts.title: 5–6 Estimating Working Capital Needs, and the Operating or Working Capital Cycle
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (Jan 2025 MCQ 8, May 2026 Q3(b)) · RTP 0 direct · MTP 0 direct
understand: ==**Three methods of estimating the requirement** (SM §5), of which ICAI says the first **'is one of the most reliable methods of Computation of Working Capital'**:==

==**(i) Current Assets Holding Period** — estimate the need **based on the average holding period of current assets, relating them to costs based on the company's experience in the previous year.** **'This method is essentially based on the Operating Cycle Concept.'**==
==**(ii) Ratio of Sales** — estimate the need **as a ratio of sales, on the assumption that current assets change with changes in sales.**==
==**(iii) Ratio of Fixed Investments** — estimate the requirement **as a percentage of fixed investments.**==

**What drives the choice of method:** **seasonal fluctuations, accurate sales forecast, investment cost and variability in sales price.** And ICAI's reminder that **the production cycle and the credit and collection policies of the firm will have an impact on working capital requirements, so they should be given due weightage in projecting them.**

==**§6 What the operating cycle is.** **'Working Capital cycle indicates the length of time between a company's paying for materials, entering into stock and receiving the cash from sales of finished goods.'** It is found by **adding the number of days required for each stage in the cycle.**==

==**ICAI's own worked sentence, which is the quickest way to fix the formula:** a company holds raw materials on average for **60 days**, gets **15 days'** credit from the supplier, the production process needs **15 days**, finished goods are held **30 days** and **30 days'** credit is extended to debtors. **The total, 120 days, is 60 − 15 + 15 + 30 + 30.**==

==**The equation** (SM §6): **Operating Cycle = R + W + F + D − C**, where **R** = raw material storage period, **W** = work-in-progress inventory holding period (ICAI notes this **'may also be termed as works cost'**), **F** = finished goods storage period, **D** = receivables (debtors) collection period and **C** = credit period allowed by suppliers (creditors).==

==**Number of Operating Cycles in a Year = 360 or 365 ÷ Operating Cycle.** And ICAI's gloss: **'more the number of operating cycles better it is for the organization as it indicates shorter operating cycle.'**==
==**The five component formulae, each a fraction with a per-day denominator** (SM §6):==
==**R = Average stock of raw material ÷ Average cost of raw material consumption per day**==
==**W = Average work-in-progress inventory ÷ Average cost of production per day**==
==**F = Average stock of finished goods ÷ Average cost of goods sold per day**==
==**D = Average receivables ÷ Average credit sales per day**==
==**C = Average payables ÷ Average credit purchases per day**==

==**The denominators are the examinable part.** Each stage is divided by the cost that *passes through* that stage: raw material by **consumption**, WIP by **cost of production**, finished goods by **cost of goods sold**, debtors by **credit sales**, creditors by **credit purchases**. ==**Getting W and F the wrong way round — dividing WIP by cost of goods sold — is the single commonest error in the chapter.**==

**Why the cycle matters, in ICAI's words:** its determination **helps in the forecasting, controlling and management of working capital**; **the length of the operating cycle is the indicator of performance of management**; and **the net operating cycle represents the time interval for which the firm has to negotiate for working capital from its lenders.**

==**The 'time is money' table, which is pure marks in a theory question** (SM §6). **Collect receivables faster → you release cash from the cycle. Collect receivables slower → your receivables soak up cash. Get better credit from suppliers (in duration or amount) → you increase your cash resources. Shift inventory faster → you free up cash. Move inventory slower → you consume more cash.**==

**And the warning about growth:** **'The faster a business expands the more cash it will need for working capital and investment. The cheapest and best sources of cash exist as working capital right within the business.'** Also: **'the cost of providing credit to customers and holding stocks can represent a substantial proportion of a firm's total profits.'**

==**The cash cycle, which is the operating cycle under another name** (SM Illustration 11). **Cash cycle = debtors days + inventory days − creditors days. Cash turnover = 360 ÷ cash cycle (in days), or 12 ÷ cash cycle in months. Minimum operating cash = Total operating annual outlay ÷ cash turnover.** ICAI's Sai Trading figures: 45 + 75 − 30 = **90 days**, turnover **4**, and on a ₹120 lakh annual spend a minimum balance of **₹30 lakhs**; cut the inventory period by 30 days and the cycle falls to **60 days**, turnover rises to **6**, the balance falls to **₹20 lakhs**, and at 10% the saving is **₹1 lakh**.==

==**The contingency or safety provision, which is where MCQ marks are lost.** 'A provision for contingencies at 20% **of working capital**' means **working capital × 1.20** — SA January 2025's JKL Company: ₹50 lakh of working capital becomes **₹60 lakh**. But 'a margin of 10% **of the working capital inclusive of the provision**' means the computed figure is only 90% of the answer, so the provision is **computed figure × 10/90** — RTP September 2024 applies exactly that as **₹4,49,792 × 1/9 = ₹49,977**. ==**Read the preposition: 'of working capital' is a mark-up; 'inclusive of the margin' is a gross-up.**==
concepts.example: May 2026's AR Ltd gives collection 60 days, inventory 90 days and payables 30 days on sales of ₹200 lakhs with a 10% net margin. Cash cycle = 60 + 90 − 30 = 120 days; cash turnover = 360 ÷ 120 = 3; total cash outlay = sales less net profit = ₹200 − ₹20 = ₹180 lakhs; minimum operating cash = ₹180 ÷ 3 = ₹60 lakhs. It is SM Illustration 11 with different numbers, and the second half of the question then prices a 2% discount against the ₹15 lakh release it would buy.

official_questions.question: JKL Company Ltd. has current assets of ₹1,00,00,000 and current liabilities of ₹50,00,000. The Financial manager of the company desires to make a provision for contingencies @20% of working capital. Accordingly, what would be the amount of working capital requirement for the company? (A) ₹55 Lakh (B) ₹60 Lakh (C) ₹65 Lakh (D) ₹70 Lakh
answer_points: **Step 1 — the working capital itself.** ₹1,00,00,000 − ₹50,00,000 = **₹50,00,000**, that is ₹50 lakh.
**Step 2 — read the preposition.** The provision is **'@20% of working capital'**, a **mark-up on the ₹50 lakh**, not a gross-up to be contained within the answer.
**Step 3.** ₹50 lakh × 1.20 = ==**₹60 lakh — option (B)**==, which is ICAI's published key.

==**Why the other options are there, and they are instructive.** **₹55 lakh** is 20% of the ₹25 lakh *difference* some candidates compute by halving, or a 10% mark-up misread. **₹65 lakh** is ₹50 lakh plus 20% of ₹75 lakh. **₹70 lakh** is the gross-up answer ₹50 lakh ÷ 0.8 rounded up from ₹62.5 lakh, or ₹50 lakh plus 40%.==

==**The transferable rule, and it is worth more than this one mark.** **'A provision at x% of working capital' multiplies by (1 + x).** **'A margin of x% of the working capital inclusive of the margin' divides by (1 − x)**, which ICAI applies in RTP September 2024 as **₹4,49,792 × 1/9 = ₹49,977** for a 10% provision inclusive of itself, and in MTP January 2025 Series II as **excess × 15/85** for a 15% safety margin inclusive of the margin amount. ==Three official questions turn on the preposition alone.==

official_questions.question: AR Ltd. has given following data for the year ended 31st March, 2026: Receivables are collected on an average after 60 days; Inventories are held for average period of 90 days before being sold; The company usually settles its payables with suppliers after 30 days; The total sales of the company amounts to ₹200 lakhs, which is earned evenly throughout the year. All sales are credit sales. Net profit margin is 10%. The company has not incurred any non-operating expenses during the year. Tax rate is 30%. Assume 360 days in a year. Opportunity cost of investment is 12%. (i) Calculate the cash cycle and the minimum cash balance to be maintained to meet its obligations. (ii) The company is planning to propose a scheme, whereby it will offer a cash discount of 2% to debtors to reduce the debtors' collection period by 30 days. It is expected that 60% of the debtors will avail the scheme. (A) What will be reduction in the minimum cash to be maintained to meet obligation after the proposed scheme is adopted? (B) What will be net saving due to such scheme? (C) Should the company adopt the scheme? (2 + 4 = 6 Marks)
answer_points: **(i) The cash cycle.** **60 days (debtors) + 90 days (inventory) − 30 days (payables) = ==120 days==**, that is **4 months**.
**Cash turnover** = 360 days ÷ 120 days = ==**3 times**== (equivalently 12 months ÷ 4 months).

**Total cash outlay** = **Sales − Net profit** = ₹200 lakhs − ₹20 lakhs (10% of sales) = ==**₹180 lakhs**==. *The question's statement that there were no non-operating expenses is what lets the whole net margin be deducted.*
**Minimum operating cash** = Total operating annual outlay ÷ cash turnover = ₹180 lakhs ÷ 3 = ==**₹60 lakhs**==.

**(ii)(A) After the scheme.** ICAI's primary answer takes the **new average collection period as 30 days** flat: **new cash cycle = 30 + 90 − 30 = ==90 days==**, new cash turnover = 360 ÷ 90 = **4 times**, and new minimum cash = ₹180 lakhs ÷ 4 = ==**₹45 lakhs**==. **Reduction = ₹60 lakhs − ₹45 lakhs = ==₹15 lakhs==.**

**(ii)(B) The net saving.** **Opportunity cost saving** = 12% of the ₹15 lakh release, post tax = ₹15 lakhs × 0.12 × (1 − 0.30) = ==**₹1.26 lakhs**==.
**Cost of the cash discount** = 2% × 60% of total sales, post tax = 0.02 × 0.60 × ₹200 lakhs × (1 − 0.30) = ₹2.40 lakhs × 0.70 = ==**₹1.68 lakhs**==.
**Net saving = ₹1.26 lakhs − ₹1.68 lakhs = ==₹(0.42) lakhs==.**
**(ii)(C) The advice.** ==**No — the company should not adopt the scheme.** The discount costs ₹1.68 lakhs to buy an opportunity saving of only ₹1.26 lakhs, a net loss of ₹42,000.==

==**ICAI also prints an alternative reading, and it is the more defensible one.** If **60% of debtors pay 30 days early (30 days) and 40% do not avail the scheme and continue at 60 days**, the new average collection period is **(0.60 × 30) + (0.40 × 60) = 18 + 24 = 42 days**, the cash cycle **90 + 42 − 30 = 102 days**, and the cash turnover **360 ÷ 102 = 3.529 times**. The release and the saving are then both smaller, so **the conclusion to reject is unchanged and in fact stronger.**==

==**Which to write.** Give the **30-day version as the main answer** because it is ICAI's own primary solution and matches the question's words 'reduce the debtors' collection period by 30 days'; then **add the 42-day working as a note**, saying the recommendation does not change. Stating that the decision is robust to the assumption is worth more than picking one and hoping.==

**One point of technique.** The discount is costed on **total sales** here, not on the 60% of *receivables*, because all sales are credit sales and the 60% take-up is applied to the sales figure. And both the saving and the cost are taken **post tax at 30%**, which is what makes them comparable.

mcqs.question: A firm has an inventory holding period of 60 days, a debtors collection period of 50 days and a creditors payment period of 20 days. Its annual cash outlay is ₹270 lakhs and it earns 9% on investments. Its minimum operating cash balance is:

options.A: ₹97.50 lakhs
options.B: ₹67.50 lakhs
options.C: ₹22.50 lakhs
options.D: ₹90.00 lakhs

mcqs.explanation: Cash cycle = 50 + 60 − 20 = 90 days. Cash turnover = 360 ÷ 90 = 4. Minimum operating cash = ₹270 lakhs ÷ 4 = ₹67.50 lakhs (SM Illustration 11). Option A adds the creditors period instead of subtracting it, giving 130 days and a turnover of 2.77. Option D divides by a cycle of 108 days. The 9% return is not needed for this part — it prices a saving, not the balance.

recap: Three methods: current assets holding period (the operating cycle, and the most reliable), ratio of sales, ratio of fixed investments.
Operating Cycle = R + W + F + D − C, and C is the only subtraction.
Each period is divided by what flows through it: consumption, cost of production, cost of goods sold, credit sales, credit purchases.
Cycles in a year = 360 or 365 ÷ cycle; working capital = annual operating cost ÷ cycles; more cycles is better.
Cash cycle = debtors + inventory − creditors; minimum cash = annual outlay ÷ cash turnover, and the outlay is sales less net profit.
'20% of working capital' multiplies by 1.20; 'inclusive of the margin' divides by (1 − x).

concepts.title: 6.1 Working Capital Based on Operating Cycle
concepts.evidence: PYQ 3 (Sep 2024 Q1(b), Jan 2025 Q2(b), Sep 2025 Part I case) · RTP 1 (May 2026 Q9) · MTP 1 (Sep 2025 Series I Q1(c))
understand: ==**The method in three steps** (SM §6.1): **(1) compute each of the five periods; (2) add them as R + W + F + D − C to get the cycle; (3) divide the year by the cycle to get the number of cycles, and divide the annual operating cost by that number to get the working capital.**==

==**SM Illustration 2 is the template, and ICAI reuses it in five official questions.** XYZ Ltd: raw material consumed ₹6,00,000 with average stock ₹50,000 → **R = 50,000 ÷ (6,00,000 ÷ 360) = 50,000 ÷ 1,667 = 30 days**. Cost of production ₹5,00,000 with average WIP ₹30,000 → **W = 30,000 ÷ 1,389 = 22 days**. Cost of goods sold ₹8,00,000 with average finished goods ₹40,000 → **F = 40,000 ÷ 2,222 = 18 days**. Collection **45 days**, credit availed **30 days**. **Net operating cycle = 30 + 22 + 18 + 45 − 30 = 85 days**, and **number of cycles = 360 ÷ 85 = 4.23 times.**==
==**Then the third step, which Illustration 2 does not show but every exam question needs:** **Amount of Working Capital Required = Annual Operating Cost ÷ Number of Operating Cycles.**==

==**Which 'annual operating cost'?** ICAI uses **cost of goods sold plus administration and selling expenses** — September 2024's SK Limited takes ₹14,61,000 + ₹4,14,000 = ₹18,75,000. Where the question simply gives an 'annual operating cost', use it as given.==

==**And whether to strip out depreciation.** January 2025's MSD Limited gives an annual operating cost of ₹60,00,000 **'including depreciation of ₹4,80,000'**, and ICAI prints **both** answers: **₹16,00,000** on the gross cost and **₹14,72,000** on the cash cost of ₹55,20,000. ==**Give the gross figure as the main answer and the cash-cost figure as a note, saying which basis each uses.** The fact that ICAI prints both means a candidate who gives one with the basis stated cannot be marked wrong.==

**Deriving periods that are not given — the skill September 2024 actually tested.** SK Limited gives cost of production ₹15,48,000, cost of goods sold ₹14,61,000, average WIP ₹94,600 and average finished goods ₹2,43,500, with R, D and C given as 65, 36 and 63 days. So **W = ₹94,600 ÷ (₹15,48,000 ÷ 360) = 22 days** and **F = ₹2,43,500 ÷ (₹14,61,000 ÷ 360) = 60 days**, giving **65 + 22 + 60 + 36 − 63 = 120 days**, **3 cycles**, and **₹18,75,000 ÷ 3 = ₹6,25,000.**

==**Running the cycle backwards — September 2025's RG Limited, the hardest question in the chapter.** The question gives the **answer** (working capital ₹1,01,850 after a 5% contingency) and **3 cycles a year**, and asks for the five periods. The chain is: **working capital before contingency = ₹1,01,850 ÷ 1.05 = ₹97,000**; **total operating cost = ₹97,000 × 3 = ₹2,91,000**; then every component unwinds from the cost sheet. ==**Learn the chain, not the numbers: contingency out → multiply by cycles → operating cost → COGS → cost of production → raw material consumed → purchases.**==

==**The cost-sheet identities that chain needs, and they are the real content of this section:**
**Cost of Goods Sold = Total operating cost − Selling and distribution expenses**
**Cost of Production = COGS + Closing finished goods − Opening finished goods**
**Raw Material Consumed = Cost of production − Wages and manufacturing expenses + Closing WIP − Opening WIP**
**Credit Purchases = Raw material consumed + Closing raw material − Opening raw material**==

**The day-count convention matters more here than anywhere else.** ICAI uses **360 days** in September 2024, January 2025 and September 2025, and **365 days** in May 2026's Puja Limited and MTP September 2025 Series I's Wint Limited. ==**The question always says which. Write it in the first line and use it in all five denominators.**==

**Average or closing?** Where opening and closing figures are both given, ICAI uses the **simple average**. Where only one is given, it uses that one. September 2025's RG Limited gives both for all three inventories and ICAI averages each.

==**The contingency sits at the end, never in the middle.** Compute the working capital from the cycle first, then add the provision. Wint Limited: ₹1,703.63 lakh from the cycle, **plus a 10% contingency reserve of ₹170.363 lakh = ₹1,874 lakh.**==
concepts.example: September 2025's RG Limited is worth working twice. From ₹1,01,850 and 3 cycles: ₹97,000 of working capital, ₹2,91,000 of operating expenses, ₹2,61,000 of COGS after taking out ₹30,000 of selling and distribution, ₹2,56,800 of cost of production after the finished-goods movement, ₹1,45,800 of raw material consumed after wages and the WIP movement, and ₹1,49,550 of credit purchases. The five periods then fall out: 65, 30, 40, 48 and 63 days — and the 48-day debtors period is itself recovered from the cycle total of 120 days, since every other figure is known. The whole case is one long substitution.

provisions.requirement: Compute the five periods; add as R + W + F + D − C; divide the annual operating cost by the number of cycles.
provisions.exam_angle: Step 3 is the one Illustration 2 omits and every exam question requires.
The template; five official questions are this illustration with different data.

provisions.requirement: Cost of goods sold plus administration and selling expenses, or the figure the question gives.
provisions.exam_angle: September 2024 adds ₹4,14,000 of administration and selling to ₹14,61,000 of COGS.

provisions.requirement: ICAI prints both the gross and the cash-cost answers where depreciation is disclosed (MSD Limited: ₹16,00,000 and ₹14,72,000).
provisions.exam_angle: Give both with the basis named; neither can then be marked wrong.

keywords: annual operating cost ÷ number of cycles
derive W and F from the cost sheet

memory.trick: **Periods, cycle, cycles, cost.** Four words in order: find the **periods**, add them into the **cycle**, divide the year to get the number of **cycles**, divide the annual **cost** by that number. ==And when the question gives you the cost and asks for the periods, run the same four words backwards.==
key: Five periods, each a labelled fraction
Cycle = R + W + F + D − C
Working capital = annual operating cost ÷ cycles
Add the contingency or safety margin last
147 days · 2.48 cycles · ₹1,874 lakh with contingency (365 days)

mistakes: Dividing the annual operating cost by the cycle in days instead of by the number of cycles. The two differ by a factor of 360.
Adding the contingency before computing the cycle. It goes on at the very end.
Using the closing inventory where opening and closing are both given. ICAI averages them.
Mixing 360 and 365 between denominators. Puja Limited and Wint Limited both use 365 throughout.
Forgetting that the number of cycles can be fractional. 3.75, 4.23, 4.244 and 2.48 all appear in official answers; do not round to a whole number.
In a reverse question, dividing by 1.05 and then forgetting to multiply by the number of cycles. Both steps are needed to reach the operating cost.
