concepts.title: 9.3–10.2 The Cash Budget, the Methods of Cash Flow Budgeting, and Cash Budgets for Short and Long Periods
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (Jan 2025 Q1(a)) · RTP 1 (Sep 2026 Q9) · MTP 0
understand: ==**What a cash budget is** (SM §9.3): **'Cash Budget is the most significant device to plan for and control cash receipts and payments. This represents cash requirements of business during the budget period.'**==

==**The four purposes, each of which is a mark:**
**1. Coordinate the timings of cash needs** — **'It identifies the period(s) when there might either be a shortage of cash or an abnormally large cash requirement';**
**2. **'It also helps to pinpoint period(s) when there is likely to be excess cash';**
**3. **'It enables firm which has sufficient cash to take advantage like cash discounts on its accounts payable';** and
**4. **'Lastly it helps to plan/arrange adequately needed funds (avoiding excess/shortage of cash) on favorable terms.'**==

**And what the firm does with the answer:** **'On the basis of cash budget, the firm can decide to invest surplus cash in marketable securities and earn profits. On the contrary, any shortages can also be managed by making overdraft or credit arrangements with banks.'**

==**The two steps in preparing it** (SM §9.3): **(a) selection of the period of time to be covered by the budget — it also defines the planning horizon; (b) selection of factors that have a bearing on cash flows**, which are divided into **operating (cash flows generated by operations of the firm)** and **financial (cash flows generated by financial activities of the firm).**==
==**§10 Three methods of cash flow budgeting, and ICAI says which one business actually uses:**==

==**1. Receipts and Payments Method.** **'In this method all the expected receipts and payments for budget period are considered. All the cash inflow and outflow of all functional budgets including capital expenditure budgets are considered. Accruals and adjustments in accounts will not affect the cash flow budget. Anticipated cash inflow is added to the opening balance of cash and all cash payments are deducted from this to arrive at the closing balance of cash.'** ==**'This method is commonly used in business organizations.'**==

==**2. Adjusted Income Method.** **'In this method the annual cash flows are calculated by adjusting the sales revenue and cost figures for delays in receipts and payments (change in debtors and creditors) and eliminating non-cash items such as depreciation.'**==

==**3. Adjusted Balance Sheet Method.** **'In this method, the budgeted balance sheet is predicted by expressing each type of asset (except cash & bank) and short-term liabilities as percentage of the expected sales. The profit is also calculated as a percentage of sales, so that the increase in owner's equity can be forecasted. Known adjustments may be made to long-term liabilities and the balance sheet will then show if additional finance is needed (if budgeted assets exceed budgeted liabilities) or if there will be a positive cash balance (if budgeted liabilities exceed budgeted assets).'**==

**One point ICAI makes twice:** **'the capital budget will also be considered in the preparation of cash flow budget because the annual budget may disclose a need for new capital investments and also, the costs and revenues of any new projects coming on stream will need to be incorporated in the short-term budgets.'**

==**§10.1 The short-period cash budget — what has to be estimated.**
**Receipts:** **(1) receipts from debtors; (2) cash sales; (3) any other source of receipt of cash** (ICAI's example is a dividend from a subsidiary company).
**Payments:** **(1) payments for purchases; (2) payments for expenses; (3) payments made periodically but not every month** — **debenture interest, income tax paid in advance, sales tax or GST**; **(4) special payments in a particular month**, for example **dividends to shareholders, redemption of debentures, repayments of loans.**==

==**§10.2 The long-period cash budget**, which **'often resembles the projected sources and application of funds statement.'** The procedure: **take the cash at bank and in hand at the beginning of the year; ADD trading profit (before tax) expected to be earned, depreciation and other development expenses to be written off, sale proceeds of assets, proceeds of fresh issue of shares or debentures, and any reduction in working capital (current assets except cash, less current liabilities); DEDUCT dividends to be paid, cost of assets to be purchased, taxes to be paid, debentures or preference shares to be redeemed, and any increase in working capital.**==

==**The layout to use for the short-period budget — the one both official questions are marked against:**
**Opening balance · Add: Receipts · = Total cash available (A) · Less: Payments (itemised) · = Total payments (B) · Closing balance before adjustment · Minimum cash balance desired · Less: Temporary investment · Add: Temporary borrowing · = Cash closing balance.**
January 2025's KP Ltd answer uses exactly those rows. ==**Keep the 'closing balance before adjustment' line visible: it is where the surplus or deficit is read off, and it is a mark.**==

==**Two ways ICAI expresses the same answer, and both appear in official papers.** KP Ltd is asked to **prepare the budget and close at the minimum balance**, borrowing or investing as needed. September 2026's Jahanara Fashions is asked for the **'surplus/deficit of cash in relation to their target cash balance'**, and ICAI's answer uses a **cumulative** layout: opening balance, inflows, outflows, net cash flow, **cumulative net cash flow**, opening plus cumulative, minimum balance required, and then **surplus or (deficit)**. ==**Read the requirement: 'prepare a cash budget' wants the first layout; 'what will be the surplus or deficit against the target' wants the second.**==
concepts.example: September 2026's Jahanara Fashions runs three months with all sales in cash, purchases paid a month in arrear (so January pays December's ₹3,50,000), rent ₹10,000, partners' drawings ₹25,000, salaries varying, and ₹40,000 of furniture bought for cash in January. Against an opening balance of ₹6,000 and a target of ₹15,000 the answer is a deficit of ₹(59,000) in January, ₹(94,000) in February and a surplus of ₹81,000 in March. The cumulative column is what makes February's figure worse than January's even though February's own net outflow is smaller.

official_questions.question: KP Ltd. has provided the following information: (i) Estimated monthly sales (₹ in lakh): April-2024 10, May-2024 12, June-2024 15, July-2024 10, August-2024 13, September-2024 14. (ii) Gross Profit Ratio is 20%. (iii) Cost of Goods sold is paid in the next month. (iv) Sales are on credit and a credit period of 2 months is allowed. (v) Indirect Expenses are paid in the same month; monthly indirect expenses (₹ in lakh): June-2024 1.0, July-2024 1.2, August-2024 1.0, September-2024 1.3. (vi) Dividend amounting ₹3 Lakh will be paid in the month of September 2024. (vii) Cash Balance on 01/07/2024 was ₹1.5 Lakh. (viii) The company has to maintain a minimum cash balance of ₹1 Lakh. If there is a cash balance deficit in any month, the company would take a temporary short term loan and if the cash balance exceeds ₹2 Lakh, then the company would invest the short term excess amount of ₹2 Lakh. (ix) Ignore the interest on short term loans and short term investments. You are required to prepare a Cash Budget for three months starting from July 2024. (5 Marks)
answer_points:
**Working Note first — the two lags, laid out as a small table.**
**Collections:** a two-month credit period means **July collects May's sales of ₹12 L, August collects June's ₹15 L, and September collects July's ₹10 L.**
**Cost of goods sold** is 80% of sales (gross profit 20%), paid the **next** month:
sales June ₹15 L → COGS ₹12 L, paid in **July**;
sales July ₹10 L → COGS ₹8 L, paid in **August**;
sales August ₹13 L → COGS ₹10.4 L, paid in **September**.
*(ICAI's own working note also computes September's COGS of ₹11.2 L, which falls due in October and so sits outside the budget.)*
==**The Cash Budget (₹ in lakh), in ICAI's rows:**==
**Opening Balance** — July **1.5**, August **1**, September **2**.
**Add: Receipts — Collection from debtors** — July **12**, August **15**, September **10**.
**Total cash available (A)** — July **13.5**, August **16**, September **12**.

**Less: Payments** — **Payment of COGS** July **12**, August **8**, September **10.4**; **Payment of indirect expenses** July **1.2**, August **1**, September **1.3**; **Payment of dividend** September **3**.
**Total payments (B)** — July **13.2**, August **9**, September **14.7**.
**Closing Balance before adjustment** — July **0.3**, August **7**, September **(2.7)**.
**Minimum cash balance desired** — **1** in each month.

**Less: Temporary Investment** — August **5**.
**Add: Temporary Borrowing** — July **0.7**, September **3.7**.
**Cash Closing Balance** — July **1**, August **2**, September **1**.

==**The adjustment rules, applied exactly as the question states them, and this is where the marks separate.**
**July:** the balance before adjustment is ₹0.3 L, below the ₹1 L minimum, so **borrow ₹0.7 L** to reach exactly ₹1 L.
**August:** ₹7 L, which exceeds ₹2 L, so **invest the excess over ₹2 L** — the question says the company invests when the balance exceeds ₹2 L, and ICAI invests **₹5 L**, leaving ₹2 L. *Note that August therefore closes at ₹2 L, not ₹1 L.*
**September:** ₹(2.7) L, so **borrow ₹3.7 L** to reach ₹1 L.==

==**The one point of interpretation worth stating as a note.** Clause (viii) reads 'if cash balance exceed 2 Lakh, then company would invest for short term excess amount of 2 Lakh'. ICAI reads this as **invest the amount in excess of ₹2 lakh** — hence ₹5 L invested out of ₹7 L, closing at ₹2 L. **Say so in a note**, because the alternative reading (invest a fixed ₹2 L) would close August at ₹5 L and change nothing else. Stating the reading taken protects the mark.==

**Why the September deficit is so much larger than July's.** September carries three payments — ₹10.4 L of COGS, ₹1.3 L of expenses and the ₹3 L dividend — against collections of only ₹10 L, because July's sales were the lowest of the six months at ₹10 L and the two-month lag lands them in September. ==**The budget's purpose is visible in that single column: it identifies the period when there is 'an abnormally large cash requirement' two months before it arrives.**==

**Three things that do not appear anywhere in the budget.** April's and September's sales collections (outside the window), September's COGS payment (falls in October), and any interest on the loans or investments (the question says to ignore it). A candidate who includes the interest introduces a circularity the question has deliberately removed.
keywords: COGS 80% of sales, paid next month
also_asked_as: RTP-S26-FQ9 asks the same structure as a surplus/deficit against a target balance

official_questions.question: You have been asked to prepare a cash budget for the next quarter, January through March, for Jahanara Fashions. (a) Sales are expected to be ₹4,00,000 in January, ₹4,00,000 in February and ₹6,00,000 in March, all in cash. (b) The estimated purchases are ₹3,80,000 in January, ₹3,60,000 in February and ₹4,50,000 in March; payments for purchases will be made after a lag of one month, and outstanding on account of purchases in December last are ₹3,50,000. (c) The rent per month is ₹10,000 and the partners' personal withdrawal per month is ₹25,000. (d) Salaries and other expenses payable in cash are expected to be ₹25,000 in January, ₹20,000 in February and ₹30,000 in March. (e) They plan to buy furniture worth ₹40,000 on cash payment in January. (f) The cash balance at present is ₹6,000. Their target cash balance, however, is ₹15,000. What will be the surplus/deficit of cash in relation to their target cash balance?
answer_points: **Note the three features that shape the answer.** **All sales are in cash**, so there is no collection lag and no debtors. **Purchases are paid a month in arrear**, so January pays December's **₹3,50,000**, February pays January's ₹3,80,000 and March pays February's ₹3,60,000 — **March's own ₹4,50,000 is not paid in the quarter.** And the question asks for the **surplus or deficit against the target**, not for a closing balance.

**Outflows, month by month.**
**January:** purchases ₹3,50,000 + rent ₹10,000 + drawings ₹25,000 + salaries ₹25,000 + furniture ₹40,000 = ==**₹4,50,000**==.
**February:** purchases ₹3,80,000 + rent ₹10,000 + drawings ₹25,000 + salaries ₹20,000 = ==**₹4,35,000**==.
**March:** purchases ₹3,60,000 + rent ₹10,000 + drawings ₹25,000 + salaries ₹30,000 = ==**₹4,25,000**==.
==**ICAI's cumulative layout, which is what the question's wording calls for:**==
**1. Opening balance** — January **₹6,000** (shown once).
**6. Opening balance + cumulative net cash flow** — ₹(44,000) · ₹(79,000) · ₹96,000.
**7. Minimum cash balance required** — ₹15,000 in each month.

==**Why the cumulative column matters, and it is the whole point of the layout.** February's own net outflow of ₹35,000 is **smaller** than January's ₹50,000, yet February's deficit of ₹(94,000) is **larger** than January's ₹(59,000). The deficit is cumulative: the shortfall carries forward, and the firm has to fund the **worst cumulative position**, not the worst monthly flow. ==**A month-by-month layout that resets the opening balance each month hides this and would give the wrong borrowing requirement.**==

**The conclusion to write.** The firm needs arrangements for about **₹94,000** — its peak requirement, reached at the end of February — and that need is **temporary**: by the end of March the cumulative position has swung to a **₹81,000 surplus** above the target, available for short-term investment. **Overdraft or credit arrangements with banks** are the right instrument precisely because the need reverses within the quarter.

**Two deliberate omissions in the data.** The **₹4,50,000 of March purchases** is never paid inside the budget, and there are **no debtors** because all sales are cash. Both simplify the arithmetic, which is how the question makes room for the cumulative point it is really testing.

**And one line worth adding on the drawings.** Partners' personal withdrawals of ₹25,000 a month are **cash payments** and belong in the budget, even though they are an appropriation rather than an expense. A cash budget records movements of cash, not items of profit and loss — which is the same reason **depreciation never appears** and **accruals do not affect it.**

mcqs.question: Which method of cash flow budgeting does the study material describe as calculating the annual cash flows by adjusting the sales revenue and cost figures for delays in receipts and payments and eliminating non-cash items such as depreciation?

options.A: The adjusted income method
options.B: The receipts and payments method
options.C: The adjusted balance sheet method
options.D: The sources and application of funds method

mcqs.explanation: SM §10 gives three methods. The adjusted income method starts from the income figures and adjusts for the change in debtors and creditors and for non-cash items. The receipts and payments method counts expected cash flows directly and is the one 'commonly used in business organizations'. The adjusted balance sheet method expresses assets and short-term liabilities as a percentage of expected sales.

mcqs.question: A firm opens a quarter with ₹10,000 of cash and a target balance of ₹20,000. Its net cash flows are ₹(40,000) in month 1, ₹(30,000) in month 2 and ₹1,00,000 in month 3. Its deficit against the target at the end of month 2 is:
mcqs.explanation: Cumulative net cash flow to the end of month 2 is ₹(70,000); adding the ₹10,000 opening balance gives ₹(60,000); deducting the ₹20,000 target gives a deficit of ₹(80,000). This is RTP September 2026's layout. Option A takes month 2's flow alone, option D stops at the cash position without applying the target, and option C omits the first month's carry-forward — the error the cumulative row exists to prevent.

concepts.title: 10.3–10.5 Managing Cash Collection and Disbursements, Accelerating Cash Collections, and Controlling Payments
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 0 — a standing gap, which is why this block carries a chapter-test descriptive question
understand: **Why the section exists** (SM §10.3): having prepared the cash budget, **'the finance manager should ensure that there is not a significant deviation between projected cash flows and actual cash flows'**, and efficiency must be brought in **by proper control of cash collection and disbursement.**

==**The twin objectives, and they pull in opposite directions by design:** **'Accelerate cash collections as much as possible; and Decelerate or delay cash disbursements within permissible time frame.'** ==Note the qualifier on the second: **within permissible time frame.** ICAI is not endorsing late payment.==

==**§10.4 Float — the four kinds, and this is the most examinable list in Unit II after Baumol.** **'The term float is used to refer to the periods that affect cash as it moves through the different stages of the collection process.'**==

==**1. Billing float** — **'An invoice is the formal document that a seller prepares and sends to the purchaser as the payment request for goods sold or services provided. The time between the sale and the mailing of the invoice is known as billing float.'**==
==**2. Mail float** — **'This is the time when a cheque is being carried by post office, messenger service or other means of delivery.'**==
==**3. Cheque processing float** — **'This is the time required for the seller to sort, record and deposit the cheque after it has been received by the company.'**==
==**4. Banking processing float** — **'This is the time from the deposit of the cheque to the crediting of funds in the sellers' account.'**==

==**How each float is attacked** (SM §10.4): **issue invoices quickly** (reducing or eliminating **billing** float); **reduce the time lag between a customer paying the bill and the cheque being collected** (reducing or eliminating **mail** float); and **make funds become available for the firm's use** (reducing or eliminating **processing** floats).==
==**Two decentralised collection systems** ICAI names — **concentration banking** and the **lock box system** — **'to speed up cash collection and reduce float time.'**==

==**(i) Concentration Banking.** **'the company establishes a number of strategic collection centers in different regions instead of a single collection center at the head office. This system reduces the period between the time a customer mails in his remittances and the time when they become spendable funds with the company. Payments received by the different collection centers are deposited with their respective local banks which in turn transfer all surplus funds to the concentration bank of head office. The concentration bank with which the company has its major bank account is generally located at the headquarters.'** ICAI calls it **'one important and popular way of reducing the size of the float.'**==

==**(ii) Lock Box System.** **'The purpose of lock box system is to eliminate the time between the receipts of remittances by the company and deposited in the bank.'** The mechanics: **the company rents the local post-office box and authorizes its bank at each of the locations to pick up remittances in the boxes. Customers are billed with instructions to mail their remittances to the lock boxes. The bank picks up the mail several times a day and deposits the cheques in the company's account.** The cheques **may be micro-filmed for record purposes and cleared for collection**, and the company receives a deposit slip and a list of all payments. **'This procedure frees the company from handling and depositing the cheques.'**==

==**The advantage, in precise terms:** **'cheques are deposited with the banks sooner and become collected funds sooner than if they were processed by the company prior to deposit. In other words, lag between the time cheques are received by the company and the time they are actually deposited in the bank (i.e. cheque processing float) is eliminated.'** ==So the lock box kills the **cheque processing float** specifically; concentration banking shortens the **mail** float.==

==**The drawback and the decision rule — the part candidates omit.** **'The main drawback of lock box system is the cost of its operation. The bank provides a number of services in addition to usual clearing of cheques and requires compensation for them. Since the cost is almost directly proportional to the number of cheques deposited, lock box arrangements are usually not profitable if the average remittance is small.'** And the rule: **'The appropriate rule for deciding whether or not to use a lock box system or for that matter, concentration banking, is simply to compare the added cost of the most efficient system with the marginal income that can be generated from the released funds. If costs are less than income, the system is profitable and if the system is not profitable, it is not worth undertaking.'**==

==**§10.5 Controlling Payments.** **'An effective control over payments can also cause faster turnover of cash. This is possible only by making payments on the due date, making excessive use of draft (bill of exchange) instead of cheques.'**==

==**Playing the float, in ICAI's own words:** **'Availability of cash can be maximized by playing the float. In this, a firm estimates accurately the time when the cheques issued will be presented for encashment and thus utilizes the float period to its advantage by issuing more cheques but having in the bank account only so much cash balance as will be sufficient to honour those cheques which are actually expected to be presented on a particular date.'** And: **'the company may make payment to its outstation suppliers by a cheque and send it through mail. The delay in transit and collection of the cheque, will be used to increase the float.'**==

==**The symmetry worth seeing, because it is what the whole section is about.** The **collection** side wants float **destroyed**; the **payment** side wants float **created**. The same four stages — billing, mail, processing, banking — are an enemy when money is coming in and an ally when money is going out. ==That symmetry is the frame for any theory answer here.==
concepts.example: ICAI's own Illustration 9 (Prachi Ltd) asks for a 'cleared funds forecast' over five days, with one customer paying by BACS — 'receipt of money by BACS is instantaneous' — and another by cheque that 'will be paid into Prachi Ltd's bank account on the same day as the sale is made and will clear on the third day following this (excluding day of payment)'. The three-day clearing gap is the banking processing float made arithmetical, and the contrast with the instantaneous BACS receipt is exactly why a company pushes customers towards electronic payment.

mcqs.explanation: SM §10.4 defines four floats. Cheque processing float runs from receipt to deposit; banking processing float runs from deposit to the crediting of funds; mail float is the cheque in transit; billing float is the gap between the sale and the mailing of the invoice. The lock box system eliminates the cheque processing float specifically, because the bank deposits the cheque before the company ever sees it.

options.C: Adopt it only if the bank will waive its charges on the clearing of cheques
options.D: Compare the added cost of the most efficient system with the marginal income that can be generated from the released funds

mcqs.explanation: SM §10.4: 'The appropriate rule ... is simply to compare the added cost of the most efficient system with the marginal income that can be generated from the released funds. If costs are less than income, the system is profitable and if the system is not profitable, it is not worth undertaking.' Option A is a rule of thumb ICAI does not give; option B ignores the cost side, which is the lock box's main drawback.

recap: Twin objectives: accelerate collections, and delay disbursements within permissible time frame.
Four floats: billing (sale to invoice), mail (cheque in transit), cheque processing (receipt to deposit), banking processing (deposit to credit).
Concentration banking uses regional collection centres whose local banks sweep surplus funds to the concentration bank at head office.

The lock box system has the bank collect from a rented PO box several times a day, eliminating the cheque processing float; its cost is proportional to the number of cheques, so it suits large remittances.
For either system, compare the added cost with the marginal income from the released funds.
On the payment side: pay on the due date, use drafts rather than cheques, and play the float by holding only what the cheques expected that day require.

understand: ==**§10.6 The question the models answer.** A firm should maintain an optimum cash balance for day-to-day operations and **'may also carry additional cash as a buffer or safety stock. The amount of cash balance will depend on the risk-return trade off.'** ICAI's framing: the firm should hold **'just enough, i.e. neither too much (to avoid any opportunity cost) nor too little cash balance (to settle day to day payments)'** — and then poses the question the two models split: **'How to determine the optimum cash balance if cash flows are predictable and if they are not predictable?'**==

==**§11 The two families.** **'All these models can be put in two categories: Inventory type models; and Stochastic models.'** **Inventory type models** — **'William J. Baumol's economic order quantity model applies equally to cash management problems under conditions of certainty or where the cash flows are predictable.'** **Stochastic models** — **'in a situation where the EOQ Model is not applicable, stochastic model of cash management helps in determining the optimum level of cash balance. It happens when the demand for cash is stochastic and not known in advance.'**==
**The purpose common to both:** **'to ensure that cash does not remain idle unnecessarily and at the same time the firm is not confronted with a situation of cash shortage.'**
==**§11.1 Baumol's model (1952).** **'According to this model, optimum cash level is that level of cash where the carrying costs and transactions costs are the minimum.'**==

==**The two costs, defined precisely:** **'The carrying costs refer to the cost of holding cash, namely, the opportunity cost or interest foregone on marketable securities. The transaction costs refer to the cost involved in getting the marketable securities converted into cash. This happens when the firm falls short of cash and has to sell the securities resulting in clerical, brokerage, registration and other costs.'**==

==**The formula** (SM §11.1): **C = √(2U × P ÷ S)**, where
**C = Optimum cash balance**
**U = Annual (or monthly) cash disbursement**
**P = Fixed cost per transaction**
**S = Opportunity cost of one rupee p.a. (or p.m.)**==

==**The four assumptions:** **(i) cash needs of the firm are known with certainty; (ii) the cash is used uniformly over a period of time and it is also known with certainty; (iii) the holding cost is known and it is constant; (iv) the transaction cost also remains constant.**==

==**SM Illustration 10, the forward computation.** Total disbursements ₹1,05,000 per month or **₹12,60,000 per year**; administrative and transaction cost of transferring cash **₹20 per transfer**; marketable securities yield **8% per annum**.
**C = √(2 × ₹12,60,000 × ₹20 ÷ 0.08) = ₹25,100.**==

==**And the reverse computation, which is what the exam actually asks.** January 2026's MCQ 7 gives **C = ₹30,000, P = ₹25 and S = 10%** and asks for **U**. Square both sides: **C² = 2UP ÷ S**, so **U = C²S ÷ 2P** = (₹30,000² × 0.10) ÷ (2 × ₹25) = ₹9,00,00,00,000 × 0.10 ÷ ₹50 = **₹18,00,000**. ==**Learn the rearranged form U = C²S ÷ 2P; two of the three official Baumol questions run backwards.**==

==**Units discipline, which is where marks are lost.** U and S must be on the **same time basis** — annual disbursement with an annual opportunity cost, or monthly with monthly. ICAI's formula note says so expressly: **'U = Annual (or monthly) cash disbursement'** and **'S = Opportunity cost of one rupee p.a. (or p.m.)'**. In Illustration 10 the monthly ₹1,05,000 is converted to the annual ₹12,60,000 before the 8% is applied; in RTP January 2025's Samvar Ltd the monthly disbursement of ₹1.50 lakh is likewise annualised to ₹18,00,000 against a 12% annual yield, giving **C = √(2 × 18,00,000 × 20 ÷ 0.12) = ₹24,495.**==

==**The limitation, and it is the bridge to Miller-Orr:** **'The limitation of the Baumol's model is that it does not allow the cash flows to fluctuate. Firms in practice do not use their cash balance uniformly nor are they able to predict daily cash inflows and outflows.'**==

==**§11.2 The Miller-Orr model (1966).** **'According to this model the net cash flow is completely stochastic.'** **'When changes in cash balance occur randomly the application of control theory serves a useful purpose. The Miller-Orr model is one of such control limit models. This model is designed to determine the time and size of transfers between an investment account and cash account.'**==
==**The three limits:** **'h as upper limit, z as the return point; and zero as the lower limit.'**==

==**The three rules:**
**'When the cash balance reaches the upper limit, the transfer of cash equal to h – z is invested in marketable securities account.'**
**'When it touches the lower limit, a transfer from marketable securities account to cash account is made.'**
**'During the period when cash balance stays between (h, z) and (z, 0) i.e. high and low limits no transactions between cash and marketable securities account is made.'**==

==**What sets the limits:** **'The high and low limits of cash balance are set up on the basis of fixed cost associated with the securities transactions, the opportunity cost of holding cash and the degree of likely fluctuations in cash balances. These limits satisfy the demands for cash at the lowest possible total costs.'**==

==**Why it is preferred:** **'The MO Model is more realistic since it allows variations in cash balance within lower and upper limits. The finance manager can set the limits according to the firm's liquidity requirements i.e., maintaining minimum and maximum cash balance.'**==

==**A point of fact worth knowing for an MCQ.** **The current SM gives no formula for h or z** — only the control-limit description. So a Miller-Orr question in Paper 6A can only be **descriptive or conceptual**: the three limits, the three rules, the three determinants, and the comparison with Baumol. ==Do not expect to compute a return point, and do not invent the cube-root formula from other syllabuses.==

memory.trick: **Baumol is a sawtooth; Miller-Orr is a corridor.** Baumol draws cash falling steadily to zero and being topped up by the same amount each time; Miller-Orr draws it wandering randomly between a floor and a ceiling and being knocked back to a **return point** only when it hits one. ==Certainty gives you a formula; randomness gives you limits.==

mistakes: Mixing a monthly disbursement with an annual opportunity cost. Annualise U first — Illustration 10 converts ₹1,05,000 a month to ₹12,60,000 a year before applying 8%.
Using the yield as a percentage rather than a decimal. S is the opportunity cost of one rupee, so 8% is 0.08.
Forgetting to double U in the numerator. The 2 is part of the formula, and omitting it understates C by about 29%.
Trying to compute Miller-Orr's return point. The current SM gives no formula; the model is examinable descriptively only.
Saying that at the upper limit the whole balance is invested. The transfer is h − z, which leaves the return point in cash.
Attributing the three motives for holding cash to Baumol. Those are Keynes's, in §9.1.
Saying Baumol assumes the transaction cost varies with the amount transferred. It is a fixed cost per transaction, and constant.

official_questions.question: A firm maintains a separate account for cash disbursement. The administrative and transaction cost of transferring cash to the disbursement account is ₹25 per transfer. Marketable securities yield 10% per annum. The firm has determined its optimum cash balance at ₹30,000, according to the William J. Baumol Model. What will be the Total Annual Cash Disbursements of the firm? (A) ₹18,00,000 (B) ₹45,00,000 (C) ₹36,00,000 (D) ₹27,00,000
answer_points: **Write the model first, with its symbols named.** **C = √(2U × P ÷ S)**, where C is the optimum cash balance, **U the annual cash disbursement**, **P the fixed cost per transaction** and **S the opportunity cost of one rupee per annum.**
**Identify what is given and what is wanted.** C = **₹30,000**; P = **₹25**; S = **0.10**. **U is the unknown.**
**Square both sides and rearrange.** C² = 2UP ÷ S, so ==**U = C²S ÷ 2P**==.

==**Why the distractors are what they are.** **₹45,00,000** is what you get by using **S = 0.04** (that is, dividing the yield by 2.5 or confusing it with a half-yearly rate); **₹36,00,000** comes from forgetting the 2 in the numerator and so solving U = C²S ÷ P; **₹27,00,000** comes from treating the yield as 15%. ==All three are reachable by a single misplaced constant, which is the mark of a well-built Baumol MCQ.==

==**The transferable point.** Of the three official Baumol questions in the period reviewed, **two run backwards** — this one for U, and RTP January 2025's Samvar Ltd for C from a monthly disbursement that must first be annualised. **Memorise the rearranged form U = C²S ÷ 2P alongside the forward form**, and treat 'the firm has determined its optimum cash balance at …' as the standing signal that the formula is to be inverted.==

**One unit check that costs nothing.** The question gives an **annual** yield and asks for an **annual** disbursement, so no conversion is needed here. Where the disbursement is given monthly — as in Illustration 10's ₹1,05,000 and Samvar's ₹1.50 lakh — **annualise it before applying an annual S**, or the answer is out by a factor of √12.
keywords: annualise U if S is annual
also_asked_as: RTP-J25-FQ1 item (i) computes C forwards from a monthly disbursement of ₹1.50 lakh and a 12% yield, giving ₹24,495

official_questions.question: Samvar Ltd, a leading FMCG company operating stores under the GoMART brand, is contemplating 50 additional stores needing ₹200 lakhs per store. Average sales would be ₹120 lakhs p.a. with a GP margin of 18%. 15% of customers pay by debit and credit card through POS systems, which take approximately 9 days for funds to be credited; installing a POS system costs 2% of total sales through POS. Perishable products are 60% of sales, semi-durable 25% and durable the balance, with inventory storage periods of 10, 30 and 60 days respectively. Suppliers provide an average 30 days' credit. Each store employs 20 personnel with monthly average salaries of ₹4 lakhs per store, paid on the 1st of the next month. Samvar plans to keep the optimum cash balance in hand as suggested by Baumol's model; excess cash is invested in marketable securities yielding 12% p.a. Total disbursement for the year is estimated at ₹1.50 lakhs per month with a transaction cost of ₹20 per transfer. Based on the above, calculate for each store: (i) The optimum cash balance — (A) ₹7,071 (B) ₹26,500 (C) ₹7,150 (D) ₹24,495. (ii) The Gross and Net Working Capital for the next year — (A) ₹6.7730 L, (5.9396 L) (B) ₹6.7730 L, 12.7125 L (C) ₹200 L, (5.9396L) (D) ₹(5.9396 L), 6.7730 L. [Items (iii) to (v) of the same case are cost-of-capital items cross-referenced to Chapter 4.]
answer_points: ==**Item (i) — the optimum cash balance. Answer (D) ₹24,495.**==

**Annualise the disbursement first.** The total disbursement is **₹1.50 lakhs per month**, so **U = ₹1,50,000 × 12 = ₹18,00,000** — and this step is the whole question, because the yield is given per annum.

==**Why option (A) ₹7,071 is there, and it is the single most instructive distractor in the chapter.** √(2 × ₹1,50,000 × ₹20 ÷ 0.12) = √₹5,00,00,000 = **₹7,071** — the answer you get by using the **monthly** disbursement against the **annual** opportunity cost. The two figures differ by exactly **√12**. ==ICAI has built the question so that the units error produces a clean, plausible number.==
**Item (ii) — Gross and Net Working Capital. Answer (A) ₹6.7730 lakh and ₹(5.9396) lakh.**

**Current assets, store by store.** **Inventory**, weighted by the three product classes on the cost of goods sold (sales ₹120 lakhs at an 18% GP margin gives a COGS of ₹98.40 lakhs): perishable 60% for 10 days, semi-durable 25% for 30 days and durable 15% for 60 days. **Debtors**, only on the **15% of sales settled through POS**, outstanding **9 days**. Plus the **₹24,495 of optimum cash** from item (i).
**Current liabilities.** **Creditors** at **30 days** of purchases, and **salaries outstanding** of **₹4 lakhs** — one month's payroll, because employees' dues are paid on the 1st of the next month.

==**Why net working capital is negative, and it is the point of the item.** The salary accrual of ₹4 lakhs plus a month of supplier credit together exceed a current-asset base built on **10-to-60-day inventory and 9-day card receivables**. A retail FMCG store collects almost everything in cash at the till and pays its suppliers and staff in arrear, so it runs on **negative working capital** — **₹(5.9396) lakh per store**. ==**A negative figure is the right answer here, not an error to be corrected**, and option (D) is offered precisely for candidates who assume the signs must be the other way round.==

**Note what the POS fee is for.** The **2% of sales through POS** is a **cost**, not a working-capital item; it belongs to the profitability of the store, and items (iii) to (v) of the case use it. It does not enter the gross or net working capital computation.

==**On the placement of this atom.** Items (i) and (ii) are Chapter 9; items (iii) to (v) — the total funds needed per store, the overall cost of capital on a 2:1 debt-equity mix with slab-based rates, and the revenue subsidy that depends on the cost of capital not exceeding 10% — are **Chapter 4 cost-of-capital items**. The case is recorded here because its opening two items are working capital and the scenario is framed around 'the additional capital needed for the smooth running of fixed assets and its daily operations'. ==**Cross-reference Chapter 4 §7 for items (iii) to (v).**==
keywords: debtors only on 15% POS sales for 9 days
negative working capital is correct for retail

mcqs.question: A firm's cash disbursements are ₹2,00,000 per month, the cost per transfer is ₹50 and marketable securities yield 9% per annum. The optimum cash balance under Baumol's model is:
mcqs.explanation: Annualise the disbursement: U = ₹2,00,000 × 12 = ₹24,00,000. C = √(2 × ₹24,00,000 × ₹50 ÷ 0.09) = √(₹24,00,00,000 ÷ 0.09) = √₹26,66,66,66,667 = ₹51,640. Option B uses the monthly ₹2,00,000 against the annual 9%, understating the answer by a factor of √12 — the error RTP January 2025's Samvar Ltd offers as its own first distractor. Option C omits the 2 as well.

mcqs.question: Under the Miller-Orr model, when the cash balance reaches the upper limit h, the firm:

options.A: Transfers the whole balance h into marketable securities, leaving the account at zero
options.B: Transfers cash equal to h − z into marketable securities, returning the balance to the return point z
options.C: Takes no action, since the upper limit is an alert rather than a trigger
options.D: Raises the return point z to equal h and leaves the cash where it is

mcqs.explanation: SM §11.2: 'When the cash balance reaches the upper limit, the transfer of cash equal to h – z is invested in marketable securities account.' The balance therefore falls to the return point z, not to zero — zero is the lower limit, at which a transfer out of securities into cash is made. Between the limits no transactions take place at all.

recap: Inventory type models (Baumol) suit predictable cash flows; stochastic models (Miller-Orr) suit cash demand not known in advance.
Baumol's optimum is where carrying cost — interest forgone on marketable securities — and transaction cost are together least.
C = √(2UP ÷ S); rearranged, U = C²S ÷ 2P. Illustration 10 gives ₹25,100; Samvar Ltd gives ₹24,495.
Keep U and S on the same time basis; a monthly U against an annual S is wrong by √12.
Baumol's limitation is that it does not allow cash flows to fluctuate.
Miller-Orr sets h, z and zero: at h invest h − z, at zero sell securities, in between do nothing. The current SM gives no formula for h or z.

concepts.title: 12–12.7 Recent Developments in Cash Management — Electronic Fund Transfer, Zero Balance Account, Money Market Operations, Petty Cash Imprest System, Management of Temporary Cash Surplus, Electronic Cash Management System and Virtual Banking
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (Jan 2025 Q4(c), Jan 2026 Q4(b)) · RTP 0 · MTP 0
understand: **Why ICAI groups these seven** (SM §12): **'Both technological advancement and desire to reduce cost of operations has led to some innovative techniques in managing cash.'** The seven are printed as a single labelled diagram, and each is a two-mark answer in its own right.

==**12.1 Electronic Fund Transfer.** With developments in information technology **'the present banking system is switching over to the computerisation of banks branches to offer efficient banking services and cash management services to their customers. The network will be linked to the different branches, banks.'** The three benefits to the customer: **instant updating of accounts; quick transfer of funds; instant information about foreign exchange rates.**==

==**12.2 Zero Balance Account.** **'For efficient cash management some firms employ an extensive policy of substituting marketable securities for cash by the use of zero balance accounts. Every day the firm totals the cheques presented for payment against the account. The firm transfers the balance amount of cash (in excess of payments) in the account if any, for buying marketable securities. In case of shortage of cash, the firm sells the marketable securities.'** ==It is the Miller-Orr corridor collapsed to a single point: the target balance is zero.==

==**12.3 Money Market Operations.** **'One of the tasks of treasury function of larger companies is the investment of surplus funds in the money market. The chief characteristic of money market banking is one of size.'** Banks obtain funds **'by competing in the money market for the deposits by the companies, public authorities, High Net worth Investors (HNI), and other banks.'** **'Deposits are made for specific periods ranging from overnight to one year; highly competitive rates which reflect supply and demand on a daily, even hourly basis are quoted. Consequently, the rates can fluctuate quite dramatically, especially for the shorter-term deposits.'**==

==**12.4 Petty Cash Imprest System.** **'For better control on cash, generally the companies use petty cash imprest system wherein the day-to-day petty expenses are estimated taking into account past experience and future needs and generally a week's requirement of cash will be kept separate for making petty expenses. Again, the next week will commence with the pre-determined balance. This will reduce the strain of the management in managing petty cash expenses and help in the managing cash efficiently.'**==

==**12.5 Management of Temporary Cash Surplus.** Temporary surpluses can be profitably invested in: **short-term deposits in banks and financial institutions; short-term debt market instruments; or long term debt instruments with flexible maturity dates; shares of blue chip listed companies.** **'Choice of investment can be based on economic situation, volatility of returns and also the risk appetite of the organization.'**==

==**12.6 Electronic Cash Management System.** **'Most of the cash management systems now-a-days are electronically based, since speed is the essence of any cash management system. Electronically, transfer of data as well as funds play a key role in any cash management system. Various elements in the process of cash management are linked through a satellite.'** The places interlinked include **where the instrument is collected, where cash is to be transferred in the company's account, and where the payment is to be transferred.**==

**ICAI's limited-access point, which is the detail that marks out a full answer:** a networked system **'may also provide a very limited access to third parties like parties having very regular dealings of receipts and payments with the company'** — its example being a finance company that gives **sub-brokers limited access to verify the collections made through them for determination of commission.**

==**The thirteen results of electronic cash management**, of which four or five should be named: **significant saving in time; increase in interest earned and decrease in interest expense; reduces paper-work and hence manpower; greater accounting accuracy as it allows easy detection of book-keeping errors; more control over time and funds; supports electronic payments; faster transfer of funds from one location to another; speedy conversion of various instruments into cash; making available funds wherever required, whenever required; reduction in the amount of 'idle float' to the maximum possible extent; ensures no idle funds are placed at any place in the organization; makes inter-bank balancing of funds much easier; a true form of centralized Cash Management; produces faster electronic reconciliation; reduces the number of cheques issued.**==

==**12.7 Virtual Banking — the most examined item in this block, asked in January 2025 and again in January 2026.** **'Broadly virtual banking denotes the provision of banking and related services through extensive use of information technology without direct recourse to the bank by the customer.'**==

**The context ICAI sets:** the practice of banking changed significantly **in the nineties**; **'while banks are striving to strengthen customer base and relationship and move towards relationship banking, customers are increasingly moving away from the confines of traditional branch banking and are seeking the convenience of remote electronic banking services including net banking & mobile banking. And even within the broad spectrum of electronic banking the virtual banking has gained prominence.'** Its origin **'in the developed countries can be traced back to the seventies with the installation of Automated Teller Machines (ATMs)'**, after which **'driven by the competitive market environment as well as various technological and customer pressures, other types of virtual banking services have grown in prominence throughout the world.'**

==**The four advantages of virtual banking** (SM §12.7) — the exact list both past-paper questions want:
**1. Lower cost of handling a transaction.**
**2. The increased speed of response to customer requirements.**
**3. The lower cost of operating branch network along with reduced staff costs leads to cost efficiency.**
**4. Virtual banking allows the possibility of improved and a range of services being made available to the customer rapidly, accurately and at his convenience.**==

==**And the separate sentence on popularity, which January 2026 asks for by name:** **'The popularity which virtual banking services have won among customers is due to the speed, convenience and round the clock access they offer.'** ==Three words — **speed, convenience, round the clock access** — and they answer 'why is it popular' as distinct from 'what are its advantages'.==

==**The RBI measures ICAI lists, which are the update-sensitive part of this block.** Since the **mid-Eighties**: **computerized settlement of clearing transactions, Magnetic Ink Character Recognition (MICR) technology, inter-city clearing facilities and high value clearing facilities, the Electronic Clearing Service Scheme (ECSS), the Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT) scheme, UPI payment platforms, Real Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS), Delivery vs. Payment (DVP) for Government securities transactions, and the Indian Financial Network (INFINET).** Further: **the Centralised Funds Management System (CFMS), the Securities Services System (SSS) and the Structured Financial Messaging System (SFMS).** ==**This list changes between editions — verify it against the edition applicable to the attempt before quoting it.**==
concepts.example: January 2025 asked for 'any two advantages of virtual banking' for two marks; January 2026 asked 'Why the Virtual banking service is popular among the customers? memory.trick: **Transfer, Zero, Market, Petty, Surplus, Electronic, Virtual.** Seven developments in the order ICAI prints them, and the mnemonic is the shape of the money: it **moves** (EFT), it is **swept to nothing** (zero balance), it is **parked** (money market), it is **rationed** (imprest), it is **invested** (surplus), it is **wired** (electronic), and the **bank itself disappears** (virtual).
key: Instant updating, quick transfer, instant forex rates
Daily sweep: excess buys securities, shortage sells them
Deposits from overnight to one year at hourly-moving rates
A week's float, each week starting at the pre-determined balance
Bank deposits, short-term debt, flexible long-term debt, blue chips
Speed is the essence; reduces idle float; true centralised cash management
Banking without direct recourse to the bank by the customer
Lower transaction cost · faster response · cheaper branch and staff · better and wider services
Speed, convenience, round the clock access

mistakes: Answering 'why is virtual banking popular' with the four advantages. ICAI gives a separate sentence — speed, convenience and round-the-clock access — and January 2026 asks both halves.

Defining virtual banking as internet banking. ICAI's definition is wider: services provided through extensive use of information technology without direct recourse to the bank, and it traces the origin to ATMs in the seventies.
Describing a zero balance account as an account that may not be overdrawn. It is an account swept daily to zero against marketable securities.

official_questions.question: State any two advantages of virtual banking. (2 Marks) [OR — the alternative part (c), on the exclusion of financing cost principle, is a Chapter 7 question.]
answer_points: **Open with one line of definition, which frames the advantages and costs nothing.** **Virtual banking denotes the provision of banking and related services through extensive use of information technology without direct recourse to the bank by the customer.**

==**Advantage 1 — Lower cost of handling a transaction.**== A transaction executed through an electronic channel costs the bank a fraction of the same transaction at a counter, and that saving is what makes the model viable.
==**Advantage 2 — The increased speed of response to customer requirements.**== Requests are acted on without the delay of physical presence or branch processing hours.

**Two more are available if the examiner wants a fuller answer**, and in a two-mark question naming all four costs three extra lines: ==**the lower cost of operating the branch network along with reduced staff costs, which leads to cost efficiency**==; and ==**the possibility of improved and a range of services being made available to the customer rapidly, accurately and at his convenience.**==

==**The two-mark discipline.** The question says **'any two'**, so **two advantages, each with a short clause of explanation, is the complete answer.** Writing all four is not penalised but earns nothing extra; writing two bare phrases with no explanation risks half a mark each. ==**Name the advantage, then say why it follows.**==

**If a sentence of context is wanted**, ICAI's own is available: virtual banking's origin **in the developed countries can be traced back to the seventies with the installation of Automated Teller Machines (ATMs)**, and its growth since has been **driven by the competitive market environment as well as various technological and customer pressures.**

official_questions.question: Why the Virtual banking service is popular among the customers? Discuss the advantages of Virtual Banking. (4 Marks)
answer_points: ==**The question has two halves, and ICAI's answer has two distinct sources. Answer them separately or half the marks go missing.**==

**Definition first.** **Virtual banking denotes the provision of banking and related services through extensive use of information technology without direct recourse to the bank by the customer.** Its origin in the developed countries **can be traced back to the seventies with the installation of Automated Teller Machines (ATMs)**, and other forms have since grown **driven by the competitive market environment as well as various technological and customer pressures.**
==**Part two — the advantages, which are the bank's side of the same coin. All four:**==
**1. ==Lower cost of handling a transaction.==**
**2. ==The increased speed of response to customer requirements.==**
**3. ==The lower cost of operating branch network along with reduced staff costs leads to cost efficiency.==**
**4. ==Virtual banking allows the possibility of improved and a range of services being made available to the customer rapidly, accurately and at his convenience.==**

==**The structural point that earns the fourth mark.** Items 1 and 3 are **benefits to the bank**; items 2 and 4 are **benefits to the customer** — and items 2 and 4 are where the popularity in part one comes from. Saying so explicitly shows the two halves of the question are connected rather than repeated.==

**If space allows, one line of context on the Indian payment system.** The RBI has taken numerous measures since the mid-Eighties to strengthen the payments mechanism, among them **MICR technology, the Electronic Clearing Service Scheme, the Electronic Funds Transfer scheme, UPI payment platforms, RTGS, Delivery versus Payment for Government securities and INFINET** — the infrastructure without which virtual banking could not operate at scale. *(This list is edition-sensitive; verify it against the Study Material applicable to the attempt.)*

**A four-mark answer in four parts, then.** Definition (quarter mark's worth of framing), the three reasons for popularity, the four advantages, and the one-line observation that two of the advantages accrue to the bank and two to the customer. ==Resist the temptation to merge the popularity line into the advantages list — January 2026 asks for both because they are separately printed in the Study Material.==

concepts.title: 13 Management of Marketable Securities
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 direct (but SM Illustration 11 underlies PYQ May 2026 Q3(b)) · RTP 0 · MTP 0
understand: ==**Why it belongs in a cash chapter** (SM §13): **'Management of marketable securities is an integral part of investment of cash as this may serve both the purposes of liquidity and cash, provided choice of investment is made correctly. As the working capital needs are fluctuating, it is possible to park excess funds in some short-term securities, which can be liquidated when need for cash is felt.'**==
==**The three principles of selection, and this is the examinable list:**==
==**Safety.** **'Return and risks go hand in hand. As the objective in this investment is ensuring liquidity, minimum risk is the criterion of selection.'**==

==**Maturity.** **'Matching of maturity and forecasted cash needs is essential. Prices of long term securities fluctuate more with changes in interest rates and are therefore, riskier. Since this is for temporary excess funds, short term securities are preferred.'**==

==**Marketability.** **'It refers to the convenience, speed and cost at which a security can be converted into cash. If the security can be sold quickly without loss of time and price it is highly liquid or marketable.'**==

==**What the choice is limited to** (SM §13): **'The choice of marketable securities is mainly limited to Government treasury bills, Deposits with banks and Inter-corporate deposits.'** Also attractive: **Units of Unit Trust of India and commercial papers of corporates**, along with **deposits with sister concerns or associate companies.** And: **'Besides this Money Market Mutual Funds (MMMFs) have also emerged as one of the avenues of short-term investment.'**==

==**SM Illustration 11 sits in this section, and it is the only numerical here — the Sai Trading computation that May 2026's AR Ltd reproduces.** Debtors collected after 45 days; inventory held 75 days; creditors paid in 30 days; ₹120 lakhs spent annually at a constant rate; 10% earned on investments.
**(a) Cash cycle = 45 + 75 − 30 = 90 days (3 months); cash turnover = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.**
**(b) Minimum operating cash = Total operating annual outlay ÷ cash turnover = ₹120 lakhs ÷ 4 = ₹30 lakhs.**
**(c) Cut the inventory holding period by 30 days: cycle = 45 + 45 − 30 = 60 days (2 months); turnover = 6; minimum cash = ₹120 lakhs ÷ 6 = ₹20 lakhs; reduction in investment = ₹10 lakhs; saving = 0.10 × ₹10 lakhs = ₹1 lakh.**==

==**Why ICAI puts that illustration here rather than in §6.** The ₹10 lakhs released by shortening the cycle has to **go somewhere**, and the 10% it earns is the **return on marketable securities**. ==The saving of ₹1 lakh is not an accounting entry — it is the yield on funds moved out of the operating cycle and into short-term securities, which is precisely what this section is about.==

==**The tension to state in any theory answer.** The three principles pull against return: **safety** rules out higher-yielding paper, **maturity** rules out long-dated paper where the yield curve is usually steeper, and **marketability** rules out illiquid paper that pays a premium for being illiquid. ==A marketable-securities portfolio is deliberately a low-return portfolio, because its job is to be **cash that happens to earn something**, not an investment.==
concepts.example: May 2026's AR Ltd asks for 'the cash cycle and the minimum cash balance to be maintained to meet its obligations' and then prices a cash discount against the balance released — which is SM Illustration 11 with ₹200 lakhs of sales, a 10% margin and a 12% opportunity cost. The ₹15 lakh release is valued at 12% post-tax, giving ₹1.26 lakhs, exactly as Illustration 11 values its ₹10 lakh release at 10%, giving ₹1 lakh. The section is the bridge between a shorter operating cycle and an actual rupee saving.

options.A: Minimum risk, since the objective in this investment is ensuring liquidity

mcqs.question: A firm's debtors are collected after 40 days, inventory is held 80 days and creditors are paid in 30 days. It spends ₹180 lakhs annually at a constant rate and earns 8% on investments. If the inventory holding period is cut by 30 days, the annual saving is:

options.A: ₹1.60 lakhs
options.B: ₹1.20 lakhs
options.C: ₹0.96 lakhs
options.D: ₹2.40 lakhs

mcqs.explanation: Cash cycle = 40 + 80 − 30 = 90 days, turnover 360 ÷ 90 = 4, minimum cash ₹180 lakhs ÷ 4 = ₹45 lakhs. After the 30-day cut: 40 + 50 − 30 = 60 days, turnover 6, minimum cash ₹180 lakhs ÷ 6 = ₹30 lakhs. Funds released = ₹45 − ₹30 = ₹15 lakhs, and the saving is 8% of ₹15 lakhs = ₹1.20 lakhs (SM Illustration 11's method). Option D applies the 8% to the ₹30 lakh revised balance instead of to the ₹15 lakh release, which is the commonest error here; option A applies it to a ₹20 lakh release.

recap: Marketable securities park a fluctuating surplus so that it serves both liquidity and cash.
Three principles: safety (minimum risk is the criterion), maturity (match forecast cash needs; short term preferred), marketability (convenience, speed and cost of conversion).
The choice is mainly limited to treasury bills, bank deposits and inter-corporate deposits; also UTI units, commercial paper, sister-concern deposits and Money Market Mutual Funds.
Illustration 11: a 90-day cycle on ₹120 lakhs needs ₹30 lakhs of cash; cutting inventory by 30 days releases ₹10 lakhs and saves ₹1 lakh at 10%.
The portfolio is deliberately low-return, because its job is to be cash that earns something.

concepts.title: 14 Inventory Management (Unit III)
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 1 (May 2025 Series II Part I case, items 3 and 5)
understand: ==**The shortest unit in the chapter, and ICAI says why.** **'Inventories constitute a major element of working capital. It is, therefore, important that investment in inventory is properly controlled.'** But then: **'Inventory Management has been discussed in detail in Chapter 2 (Material Cost) Paper 4: Cost and Management Accounting. Students are advised to refer the same.'**==

==**What ICAI does state here, and it is the examinable content of Unit III.** **'The objectives of inventory management are, to a great extent, similar to the objectives of cash management.'** That is the sentence to open any answer with: adequate stock for operations, nothing blocked in idle stock, and the surplus avoided rather than invested.==

==**The nine problems inventory management covers** (SM §14): **fixation of minimum and maximum levels; determining the size of inventory to be carried; deciding about the issues, receipts and inspection procedures; determining the economic order quantity; proper storage facilities; keeping check over obsolescence; and ensuring control over movement of inventories.**==

==**What this means for Paper 6A.** **No EOQ computation has been asked in any Paper 6A past paper, RTP or MTP in the period reviewed**, and the SM gives no formula here. What *has* been asked is **inventory as a component of the working-capital decision** — the holding period that feeds R, W and F in the operating cycle, the trade-off in §4.1, and the **ranking of inventory-reduction proposals by their benefit**, which is what MTP May 2025 Series II's AMPL case does. ==**Revise this unit as a theory section and as a feeder into Units I and IV, not as a quantitative topic.**==
**The cross-references that make the unit usable.** Inventory appears five times elsewhere in this chapter, and each appearance is where a question is likely to come from:

==**§3, factor 2 — Desired level of Inventory:** identify the level that **allows uninterrupted production but reduces investment in raw materials and hence increases cash flow**, using **JIT and EOQ**.==

==**§4.1 — the trade-off row:** the higher side gives **fewer stock-outs and so higher profitability**; the lower side **requires less capital but endangers stock-out and loss of goodwill**; the balancing tools are **EOQ and JIT to carry the optimum level**.==

==**§4.2 — the level of investment:** a **manufacturing** entity holds **three levels of inventory** (raw material, work-in-process, finished goods), a **trading** entity only **trading stock**, a **service** entity only **consumables**; and **consumer durables carry large inventory compared with perishable products.**==

==**§4.3 — the approaches:** an **aggressive** policy **holds a lower level of inventory** and risks stock-outs; a **conservative** policy keeps **inventory level higher** and risks **inventory obsolescence** and **shortage of liquidity in the long run due to longer operating cycles.**==

==**§6 — the operating cycle:** **R**, **W** and **F** are three of the five periods, and together they are usually the largest part of the cycle. MTP September 2025 Series I's Wint Limited runs 53 + 35 + 45 = **133 days of inventory** inside a 147-day cycle.==

==**The one quantitative skill Unit III has actually been tested on — ranking inventory proposals by benefit.** MTP May 2025 Series II's AMPL gives three schemes to cut a finished-goods holding period that has stretched from 2–2½ months to 4–4½ months: **(1) a discount of up to 12% expected to sell 1,000 units a quarter; (2) an exchange scheme offsetting an average ₹3,500 a machine, expected to sell 4,650 units a year; (3) an advance-order scheme — ₹3,000 on order, ₹9,500 on delivery 1½ months later, a ₹4,500 benefit to the customer — expected to sell 400 machines a month.** The MCQ asks for the three ranked **'based on benefit analysis to the company in the form of sales'**, and a further MCQ asks for the **optimum combination of inventory proposal and credit policy.** ==**The method is to convert each scheme to annual units and then to annual contribution, and rank on that — not on the per-unit concession.**==
concepts.example: MTP May 2025 Series II's AMPL case is the only place inventory management carries marks in its own right in the period reviewed, and it does so by asking for a ranking rather than a formula. Proposal 2's exchange scheme sells 4,650 units a year at an average ₹3,500 offset; proposal 3's advance scheme sells 400 a month, that is 4,800 a year, and collects ₹3,000 up front; proposal 1's discount sells only 1,000 a quarter, 4,000 a year. Annualising each is the whole computation, and the case then pairs the best inventory proposal with the better of two credit policies.

official_questions.question: AMPL, a washing-machine manufacturer facing declining sales, identified poor inventory management (piling stocks, high imports, high selling price) and poor receivables management (poor credit policy and collection, bad debts). Four plans were presented. (1) A 5% average discount giving ₹15,675 per machine had no significant impact; a reduction above 10% was associated with increased demand, and a plan of up to 12% was estimated to sell about 1,000 units every quarter. (2) An exchange scheme, offsetting ₹3,000 to ₹4,000 of price (an average offset of ₹3,500 per machine), estimated at 4,650 units in the next year. (3) An all-round inventory reduction: the total inventory holding period is about 3½ months of which finished goods alone is 2 to 2½ months, recently stretched to 4 to 4½ months; under a proposed scheme a customer paying ₹3,000 in advance takes delivery after 1½ months and pays ₹9,500 on delivery, a benefit of ₹4,500 for waiting, with an estimated 400 machines a month. (4) Dealership sales are ₹3,65,00,000 with a present policy of 60 days' credit but an average collection period of about 120 days; 90% of sales are on credit, of which 15% is to customers whose financial position is not sound with bad debt losses of 2% of sales to those customers; cost of sales is 80% and collection expenses ₹5,00,000 a year. Policy A: terms of "2/15, net 60", two-thirds expected to take the discount, no change in sales, collection period for the rest falling to 80 days, no change in bad debts, collection cost down 30%. Policy B: relax credit standards by 20 days, sales up 10%, marginal customers taking an average 150 days with bad debts rising to 2.5% on sales to financially unsound customers, collection expenses up ₹1,00,000. Required rate of return 15%, 360 days a year. (MCQs 1–5, 2 marks each)
answer_points:
==**MCQ 1 — the incremental benefit of Policy A. ICAI's answer: (a) ₹6,24,500.**==
**Credit sales** = ₹3,65,00,000 × 0.90 = **₹3,28,50,000**, unchanged under Policy A because sales do not change.
**Cost of sales at 80%** = ₹2,62,80,000, so **operating profit = ₹65,70,000** on both the current policy and Policy A.
The gain comes from three sources: **a shorter collection period** (two-thirds pay on day 15, the rest on day 80, against a current 120 days) releasing investment in receivables at 15%; **collection costs down 30%** of ₹5,00,000, that is ₹1,50,000; against **the cost of the 2% discount** on the two-thirds who take it.
==**Net: ₹6,24,500 in favour of Policy A.** Note that option (d) offers **₹(−)6,24,500**, the same figure signed the other way — so the direction of the comparison must be stated, not just the magnitude.==

==**MCQ 2 — the incremental benefit of Policy B. ICAI's answer: (d) ₹2,31,444.**==
**Sales rise 10%**, so credit sales become ₹3,28,50,000 × 1.10 = **₹3,61,35,000**, and the incremental contribution is 20% of the incremental credit sales.
Against that: the **marginal customers take 150 days**, so the investment in receivables rises sharply at 15%; **bad debts rise to 2.5%** on the 15% of sales to financially unsound customers; and **collection expenses rise ₹1,00,000**.
==**Net: ₹2,31,444** — positive, but **well below Policy A's ₹6,24,500**, which is what decides MCQ 5.==

==**MCQ 3 — ranking the three inventory proposals by benefit in the form of sales. The method, which is the examinable skill:** annualise each scheme's units, then value them.==
**Proposal 1** — a 12% discount, **1,000 units a quarter = 4,000 units a year**, each sold at 88% of the list price.
**Proposal 2** — the exchange scheme, **4,650 units a year**, each with an average ₹3,500 offset.
**Proposal 3** — the advance-order scheme, **400 machines a month = 4,800 units a year**, with ₹3,000 collected 1½ months before delivery and a ₹4,500 concession.
==**Ranked on annual units the order is 3, 2, 1 — and proposal 3 also collects part of the price in advance, which shortens the cycle as well as moving the stock.** Proposal 1 offers the deepest concession and shifts the fewest units, so it ranks last.==

==**MCQ 4 — the bad debt expense under each policy.** Policy A leaves bad debts unchanged, so the figure is the current one; Policy B raises the rate from 2% to **2.5% on sales to financially unsound customers** and raises sales 10%, so its figure is higher. **The pairing to look for is 'same under A, higher under B'** — ICAI's options are built so that two of them give the same figure twice, which cannot be right for a policy that changes both the rate and the volume.==

==**MCQ 5 — the optimum combination. The logic, and it is the point of the whole case:** take the **best inventory proposal** from MCQ 3 and the **better credit policy** from MCQs 1 and 2. Policy A's ₹6,24,500 beats Policy B's ₹2,31,444, and proposal 3 leads the inventory ranking. ==**The two decisions are independent — one is about how fast stock moves, the other about how fast cash comes back — so the optimum is simply the better of each, not a trade-off between them.**==

==**Why this case is worth working even though it looks like four unrelated plans.** It is the only official question that puts **inventory management and receivables management in the same decision**, and its structure is ICAI's own answer to the §4.1 trade-off table: **inventory and receivables are two of the five components, and a company in trouble has usually got both wrong at once.** The AMPL narrative — piling stocks *and* a 120-day collection period against a 60-day policy — is that table in prose.==

**One technique note.** Every figure in the credit-policy half rests on **₹3,28,50,000 of credit sales (90% of ₹3,65,00,000)**, not on the ₹3,65,00,000 of total sales. Using the gross figure inflates the contribution, the bad debts and the receivables investment together, and produces a plausible-looking wrong answer in every one of the three credit MCQs.

concepts.title: 15–16 Meaning and Objective of Receivables Management, and the Aspects of Management of Debtors
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 direct · RTP 0 · MTP 1 (May 2026 Series I Q3(ii))
understand: ==**The definition** (SM §15): **'Management of receivables refers to planning and controlling of debt owed to the firm from customer on account of credit sales. It is also known as trade credit management.'**==

==**The objective:** **'The basic objective of management of receivables (debtors) is to optimise the return on investment on these assets.'** Note the word — **optimise**, not maximise or minimise.==

==**Why there is an optimum at all, in ICAI's own balance:** **'When large amounts are tied up in receivables, there are chances of bad debts and there will be cost of collection of debts. On the contrary, if the investment in receivables is low, the sales may be restricted, since the competitors may offer more liberal terms. Therefore, management of receivables is an important issue and requires proper policies and their implementation.'**==
==**§16 The three aspects of management of receivables — the list May 2026 asks for by name:**==

==**1. Credit Policy.** **'A balanced credit policy should be determined for effective management of receivables. Decision of Credit standards, Credit terms and collection efforts is included in Credit policy. It involves a trade-off between the profits on additional sales that arise due to credit being extended on the one hand and the cost of carrying those debtors and bad debt losses on the other. This seeks to decide credit period, cash discount and other relevant matters.'**==

==**How credit terms are written, and this is tested in every credit-policy question.** **'The credit period is generally stated in terms of net days. For example, if the firm's credit terms are "net 50". It is expected that customers will repay credit obligations not later than 50 days.'** And the cash discount policy specifies **(a) the rate of cash discount, (b) the cash discount period, and (c) the net credit period** — so **'3/15 net 60' means a 3% discount if the customer pays within 15 days; if he does not avail the offer he must make payment within 60 days.**==

==**2. Credit Analysis.** **'This requires the finance manager to determine as to how risky it is to advance credit to a particular party. This involves due diligence or reputation check of the customers with respect to their credit worthiness.'**==

==**3. Control of Receivable.** **'This requires finance manager to follow up debtors and decide about a suitable credit collection policy. It involves both laying down of credit policies and execution of such policies.'**==

==**The four costs of maintaining receivables, which ICAI prints under aspect 3 and which belong in any answer on the subject:**
**(i) 'The company requires additional funds as resources are blocked in receivables which involves a cost in the form of interest (loan funds) or opportunity cost (own funds)';**
**(ii) 'Administrative costs which include record keeping, investigation of credit worthiness etc.';**
**(iii) 'Collection costs';**
**(iv) 'Defaulting costs'.**==

**One vocabulary point.** ICAI uses **'management of receivables'**, **'management of debtors'** and **'trade credit management'** interchangeably in this unit, and the SM's own chapter summary switches to **'management of sundry debtors'**. All four mean the same thing; do not read a distinction into the change of word.
concepts.example: MTP May 2026 Series I Q3 is a ten-mark question whose part (i) computes the effective cost of a debtors' ageing policy and whose part (ii) simply says 'EXPLAIN three aspects of management of receivables'. Part (ii) is this section verbatim — credit policy, credit analysis and control of receivable — and it is free marks for anyone who has learnt the three headings, sitting at the end of a demanding arithmetical part.
