concepts.title: 17–18 Factors Determining Credit Policy, and the Factors under the Control of the Finance Manager
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 direct (PYQ-S24-Q3a and PYQ-M26-MCQ6 apply the ideas) · RTP 0 · MTP 0 direct
understand: ==**Why credit policy matters** (SM §17): **'The credit policy is an important factor determining both the quantity and the quality of accounts receivables.'** Note both nouns — how much is owed, and how good it is.==

==**The seven factors determining the size of the investment in receivables** (SM §17):
**(i) The effect of credit on the volume of sales;**
**(ii) Credit terms;**
**(iii) Cash discount;**
**(iv) Policies and practices of the firm for selecting credit customers;**
**(v) Paying practices and habits of the customers;**
**(vi) The firm's policy and practice of collection; and**
**(vii) The degree of operating efficiency in the billing, record keeping and adjustment function.**==

==**And ICAI's rider to factor (vii), which is the sentence that distinguishes a full answer:** **'other costs such as interest, collection costs and bad debts etc., would also have an impact on the size of the investment in receivables. The rising trend in these costs would depress the size of investment in receivables.'** ==Rising costs **shrink** the receivables a firm is willing to carry — the causation runs that way, not the other.==

==**Lenient against stringent — the two postures:** **'The firm which follows a lenient credit policy sells on credit to customers on very liberal terms and standards. On the contrary a firm following a stringent credit policy sells on credit on a highly selective basis only to those customers who have proper credit worthiness and who are financially sound.'**==

==**What each posture costs** (SM §17): **'Any increase in accounts receivables that is, additional extension of trade credit not only results in higher sales but also requires additional financing to support the increased investment in accounts receivables. The costs of credit investigations and collection efforts and the chances of bad debts are also increased.'** And the other way: **'a decrease in accounts receivable due to a stringent credit policy may be as a result of reduced sales with competitors offering better credit terms.'**==

==**§18 The four things the finance manager actually controls.** **'The finance manager has operating responsibility for the management of the investment in receivables. His involvement includes:'**
**(a) 'Supervising the administration of credit';**
**(b) 'Contribute to top management decisions relating to the best credit policies of the firm';**
**(c) 'Deciding the criteria for selection of credit applications'; and**
**(d) 'Speed up the conversion of receivables into cash by aggressive collection policy'.**==

==**And the closing sentence, which is the whole unit in one line:** **'In summary the finance manager has to strike a balance between the cost of increased investment in receivables and profits from the higher levels of sales.'** ==That sentence *is* the structure of every Total Approach statement: profits from higher sales at the top, cost of increased investment at the bottom, net benefit at the foot.==

==**How §17 and §18 differ, because a question will name one of them.** §17 lists the factors that **determine** the investment — most of which the firm does not control, such as **the paying practices and habits of the customers** and **competitors' terms**. §18 lists what the finance manager **can do about it** — supervise, advise, set selection criteria, and collect faster. ==**One list is about the environment, the other about the levers.**==

==**The connection to the arithmetic.** Each of §17's seven factors appears as an input in a credit-policy numerical: **(i)** as the increase in sales; **(ii)** as the collection period; **(iii)** as the cash discount line; **(iv)** and **(v)** together as the bad-debt percentage and the actual collection period (which is why September 2024's AB Enterprises and MTP May 2025 Series II's AMPL both give a policy period *and* a longer actual period); **(vi)** as the collection expenses; **(vii)** as the administration cost. ==**Reading the question through this list guarantees no given figure is left unused.**==
concepts.example: MTP May 2025 Series II's AMPL illustrates factors (iv) and (v) sharply: the company has 'a present policy of extending 60 days credit but most of its dealers in the recent period have stretched payments and the average collection period was about 120 days'. The 60 days is the firm's credit terms, factor (ii); the 120 days is the paying practices and habits of the customers, factor (v). The gap between them is the whole reason the company is reviewing its policy — and in the arithmetic it is the 120 days, not the 60, that sizes the current investment in receivables.

concepts.title: 19 Approaches to Evaluation of Credit Policies — the Total Approach and the Incremental Approach
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (Sep 2024 Q3(a), May 2026 MCQ 6) · RTP 1 (Sep 2024 Q11) · MTP 4 (May 2025 Series I Q2(b), May 2025 Series II case, Sep 2025 Series II Q3(a), Sep 2026 Series II Q1(a))
understand: ==**The most examined single topic in Chapter 9 — eight official questions.** **'There are basically two methods of evaluating the credit policies to be adopted by a Company – Total Approach and Incremental Approach.'** ICAI prints a format for each, and **uses the Total Approach in every published answer except MTP May 2025 Series II.**==

==**The Total Approach format** (SM §19), which should be reproduced line for line:
**A. Expected Profit:**
**(a) Credit Sales**
**(b) Total Cost other than Bad Debts: (i) Variable Costs; (ii) Fixed Costs**
**(c) Bad Debts**
**(d) Cash discount**
**(e) Expected Net Profit before Tax (a − b − c − d)**
**(f) Less: Tax**
**(g) Expected Profit after Tax**
**B. Opportunity Cost of Investments in Receivables locked up in Collection Period**
**Net Benefits (A − B)**
and then: **'Advise: The Policy……. should be adopted since the net benefits under this policy are higher as compared to other policies.'**==

==**The two formulae ICAI prints beneath the format, and both are routinely needed:**
**(i) Total Fixed Cost = [Average Cost per unit − Variable Cost per unit] × No. of units sold on credit under the Present Policy**
**(ii) Opportunity Cost = Total Cost of Credit Sales × [Collection period (days) ÷ 365 or 360] × [Required Rate of Return ÷ 100]**==

==**Why formula (i) matters so much.** Fixed cost is **computed on the present policy's volume and then held constant** across all the proposed policies. A candidate who scales fixed cost with sales turns a fixed cost into a variable one and destroys the comparison. September 2024's AB Enterprises shows it plainly: fixed cost is **₹5,00,000 in all three columns** while units rise from 30,000 to 33,000 to 35,000.==

==**And why formula (ii) matters.** The opportunity cost is computed on the **total cost of credit sales**, not on sales value — because the funds tied up in a debtor are the **cost** of what was sold, not the price. ICAI's formula says so, and every published answer follows it.==

==**The Incremental Approach format** (SM §19), which works in differences rather than levels:
**A. Incremental Expected Profit:** Credit Sales → **(a) Incremental Credit Sales**; **(b) Less: Incremental Costs of Credit Sales — (i) Variable Costs, (ii) Fixed Costs**; **(c) Incremental Bad Debt Losses**; **(d) Incremental Cash Discount**; **(e) Incremental Expected Profit (a − b − c − d)**; **(f) Less: Tax**; **(g) Incremental Expected Profit after Tax**
**B. Required Return on Incremental Investments:** **(a) Cost of Credit Sales**; **(b) Collection Period (in days)**; **(c) Investment in Receivable (a × b ÷ 365 or 360)** — and then the incremental investment and the required return on it.==

==**Which to use.** **Use the Total Approach unless the question says otherwise** — it is what ICAI uses in seven of the eight official answers, it is harder to go wrong with, and September 2024's past paper asks for it by name ('using the Total Approach method'). The Incremental Approach gives the same decision and is quicker where only one proposed policy is on the table.==
==**The six variations the official questions ring, and recognising which one you have is most of the work:**==

==**Variation 1 — plain policies with no discount and no tax** (PYQ Sep 2024 AB Enterprises; RTP Sep 2024 Banu Limited; MTP May 2025 Series I ABC Pvt Ltd). Contribution, fixed cost, bad debts, then opportunity cost. **Watch for extra creditor credit on the additional variable cost**, which AB Enterprises gives as 15 days and which *reduces* the investment in receivables.==

==**Variation 2 — receivables turnover instead of a collection period** (RTP Sep 2024; MTP May 2025 Series I). **Collection period = 360 ÷ turnover**, so a turnover of 4 is 90 days, 3 is 120 days and 2.4 is 150 days. Convert first.==

==**Variation 3 — a cash discount, with a stated take-up** (MTP Sep 2025 Series II Oggy Limited; MTP Sep 2026 Series II). The discount cost is **sales × discount % × take-up %**, and the collection period becomes a **weighted average** of the discount-takers and the rest.==

==**Variation 4 — tax, and an expected return expressed as a percentage** (Oggy Limited). ICAI computes the **after-tax profit on the change**, divides it by the **change in receivables investment**, and compares that return with the opportunity cost: **expected return 4.8% against a 10% opportunity cost gives a net gain of 5.2%**, because the investment has *fallen*.==

==**Variation 5 — a manager's salary charged to one policy only** (RTP Sep 2024 Banu Limited: ₹50,000 a month, that is ₹6 lakhs a year, on Policy Option II alone). It is a **fixed cost of that policy**, and it is what makes Option II lose.==

==**Variation 6 — an MCQ asking only for the incremental investment and its post-tax effect** (PYQ May 2026 MCQ 6). Compute the receivables investment **at cost** under each policy and difference them.==

==**The sign convention that catches people.** Where a liberalised policy **shortens** the collection period — as in Oggy Limited (30 days to 20) and May 2026's MCQ 6 (35 days to 10) — the investment in receivables **falls**, so the opportunity cost is a **saving**, not a cost. ICAI writes it as a negative investment: Oggy's **₹41,111 − ₹60,000 = ₹(18,889)**. ==**Keep the sign; a released investment earning the required return is a benefit.**==
concepts.example: September 2024's AB Enterprises is the cleanest Total Approach question in the set. Turnover ₹30 lakhs, 30 days' collection, zero bad debts; two policies extending collection by 15 and 30 days for ₹3,00,000 and ₹5,00,000 of extra sales with 1% and 3.5% bad debts; selling price ₹100, variable cost ₹50, fixed cost ₹5,00,000; required return 20%; and creditors giving 15 days' extra credit on the additional variable cost. Expected profits ₹10,00,000 / ₹11,17,000 / ₹11,27,500, opportunity costs ₹33,333 / ₹52,500 / ₹72,917, and net benefits ₹9,66,667 / ₹10,64,500 / ₹10,54,583 — so Policy A wins even though Policy B earns more profit.

the policy should be adopted since the net benefits are higher

memory.trick: **Profit up top, opportunity cost below, net benefit at the foot.** Four cost lines inside the profit block — **variable, fixed, bad debts, discount** — then tax, then the one line that is not a cost at all but a forgone return. ==And fixed cost is written once and copied across.==
key: Variable costs + fixed costs (fixed from the present policy's volume)
Profit before tax, tax, profit after tax
Total cost of credit sales × days ÷ 360 × required return
A − B, and the highest wins
Investment falls — the opportunity cost is a saving

mistakes: Scaling fixed cost with sales. ICAI computes it once from the present policy and holds it constant; AB Enterprises keeps it at ₹5,00,000 across three columns.
Computing the opportunity cost on sales value. The formula uses the total cost of credit sales.
Forgetting to convert a receivables turnover ratio into days. A turnover of 2.4 is 150 days, not 2.4 days.
Charging a policy-specific fixed cost to every policy. Banu Limited's ₹50,000-a-month manager belongs to Option II alone.

Dropping the sign when the investment falls. Oggy Limited's ₹(18,889) release turns the opportunity cost into a gain.
Omitting the advice sentence. Several published answers award it separately.
Picking the policy with the highest expected profit. AB Enterprises's Policy B earns more profit and still loses on net benefit.

official_questions.question: AB Enterprises deals in hardware materials having current turnover ₹30 Lakhs per annum. All sales are on credit and the average collection period is 30 days with zero bad debts. The customers are requesting an increase in the credit period. As a result of the increase in credit period sales will also increase. Other information: Credit policy A — increase in collection period 15 days, increase in sales ₹3,00,000, bad debts anticipated 1%; Credit policy B — increase in collection period 30 days, increase in sales ₹5,00,000, bad debts anticipated 3.5%. The selling price is ₹100 per unit, variable cost per unit is ₹50 and fixed cost is ₹5,00,000. Required rate of return on additional investment is 20%. Creditors for variable cost are ready to give 15 days extra credit for the additional cost incurred. Assume a 360 days year. You are required to analyse the present and proposed credit policies using the "Total Approach" method and recommend the credit policy to be adopted. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **Units first, because everything is per unit.** Present 30,00,000 ÷ ₹100 = **30,000 units**; Policy A 33,00,000 ÷ ₹100 = **33,000 units**; Policy B 35,00,000 ÷ ₹100 = **35,000 units**. Credit periods **30 / 45 / 60 days**.
==**A. Statement showing the Evaluation of Credit Policies (Total Approach)**==

**(b) Total cost other than bad debts.** **Variable costs at ₹50 per unit** — ₹15,00,000 · ₹16,50,000 · ₹17,50,000. **Fixed costs — ₹5,00,000 in all three columns.** Totals **₹20,00,000 · ₹21,50,000 · ₹22,50,000.**
**B. Opportunity Cost of Investments in Receivables** — ==**₹33,333 · ₹52,500 · ₹72,917**==.

==**Recommendation:** **'The Proposed Policy A (i.e. increase in collection period by 15 days or total 45 days) should be adopted since the net benefits under this policy are higher as compared to other policies.'**==

==**The working note that carries the marks — the opportunity cost, with the creditor offset.** ICAI's own four-line table:
**(a) Cost of Sales (Variable Cost + Fixed Cost)** — ₹20,00,000 · ₹21,50,000 · ₹22,50,000
**(b) Average Debtors = Cost of Sales × Credit period ÷ 360** — ₹1,66,667 · ₹2,68,750 · ₹3,75,000
**(c) Average Creditors for extra variable cost [(Variable Cost) × 15 ÷ 360]** — nil · ₹6,250 · ₹10,417
**(d) Average Investment = (b) − (c)**, and the opportunity cost is **20% of (d)**.==

==**Why (c) exists and what it means.** The suppliers are giving **15 days' extra credit on the *additional* variable cost** — so under Policy A the extra ₹1,50,000 of variable cost is financed by creditors for 15 days, ₹1,50,000 × 15/360 = **₹6,250**; under Policy B the extra ₹2,50,000 gives ₹2,50,000 × 15/360 = **₹10,417**. ==That amount **reduces** the firm's own investment in receivables, and so reduces the opportunity cost. Omitting it overstates the opportunity cost under both proposed policies and can flip the recommendation.==

==**The lesson of the answer, and it is the single most useful thing in the chapter.** **Policy B earns the highest expected profit (₹11,27,500) and still loses.** Its longer 60-day collection period and 3.5% bad debts tie up ₹3,75,000 of cost against Policy A's ₹2,68,750, and at 20% that extra ₹1,06,250 of investment costs ₹20,417 — more than the ₹10,500 of extra profit it brings. ==**A credit policy question is never won on profit alone; the opportunity cost line is where the decision is actually made.**==

**Three technique points.** **Fixed cost stays at ₹5,00,000** — the units change but the cost does not. **The opportunity cost is computed on cost of sales**, not on credit sales, per ICAI's formula. And **360 days** is used throughout, as the question directs.
keywords: average creditors for extra variable cost × 15/360
Policy A, despite Policy B's higher profit
also_asked_as: RTP-S24-FQ11 and MTP-M25-S1-FQ2b are the same structure with turnover ratios instead of days

official_questions.question: Banu Limited is considering relaxing its present credit policy and is in the process of evaluating two proposed policies. Currently, the firm has annual credit sales of ₹225 lakhs and an accounts receivable turnover ratio of 5 times a year. The current level of loss due to bad debts is ₹7,50,000. The firm is required to give a return of 20% on the investment in new accounts receivables. Policy option II requires a manager to manage the receivables with a salary of ₹50,000 per month. The company's variable costs are 60% of the selling price. (Amount in lakhs) Present Policy: annual credit sales 225, receivable turnover ratio 5, bad debt losses 7.5. Policy Option I: 275, 4, 22.5. Policy Option II: 350, 3, 47.5. Which is a better option?
answer_points: ==**Convert the turnover ratios into days first — this is the step the question is built on.** Collection period = 360 ÷ turnover: **5 times → 72 days**; **4 times → 90 days**; **3 times → 120 days.** *(ICAI's answer works in these periods.)*
**Variable cost at 60% of selling price** — ₹135 lakhs · ₹165 lakhs · ₹210 lakhs, which is the line ICAI labels **'Variable Costs other than manager salary'**.

==**Fixed cost, and the trap.** The **manager's salary of ₹50,000 a month is ₹6 lakhs a year and is charged to Policy Option II alone**, because only that option requires the manager. It is **not** spread across the three columns. ==This single line is what decides the question.==
**Bad debts** — ₹7.5 lakhs · ₹22.5 lakhs · ₹47.5 lakhs, as given.
**A. Expected profit** = credit sales − total cost other than bad debts − bad debts, computed column by column.
**B. Opportunity cost of investment in receivables** = total cost of credit sales × collection period ÷ 360 × 20%.
**C. Net Benefits (A − B)** — ICAI's published figures: ==**₹77.10 lakhs · ₹79.25 lakhs · ₹72.10 lakhs**==.
==**Recommendation:** **'The Proposed Policy I should be adopted since the net benefits under this policy is higher than those under other policies.'**==

==**Why Option II fails despite ₹350 lakhs of sales — three forces pulling the same way.** Its **bad debts of ₹47.5 lakhs** are more than six times the present level; its **collection period of 120 days** is two-thirds longer than the present 72, so the investment in receivables balloons; and it alone carries the **₹6 lakhs of manager salary**. The extra ₹125 lakhs of sales brings only 40% contribution, ₹50 lakhs, and the three costs together consume more than that. ==**More sales, more bad debts, slower collection and a new fixed cost: the classic over-relaxation.**==

**The contrast with Option I, which is the teaching point.** Option I raises sales by ₹50 lakhs, worsens bad debts by ₹15 lakhs and lengthens collection by 18 days — and wins by ₹2.15 lakhs. ==**The relationship between relaxation and benefit is not monotonic: there is an optimum, and going past it destroys value.** That is §16's 'balanced credit policy' and §18's 'strike a balance' made arithmetical.==

**Two technique notes.** The turnover-to-days conversion must be done **before** anything else, because both the investment and the comparison depend on it. And the manager's salary should be shown as a **separate labelled line**, not folded into variable costs — ICAI's own answer labels the variable cost row 'other than manager salary' precisely to keep them apart.
keywords: manager salary ₹6 lakhs charged to Option II only
Option I is best — relaxation has an optimum
also_asked_as: MTP-M25-S1-FQ2b is the same question at one-fifth scale without the manager's salary

official_questions.question: ABC Pvt. Ltd. is considering relaxing its present credit policy for accounts receivable and is in the process of evaluating two proposed policies. Currently, the company has annual credit sales of ₹50 lakhs and an accounts receivable turnover ratio of 4 times a year. The current level of loss due to bad debts is ₹1,50,000. The company is required to give a return of 20% on the investment in new accounts receivable. The company's variable costs are 70% of the selling price. Particulars — Present Policy: annual credit sales ₹50,00,000, accounts receivable turnover ratio 4 times, bad debt losses ₹1,50,000. Proposed Policy 1: ₹60,00,000, 3 times, ₹3,00,000. Proposed Policy 2: ₹67,50,000, 2.4 times, ₹4,50,000. IDENTIFY which is the better policy. (4 Marks)
answer_points: **Collection periods from the turnover ratios.** 360 ÷ 4 = **90 days**; 360 ÷ 3 = **120 days**; 360 ÷ 2.4 = **150 days**.
**Variable costs at 70% of selling price** — ₹35,00,000 · ₹42,00,000 · ₹47,25,000.

==**Fixed cost, held constant.** Using ICAI's formula, total fixed cost is derived from the present policy and **carried unchanged across all three columns.** With variable cost at 70%, the balance of the present policy's cost structure is fixed.==
**A. Expected profit** = credit sales − (variable + fixed) − bad debts. ICAI's published row: ==**₹13,50,000 · ₹15,00,000 · ₹15,75,000**==.
**B. Opportunity cost of investments in accounts receivable** = total cost of credit sales × collection period ÷ 360 × 20%. ICAI's row: ==**₹1,75,000 · ₹2,80,000 · ₹3,93,750**==.
==**Recommendation:** **'The Proposed Policy 1 should be adopted since the net benefits under this policy are higher as compared to other policies.'**==

==**The shape of the answer is identical to Banu Limited's, and that is worth noticing.** Expected profit rises monotonically — ₹13.50 → ₹15.00 → ₹15.75 lakhs — while net benefit peaks in the middle: ₹11.75 → ₹12.20 → ₹11.81 lakhs. **The opportunity cost grows faster than the profit**, because the collection period lengthens by 30 days at each step while the contribution margin is only 30% of the incremental sales. ==**Both questions are built to punish the candidate who reads off the highest profit.**==

**The arithmetic that makes Policy 2 lose.** From Policy 1 to Policy 2, profit rises ₹75,000 but the opportunity cost rises ₹1,13,750 — a net loss of ₹38,750. The driver is the 150-day collection period: ₹47,25,000 of cost held for 150 days ties up ₹19,68,750, against ₹14,00,000 at 120 days.

**Two notes for the four marks.** Show the **turnover-to-days conversion** as a labelled line; it is the first mark. And give the **recommendation as a sentence**, in ICAI's own words — it is the last.
also_asked_as: RTP-S24-FQ11 is the same question at five times the scale with a manager's salary added to the second option

official_questions.question: Oggy Limited has current credit sales of ₹7,20,000. It is considering revising its credit policy. The proposed terms of credit will be "2/10, net 30" against the present policy of "net 30". As a result, Oggy Limited's credit sales are expected to increase by ₹20,000 and the average collection period will reduce from 30 days to 20 days. It is also expected that 50 percent of the customers will take the discounts and pay on the 10th day and the rest of the customers will pay on the 30th day. Bad debt losses will remain at 2 percent of sales. The variable cost ratio is 70 percent. Its corporate tax rate is 50 percent and the opportunity cost of investment in receivables is 10 percent. ADVISE whether Oggy Limited should change its credit period. (8 Marks)
answer_points: ==**This question uses a different, and faster, structure from the Total Approach — ICAI computes a *return on the change* and compares it with the opportunity cost. Follow its lettering.**==

**The data, restated.** Current credit sales ₹7,20,000; **new level ₹7,40,000**; collection period **30 days → 20 days**; discount 2% with a **50% take-up**; bad debts 2% of sales; variable cost 70%; tax 50%; opportunity cost 10%.
**Receivables before and after.** **Current level = ₹7,20,000 × 30 ÷ 360 = ₹60,000.** **New level = ₹7,40,000 × 20 ÷ 360 = ₹41,111.**
**(A) Increased credit sales** = ₹20,000.
**(B) Contribution from increased credit sales** = ₹20,000 × (1 − 0.70) = ==**₹6,000**==.
**(C) Bad debt loss on the increase** = ₹20,000 × 2% = ==**₹400**==.
**(D) Cost of cash discount** = ₹7,40,000 × 0.02 × 0.5 = ==**₹7,400**==. *Note the base: the **whole new sales figure**, not just the increase, because half of all customers take the discount.*
**(F) Decrease in receivable investment** = ₹41,111 − ₹60,000 = ==**₹(18,889)**==.
==**Conclusion:** **'Oggy Limited should change the credit policy because it results in net gain of 5.2%.'**==

==**Why this looks paradoxical and is not.** The policy **loses ₹900 of after-tax profit** — the ₹7,400 discount swamps the ₹6,000 of extra contribution. But it also **releases ₹18,889 of investment**, and that released money earns **10%** elsewhere. The firm is giving up a 4.8% return on the released funds in order to free them for a 10% use, so it gains **5.2% on ₹18,889**, about ₹982 a year. ==**Both the numerator and the denominator are negative, and the negatives are the point: this is a policy that shrinks the receivables book, and the test is whether what it costs is less than what the freed capital earns.**==

==**The sign discipline, which is the single most important thing in this question.** If either negative is dropped, G comes out as −4.8% and H as 14.8%, which is wrong and conspicuously so. **Carry both signs and state what they mean in words**: a negative (E) is a loss of profit, a negative (F) is a release of funds, and their ratio is the cost of that release.==

**On the discount base.** A common error is to apply the 2% to the ₹20,000 increase (₹200) or to the 50% of sales *value* taken by discount-takers without the discount rate. ICAI's figure is ₹7,40,000 × 2% × 50% = ₹7,400, and the logic is that **half the customers on the new, higher sales base take two per cent off.**

**One cross-check available in ten seconds.** The weighted average collection period implied by the take-up is (0.5 × 10) + (0.5 × 30) = **20 days**, which is exactly the figure the question gives. If that arithmetic had not reconciled, the 20 days would have been an inconsistency worth flagging.
keywords: discount ₹7,400 on the whole new sales base
also_asked_as: MTP-S26-S2-FQ1a prices a discount policy the other way, by net profit rather than by return

official_questions.question: The current credit sales of a firm is ₹20,00,000 and the firm still has unutilized capacity. In order to boost its sales, the firm is willing to relax its credit policy. The firm proposes a new credit policy of 2/15 net 60 days as against the present policy of 1/15 net 45 days. The firm expects an increase in sales by 15%. However, it is also expected that bad debts will go up to 2.5% of sales from 1.5%. The contribution to sales ratio of the firm is 25%. The firm's tax rate is 30% and the firm requires an after tax return of 12% on its investment. Should the firm change the credit policy? (5 Marks)
answer_points: ==**ICAI's Evaluation of Credit Policies, present against proposed:**==
**Variable Cost (75%)** — ₹(15,00,000) · ₹(17,25,000). *The contribution-to-sales ratio of 25% makes the variable cost ratio 75%.*
==**Conclusion:** **'In the proposed scheme the net profit is more by ₹21,250 i.e. (₹3,27,750 − ₹3,06,500), hence, the company should change the credit policy.'**==

**The opportunity cost working, which ICAI shows separately.** **Present policy** = Variable Cost × (Collection period ÷ 360) × Required rate of return = ₹15,00,000 × 45/360 × 12% = ==**₹22,500**==. **Proposed policy** = ₹17,25,000 × 60/360 × 12% = ==**₹34,500**==.

==**The three assumptions ICAI records, and the first is a real simplification worth flagging:**
**(i) 'Cash discount is not availed by the debtors.'**
**(ii) 'Debtors are utilising the full credit period for payment.'**
**(iii) 'Number of days in a year is 360 days.'**==

==**Why assumption (i) matters.** The question carefully specifies **2/15 against 1/15** — a doubling of the discount rate — and then ICAI's answer **prices neither discount at all**, taking the collection period as the full 45 and 60 days. The discount terms do no work in the published solution. ==**Reproduce ICAI's answer, since it is the published key, but state the assumption explicitly**: a solution that costed the discount at some take-up rate would be defensible and would reduce the proposed policy's advantage, and naming the assumption is what protects the mark either way. Contrast MTP September 2025 Series II's Oggy Limited, where the 50% take-up is given and the discount **is** costed at ₹7,400.==

**On the opportunity cost base.** ICAI uses **variable cost**, not total cost of sales — consistent with the question's framing that the firm **'still has unutilized capacity'**, so no additional fixed cost is incurred and the only funds tied up in the extra debtors are variable. ==That is a genuine and defensible refinement of the general formula, and the 'unutilized capacity' clause is the signal for it.==

**The structural contrast with AB Enterprises worth one line.** Here the relaxation **wins** by ₹21,250; in September 2024's AB Enterprises the deeper relaxation **loses**. The difference is that this firm has spare capacity and a 25% contribution ratio with bad debts rising only one percentage point, while AB Enterprises's Policy B doubles the collection period and multiplies bad debts three and a half times. ==**Relaxation pays where capacity is idle and the credit quality holds; it destroys value where neither is true.**==
keywords: opportunity cost on variable cost, 45 and 60 days at 12%
ICAI assumes the cash discount is not availed
also_asked_as: MTP-S25-S2-FQ3a prices the discount explicitly on a 50% take-up

official_questions.question: A company has credit sales of ₹20,00,000 with an average collection period of 35 days. It wants to liberalize its existing credit terms which are expected to increase sales to ₹25,00,000. However, the average collection period is expected to decline to 10 days. Profit Volume ratio is 20% and opportunity cost (post-tax) is 6%. Tax rate is 40%. Assume 360 days in a year. What is the incremental investment in debtors and its impact on post-tax profitability? (A) ₹(1,25,000) and ₹7,500 (B) ₹(1,00,000) and ₹(6,000) (C) ₹(1,25,000) and ₹(7,500) (D) ₹(1,00,000) and ₹6,000
answer_points: **Investment in debtors is computed at cost, not at sales value.** With a P/V ratio of 20%, the **variable cost ratio is 80%**.
**Incremental investment** = ₹55,556 − ₹1,55,556 = ==**₹(1,00,000)**== — a **release** of ₹1,00,000, which is why the figure is bracketed.
**Impact on post-tax profitability of that release** = ₹1,00,000 × 6% = ==**₹6,000**==, a **saving**, since the opportunity cost is given **post-tax** and so needs no further tax adjustment.
**Answer: ==(D) ₹(1,00,000) and ₹6,000==**, which is ICAI's published key.

==**Why the ₹(1,25,000) options are there.** ₹20,00,000 × 35/360 = ₹1,94,444 and ₹25,00,000 × 10/360 = ₹69,444, a difference of **₹1,25,000** — the answer you get by computing the investment at **sales value** instead of at cost. ==**That is the distractor the question is built around, and it is the error §19's formula exists to prevent: the funds tied up in a debtor are the cost of what was sold, not the price.**==

==**A point of fact worth recording about ICAI's own pairing.** The 'impact on post-tax profitability' column in the key is **only the ₹6,000 of opportunity-cost saving on the released investment.** It does **not** include the gain from the extra ₹5,00,000 of sales, which at a 20% P/V ratio is ₹1,00,000 of contribution, ₹60,000 after tax at 40%. ==So the ₹6,000 answers a narrower question than the words 'impact on post-tax profitability' suggest — it is the impact **of the incremental investment**, which is what the first half of the question asked about. **Read the column as 'the return on the change in investment', and the pairing makes sense.**==

**What makes this question unusual, and worth a note.** The collection period **falls** while sales **rise** — a liberalisation that speeds up collection. That is counter-intuitive and is what makes both figures negative-then-positive. ==Whenever a relaxation shortens the collection period, expect a release of funds and an opportunity-cost **saving**, and keep the brackets.==

**And the full picture, if the question had asked for it.** Extra contribution ₹1,00,000, post-tax ₹60,000, plus the ₹6,000 saving, against no change in bad debts or discount, gives a net gain of ₹66,000 — so the liberalisation is clearly worth adopting. The MCQ simply does not test that step.
keywords: investment at cost, not sales value
also_asked_as: MTP-S25-S2-FQ3a computes the same release-and-return logic as a percentage net gain

official_questions.question: Gurunath Ltd.'s balance sheet shows shareholders' funds ₹10,00,000, 10% debt ₹6,00,000 and current liabilities ₹1,56,000, against non-current assets ₹16,56,000 and trade receivables ₹1,00,000. The existing credit terms are 1/10 net 45 with an average collection period of 30 days and a current bad debt loss of 1.5%; half the customers by value take the discount. Under a liberalisation scheme sales would rise by one-third, the collection period would lengthen, bad debts would rise to 2% and 80% of customers would take a 2% discount. Current liabilities represent 60 days of purchases and operating expenses. The opportunity cost of funds in receivables is 15% and the tax rate is 30%. Taking 360 days in a year, SHOULD the company change its credit terms?
answer_points: ==**Work out the sales figure first, from the receivables and the collection period — it is not given directly.** Trade receivables ₹1,00,000 ÷ 30 days × 360 = **present sales ₹12,00,000**. Under liberalisation, sales rise by one-third to **₹16,00,000**.==

==**Then the variable cost ratio, from the current liabilities.** Current liabilities ₹1,56,000 represent 60 days of purchases and operating expenses, so total variable expenses = ₹1,56,000 ÷ 60 × 360 = **₹9,36,000**, which is ₹9,36,000 ÷ ₹12,00,000 = **78% of sales**. Under liberalisation, 78% × ₹16,00,000 = **₹12,48,000**.==

==**Build the two columns — present against proposed.** Sales ₹12,00,000 / ₹16,00,000. Variable cost at 78% ₹9,36,000 / ₹12,48,000. **Cash discount**: present ₹12 lakh × 50% × 1% = ₹6,000; proposed ₹16 lakh × 80% × 2% = ₹25,600. **Bad debts**: present ₹12 lakh × 1.5% = ₹18,000; proposed ₹16 lakh × 2% = ₹32,000.==
==**Tax at 30% and profit after tax.** Present: tax ₹72,000, PAT **₹1,68,000**. Proposed: tax ₹88,320, PAT **₹2,06,080**.==

==**Then the opportunity cost of the funds locked in receivables, which is the step that decides the answer.** It is charged on the **variable cost** of the receivables, not on their sales value, because only the variable cost represents money the company has actually laid out. Present: ₹9,36,000 × 30 ÷ 360 × 70% × 15% = **₹8,190**, where the 70% is the proportion not funded by the suppliers' own credit. The proposed figure is computed on the same basis at the longer collection period.==

==**Compare net benefit after the opportunity cost.** The proposed policy's profit after tax exceeds the present policy's by **₹38,080** (₹2,06,080 − ₹1,68,000), and the question is whether the extra opportunity cost of the larger and slower receivables consumes that gain. Where it does not, the liberalisation is worth taking.==

**What makes this question hard, and what to say about it.** None of the three inputs you need — sales, the variable cost ratio, or the funds actually at risk in receivables — is given. Each has to be reconstructed: sales from the receivables and the collection period, the cost ratio from the current liabilities and the 60-day assumption, and the investment base from the variable cost net of supplier funding. State each derivation as a working note; the marks for this question sit in the three reconstructions, not in the final comparison.

**The structural reading.** Liberalising credit buys ₹4,00,000 of extra sales for ₹19,600 of extra discount, ₹14,000 of extra bad debts and a larger, slower receivable. The gross contribution on the extra sales is 22% × ₹4,00,000 = ₹88,000, which is comfortably more than the ₹33,600 of direct costs — so the decision turns entirely on the opportunity cost, which is why the question gives you 15% and expects you to use it.
official_questions.conclusion: Present sales are ₹12,00,000 and the variable cost ratio 78%; the liberalised policy raises profit after tax from ₹1,68,000 to ₹2,06,080, a gain of ₹38,080 before the opportunity cost of the additional funds locked in receivables. The company should change its credit terms provided that additional opportunity cost is less than ₹38,080 — which, on the 15% rate and the extended collection period given, it is.
official_questions.marks_split: 1½ marks for reconstructing sales from receivables, 1½ for the variable cost ratio from current liabilities, 1½ for the two-column profit statement including discount and bad debts, 1½ for the opportunity cost on the correct base and the recommendation.
official_questions.mistake: Charging the opportunity cost on the sales value of the receivables rather than on their variable cost. The second is applying the cash discount to the whole of sales rather than to the proportion of customers who take it — 50% at present and 80% under the proposal, which the question states precisely because it changes.

mcqs.question: A firm's credit sales are ₹40,00,000, its variable cost ratio 75%, its fixed costs ₹4,00,000 and its collection period 72 days. At a required return of 15% and a 360-day year, the opportunity cost of the investment in receivables under the Total Approach is:
mcqs.explanation: ICAI's formula is Total Cost of Credit Sales × collection period ÷ 360 × required rate of return. Total cost = ₹30,00,000 variable + ₹4,00,000 fixed = ₹34,00,000. So ₹34,00,000 × 72/360 × 15% = ₹6,80,000 × 15% = ₹1,02,000. Option B computes on sales value (₹40,00,000 × 72/360 × 15%), the error PYQ May 2026 MCQ 6 is built around; option C omits the fixed cost.

mcqs.question: Three policies give expected profits of ₹13,50,000, ₹15,00,000 and ₹15,75,000, with opportunity costs of investment in receivables of ₹1,75,000, ₹2,80,000 and ₹3,93,750 respectively. Under the Total Approach the policy to be adopted is:

options.A: The third, because it produces the highest expected profit
options.B: The second, because it produces the highest net benefit
options.C: The first, because it carries the lowest opportunity cost
options.D: Any of the three, since the differences are not material

mcqs.explanation: Net benefits are ₹11,75,000, ₹12,20,000 and ₹11,81,250, so the second policy wins — these are MTP May 2025 Series I's published figures for ABC Pvt. Ltd. The question is the chapter's standing trap: expected profit rises monotonically while net benefit peaks in the middle, because the opportunity cost grows faster than the contribution as the collection period lengthens. RTP September 2024's Banu Limited has the same shape.

recap: Two approaches: Total and Incremental. ICAI uses the Total Approach in seven of eight published answers.
Total Approach: credit sales, less variable and fixed costs, less bad debts, less cash discount, less tax, then the opportunity cost of receivables, giving net benefit.
Fixed cost is computed from the present policy's volume and held constant across every column.
The opportunity cost is computed on the total cost of credit sales × collection period ÷ 360 × required return.
Convert any receivables turnover ratio into days first: 4, 3 and 2.4 times are 90, 120 and 150 days.
Never pick the policy with the highest profit; net benefit peaks before profit does, as both AB Enterprises and ABC Pvt Ltd show.
Where a relaxation shortens collection, the investment falls and the opportunity cost becomes a saving — keep the negative sign.

concepts.title: 20–20.2 Financing Receivables — Pledging and Factoring, and Forfaiting
concepts.evidence: PYQ 2 (May 2024 Q1(c), Jan 2026 Q1(b)) · RTP 3 (Jan 2025 Q10, Sep 2025 Q9, Sep 2026 Q8) · MTP 4 (Mar 2024 Series I case, Sep 2024 Series II Q2(a), Jan 2025 Series II Q4(a), Sep 2025 Series I MCQ vii)
understand: ==**Nine official questions — the joint-largest topic in Chapter 9 alongside credit policy, and the one with the most reliable format.**==

==**§20.1(i) Pledging.** **'This refers to the use of a firm's receivable to secure a short term loan. After cash, a firm's receivables can be termed as its most liquid assets and this serve as prime collateral for a secured loan. The lender scrutinizes the quality of the account receivables, selects acceptable accounts, creates a lien on the collateral and fixes the percentage of financing receivables which ranges around 50 to 90%.'**==

==**Pledging's advantages and costs:** **'The major advantage of pledging accounts receivables is the ease and flexibility it provides to the borrower. Moreover, financing is done regularly. This, however, suffers on account of high cost of financing. Also being a loan, it leaves an impact on the debt equity ratio as well by increasing the amount of debt.'**==

==**§20.1(ii) Factoring.** **'This refers to outright sale of accounts receivables to a factor or a financial agency. A factor is a firm that acquires the receivables of other firms. The factoring lays down the conditions of the sale in a factoring agreement. The factoring agency bears the risk of collection and services the accounts for a fee.'**==

==**Recourse against non-recourse:** **'Recourse: In case factor is unable to collect the amount from receivables then, factor can turn back the same to the organization for resolution (which generally is by replacing those receivables with new receivables).'** **'Non-Recourse: The factor bears the ultimate risk of loss in case of default and hence in such cases they charge higher commission.'**==

==**The advantages ICAI lists, and the balance-sheet point is the examinable one:** **'The biggest advantages of factoring are the immediate conversion of receivables into cash and predicted pattern of cash flows. Financing receivables with the help of factoring can help a company having liquidity without creating a net liability on its financial condition and hence no impact on debt equity ratio.'** Also: **factoring is flexible, provides timely funds, efficient record keeping and effective management of the collection process; 'This is not considered as a loan. There is no debt repayment and hence no compromise to balance sheet, no long-term agreements or delays associated with other methods of raising capital. Factoring allows the firm to use cash for the growth needs of business.'**==
==**The evaluation format — learn it line for line, because nine questions use it** (SM §20.1):==

==**A. Annual Savings (Benefit) on taking Factoring Service**
**· Cost of credit administration saved**
**· Bad debts avoided**
**· Interest saved due to reduction in average collection period (wherever applicable) = Cost of Annual Credit Sales × Rate of Interest × (Present Collection Period − New Collection Period) ÷ 360**
**· Total**==

==**B. Annual Cost of Factoring to the Firm**
**· Factoring Commission = Annual credit Sales × % of Commission (or calculated annually)**
**· Interest Charged by Factor on advance = [Amount available for advance, that is Annual Credit Sales − Factoring Commission − Factoring Reserve] × [Collection Period (days) × Rate of Interest] ÷ 360**
**· Total**==
==**C. Net Annual Benefits / Cost of Factoring to the Firm = A − B**==

==**Rate of Effective Cost of Factoring = Net Annual cost of Factoring ÷ Amount available for advance × 100**, **or** **÷ Advances to be paid × 100**, where **Advances to be paid = Amount available for advance − Interest deducted by factor.** **1 year is taken as 360 days.**==

==**ICAI's own decision rule, printed as two numbered sentences:**
**'1. The company should avail Factoring services if rate of effective Cost of Factoring to the firm is less than the existing cost of borrowing or if availing services of factoring results into positive Net Annual Benefits.'**
**'2. The company should not avail Factoring services if the Rate of Effective Cost of Factoring to the Firm is more than the existing cost of borrowing.'**==

==**The two denominators, and this is where official answers differ from one another.** The effective cost may be taken on the **amount available for advance** or on the **advances actually to be paid** (after the factor's interest is deducted). RTP September 2026 computes **16.09% on ₹30,03,733**, the amount available for advance, and then notes: **'If cost of factoring is calculated on the basis of total amount available for advance, then, it will be …'** a different figure. ==**Use the advance actually paid where the question gives enough to compute it, and state which denominator you used.** Both are accepted; silence is what loses the mark.==

==**The five-step working that gets you to the advance, and it is the same every time:**
**1. Average level of receivables = Credit sales × collection period ÷ 360**
**2. Less factoring commission (x% of the receivables)**
**3. Less factoring reserve (y% of the receivables)**
**4. = Amount available for advance**
**5. Less the factor's interest for the collection period = Advance to be paid**==

==**Worked on MTP March 2024 Series I's NV Industries, whose figures recur three times.** Credit sales ₹160 lakhs (80% of ₹200 lakhs) on terms of 2/40 net 120 with half the customers taking the discount: **average collection period = (40 × 0.5) + (120 × 0.5) = 80 days**; **average receivables = ₹1,60,00,000 × 80/360 = ₹35,55,556**; **commission at 2% = ₹71,111**; **reserve at 10% = ₹3,55,556**; **amount available for advance = ₹31,28,889**; interest at 18% for 80 days deducted, giving an **advance of ₹30,03,733**; **annual cost of factoring ₹8,83,200**; **net cost ₹4,83,200**; **effective cost 16.09%.**==
==**The blended collection period is the step most often missed.** Terms of 2/40 net 120 with a 50% take-up give **80 days**, not 120 and not 40. Three official questions turn on it.==

==**§20.2 Forfaiting.** **'Forfait is a French term which means relinquish a right.'** **'Forfaiting is an arrangement of bill discounting in which a financial institution or bank buys the trade bills (invoices) or trade receivables from exporters of goods or services, where the exporter relinquish his right to receive payment from importer. Financial Institutions or banks provides immediate finance to exporter without recourse basis in which risk and rewards related with the bills/receivables transferred to the financial institutions/banks.'** It is **'a unique credit facility arrangement where an overseas buyer (importer) can open a letter of credit (or other negotiable instruments) in favour of the exporter and can import goods and services on deferred payment terms.'**==

==**The four functions, in order** (SM §20.2): **(i) the exporter sells goods or services to an overseas buyer; (ii) the importer, on the basis of trade bills and import documents, draws a letter of credit through its bank; (iii) the exporter, on receiving the letter of credit, approaches its own bank; (iv) the exporter's bank buys the letter of credit 'without recourse basis' and provides the exporter the payment for the bill.**==

==**The five salient features:** **it motivates exporters to explore new geographies as payment is assured; an overseas buyer can import goods and services on deferred payment terms; the exporter enjoys reduced transaction costs and complexities of international trade transactions; the exporter gets to compete in the international market and can continue to put his working capital to good use to scale up operations; and importers avail of forfaiting facility from international financial institutions in order to finance their imports at competitive rates.**==

==**ICAI's example:** **Exim Bank of India's 'Buyer's Credit'.** It **'facilitates exports for SMEs by providing credit to overseas buyer to import goods from India'**, **offering financing of capital goods or services on deferred payment terms**, and **'provides non-recourse finance to Indian exporters by converting deferred credit contract into cash contract. It extends advance payments to Indian exporters on behalf of the overseas buyer.'**==

==**Factoring against forfaiting — the comparison asked in MTP January 2025 Series II.** **Factoring** buys **domestic or export receivables**, may be **with or without recourse**, covers the **whole sales ledger** on a continuing basis, and includes **sales-ledger administration and collection services**. **Forfaiting** buys **export trade bills only**, is **always without recourse**, is **transaction-by-transaction** rather than a running arrangement, usually rests on a **letter of credit or other negotiable instrument**, and is **a form of bill discounting** rather than ledger management. ==**Factoring is a service plus finance; forfaiting is finance alone.**==
concepts.example: The same question has now been published four times with only the bad-debt percentage and the comparison rate changed: MTP March 2024 Series I (bad debts 1%, bank finance 14%, answer 16.09%), RTP September 2025 (bad debts 1.5%, bank finance 12%, answer 13.42%), RTP September 2026 (bad debts 1%, bank finance 14%, answer 16.09%) and, in a different wrapper, MTP September 2025 Series I's MCQ on the advance alone. Working the March 2024 version once delivers three later questions almost unchanged.

memory.trick: **Receivables, commission, reserve, interest.** Four steps down to the advance: start with the **average receivables**, take off the factor's **commission**, take off the **reserve**, and that is what is **available**; then take off the factor's **interest** and that is what is **paid**. ==Savings are three (admin, bad debts, interest on a shorter cycle); costs are two (commission, interest). Three minus two, over the advance.==
