official_questions.question: Following is the sales information in respect of Bright Ltd: Annual Sales (90% on credit) ₹7,50,00,000; Credit period 45 days; Average Collection period 70 days; Bad debts 0.75%; Credit administration cost (out of which 2/5th is avoidable) ₹18,60,000. A factor firm has offered to manage the company's debtors on a non-recourse basis at a service charge of 2%. The factor agrees to grant advance against debtors at an interest rate of 14% after withholding 20% as reserve. The payment period guaranteed by the factor is 45 days. The cost of capital of the company is 12.5%. One-time redundancy payment of ₹50,000 is required to be made to the factor. Calculate the effective cost of factoring to the company. (Assume 360 days in a year)
answer_points: ==**A. Savings due to factoring**==
**Administration cost saved** = ₹18.6 lakhs × 2/5 = ==**₹7,44,000**==. *Only the avoidable fraction is a saving — the question gives 2/5 for that purpose.*

**Interest saved due to reduction in the average collection period** = ₹7.5 crores × 90% × (70 − 45) ÷ 360 × 12.5% = ==**₹5,85,937.50**==. *The factor guarantees 45 days against an actual 70, and the saving is valued at the company's own 12.5% cost of capital.*
==**B. Costs of factoring**==
**Redundancy payment** = ==**₹50,000**==.
**C. Net annual cost to the firm (A − B) = ==₹4,85,187.50==** (a net cost, since the costs exceed the savings).

==**The working note that produces the advance, and it must be shown:**
**Average level of receivables** = ₹6.75 crores × 45/360 = **₹84,37,500** *(on the factor's guaranteed 45 days, not the present 70)*
**Service charge** = 2% of ₹84,37,500 = ₹1,68,750
**Reserve** = 20% of ₹84,37,500 = ₹16,87,500
**Total deductions = ₹18,56,250**
**Amount available for advance = ₹84,37,500 − ₹18,56,250 = ₹65,81,250**
**Less interest at 14% for 45 days = ₹1,15,171.875**
**Net amount of advance available = ==₹64,66,078.125==**==
==**The advice:** **'Since the rate of effective cost of factoring is less than the existing cost of capital, therefore, the proposal is acceptable.'** 7.504% against a cost of capital of 12.5%.==

==**ICAI prints three answers to this question, and all three should be known.**
**(1) ₹4,85,187.50 and 7.504%** — the main answer, with the redundancy payment included.
**(2) ₹4,35,187.50 and 6.730%** — ICAI's own note: **'Alternatively, if redundancy cost is taken as irrelevant for decision making, then Net Annual cost to the Firm will be ₹4,35,187.5 and Rate of effective cost of factoring will be 6.730%.'** The argument is that a **one-time** payment is not an annual cost and so does not belong in an annual rate.
**(3) A third variant** computing the average level of receivables **on 70 days** rather than 45, giving receivables of ₹1,31,25,000, a service charge of ₹2,62,500 and a reserve of ₹26,25,000.
==**Give answer (1) and note answer (2) in a line.** The three-way split is recorded as an open item in this chapter's verification block; it is ICAI's ambiguity, not the candidate's.==

**The two reading decisions that drive everything.** **Which collection period?** The factor guarantees 45 days, so the post-factoring receivables are sized on 45 — and the 25-day improvement is itself one of the savings. **Which administration cost?** Only the avoidable 2/5, because the other 3/5 continues whether or not the factor is appointed.
keywords: only 2/5 of administration cost is avoidable
also_asked_as: PYQ-J26-Q1b is the same computation with credit sales to be derived; MTP-S24-S2-FQ2a adds a recourse basis and an overdraft comparison

official_questions.question: X Ltd. has average debtors of ₹90,00,000. The company's average collection period is 60 days. At present, it incurs credit administration expenses of ₹4,00,000 per year and bad-debt losses amounting to 1% of credit sales. A factoring company has proposed to purchase these receivables by charging a commission of 2% on credit sales. The factor will provide an advance of 85% of receivables, after keeping 15% as reserve, and will charge interest at 15% per annum for the collection period. Assume 360 days in a year. Required: (i) Calculate the effective cost of factoring. (ii) As a financial consultant, advise whether X Ltd. should accept the factoring proposal. (5 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Step 1 — back out the credit sales, which is the step the question is built on.** Average debtors = Credit sales × collection period ÷ 360, so **Credit sales = ₹90,00,000 × 360 ÷ 60 = ==₹5,40,00,000==.**==
==**A. Annual savings (benefit) on taking factoring service**==
**Cost of credit administration saved** = ==**₹4,00,000**==.
**Total = ==₹9,40,000==.** *There is no 'interest saved' line here, because the factor does not shorten the collection period — it stays at 60 days.*
==**B. Annual cost of factoring to the firm**==
**C. Net cost of factoring to the firm = ₹22,00,500 − ₹9,40,000 = ==₹12,60,500==.**

==**(ii) The advice: reject.** An effective cost of **17.307%** is well above any plausible short-term borrowing rate, and ICAI's own rule is that **'the company should not avail Factoring services if the Rate of Effective Cost of Factoring to the Firm is more than the existing cost of borrowing.'** The proposal costs ₹12,60,500 a year net and buys nothing but the transfer of a collection function that was costing ₹4,00,000 to run. ==**X Ltd should not accept.**==

==**An inconsistency inside ICAI's own answer, which this book records rather than smooths over.** The **commission in the cost block is 2% of credit sales (₹5,40,00,000 × 2% = ₹10,80,000)**, but the **commission deducted in arriving at the advance is 2% of receivables (₹90,00,000 × 2% = ₹1,80,000)**. The same 2% is applied to two different bases in the same solution. ==ICAI's printed format permits both — **'Factoring Commission [Annual credit Sales × % of Commission (or calculated annually)]'** — but using both at once in one answer is not internally consistent. **Reproduce ICAI's figures, since they are the published key, and note the point.** It is recorded as an open item in the verification block.==

**ICAI also notes a second denominator.** Its answer adds that **'Rate of Effective Cost of Factoring to the Firm can also be calculated for advance without taking Interest into consideration'** — that is, on ₹74,70,000 rather than ₹72,83,250, giving 16.874%. Say which denominator you used.

==**The contrast with May 2024's Bright Ltd is the lesson.** Bright Ltd's factor **shortens collection from 70 days to a guaranteed 45**, and that single improvement generates ₹5,85,937 of interest saved — enough to bring the effective cost down to 7.504% and make the proposal acceptable. X Ltd's factor **changes nothing about the collection period**, so the savings block has only two lines instead of three and the cost is more than double. ==**In a factoring question, always look first for whether the collection period improves: that line is usually the difference between accept and reject.**==
keywords: no interest-saved line — collection period unchanged
also_asked_as: PYQ-M24-Q1c is the same format where the factor does shorten the collection period

official_questions.question: Sukrut Limited has annual credit sales of ₹75,00,000. Actual credit terms are 30 days, but its management of receivables has been poor and the average collection period is about 60 days. Bad debt is 1 per cent of total sales. A factor has offered to take over the task of debt administration and credit checking at an annual fee of 1.5 per cent of credit sales. Sukrut Limited estimates that it would save ₹45,000 per year in administration costs as a result. Due to the efficiency of the factor, the average collection period would come back to the original credit offered of 30 days and bad debts would come to 0.5% on recourse basis. The factor would pay a net advance of 80 per cent to the company at an annual interest rate of 12 per cent after withholding a reserve of 10%. Sukrut Limited is currently financing its receivables from an overdraft costing 10 per cent per year and will continue to finance the balance fund needed (which is not financed by the factor) through the overdraft facility. If the occurrence of credit sales is throughout the year, COMPUTE whether the factor's services should be accepted or rejected. Assume 360 days in a year. (7 Marks)
answer_points: ==**ICAI's published figures: factor commission ₹1,12,500, interest cost on net advances ₹53,100, total cost ₹1,65,600, and Net Benefits to the Firm ₹23,650 — so the proposal is accepted.**==
==**A. Savings, and all three lines are live here.**==
**Administration cost saved** = ==**₹45,000**==, as given.

**Bad debts saved** = 1% − 0.5% = 0.5% of ₹75,00,000 = ==**₹37,500**==. *On a **recourse** basis bad debts are **halved, not eliminated** — the factor can turn uncollected receivables back to Sukrut, so the company retains half the loss.*

**Savings in interest cost of carrying debtors**, which ICAI sets out as its working note 1: the collection period falls from **60 days to 30 days**, so the debtors financed by the 10% overdraft halve. **In-house: ₹75,00,000 × 60/360 × 10% = ₹1,25,000.** Under factoring the company finances only the portion the factor does not advance, for 30 days.
==**B. Costs of factoring.**==
**Factor commission** = annual credit sales × commission = ₹75,00,000 × 1.5% = ==**₹1,12,500**==.
**Interest cost on net advances** = ==**₹53,100**== (ICAI's working note 1 computes the factor's 12% on the advance for 30 days, against the 10% overdraft the company would otherwise have paid).
**C. Net Benefits to the Firm (A − B) = ==₹23,650==.**
==**Advice:** **'Since the savings to the firm exceed the cost due to factoring, the proposal is acceptable.'**==

==**What makes this question harder than the others, and worth the seven marks.** There are **two interest rates in play** — the factor's **12%** on what it advances, and the company's own **10% overdraft** on the balance it still has to fund. ICAI's phrasing is explicit: Sukrut **'will continue to finance the balance fund needed (which is not financed by the factor) through the overdraft facility.'** ==So the comparison is not 'factoring against the overdraft' but 'factoring plus a smaller overdraft against a larger overdraft', and the interest line is a **net** figure.==

==**The recourse point is the second trap.** 'Bad debts would come to 0.5% **on recourse basis**' — so the saving is the **difference** of half a percentage point, ₹37,500, and **not** the full 1% of ₹75,000. A non-recourse arrangement would have saved the whole ₹75,000, and would have carried a higher commission for that reason: SM §20.1 says the factor **'bears the ultimate risk of loss in case of default and hence in such cases they charge higher commission.'**==

**Why the proposal wins where X Ltd's loses.** Sukrut gets **all three savings** — administration, bad debts and a 30-day improvement in collection — against a commission of only **1.5%**. X Ltd gets two savings against a **2%** commission and no improvement in collection. ==Three savings and a cheap commission beat two savings and a dear one.==

**One presentational note for seven marks.** Show working note 1 — the comparison of the in-house interest cost with the post-factoring interest cost — as a separate labelled table. It is where three of the seven marks sit, and burying it inside the cost block makes it invisible.
keywords: bad debts 1% to 0.5% on recourse = ₹37,500 saved
also_asked_as: PYQ-M24-Q1c is the non-recourse version where bad debts are fully saved

official_questions.question: A firm has total sales of ₹200 lakhs of which 80% is on credit. It is offering credit terms of 2/40, net 120. Of the total, 50% of customers avail of the discount and the balance pay in 120 days. Past experience indicates that bad debt losses are around 1.5% of credit sales. The firm spends about ₹2,40,000 per annum to administer its credit sales. These are avoidable as a factor is prepared to buy the firm's receivables. He will charge 2% commission. He will pay advance against receivables to the firm at an interest rate of 18% after withholding 10% as reserve. (i) DETERMINE the effective cost of factoring. Consider year as 360 days. (ii) If bank finance for working capital is available at 12% interest, ADVISE, should the firm avail of factoring service.
answer_points: ==**The blended collection period, which is the first mark.** 50% of customers take the discount and pay on day 40; 50% pay on day 120. **Average collection period = (40 × 0.5) + (120 × 0.5) = ==80 days==.**==
**Less the factor's interest at 18% for 80 days** = ₹31,28,889 × 0.18 × 80 ÷ 360 = ₹1,25,156, giving an **advance of ==₹30,03,733==**.

==**A. Savings.** Administration cost saved **₹2,40,000**; bad debts avoided 1.5% of ₹1,60,00,000 = **₹2,40,000**. **Total = ₹4,80,000.** *No interest-saved line: the collection period is unchanged at 80 days.*==
==**B. Costs.** ICAI's figure for the **annual cost of factoring is ₹8,83,200** — the commission annualised plus the factor's interest annualised over the 80-day cycle.==

==**(ii) The advice: reject.** **13.42% exceeds the 12% at which bank finance for working capital is available**, so by ICAI's rule — avail factoring only if the effective cost is **less** than the existing cost of borrowing — **the firm should not avail of the factoring service** and should fund its receivables through the bank instead.==

==**This is the same question as MTP March 2024 Series I's NV Industries and RTP September 2026 Q8, with two numbers changed.** Bad debts are **1.5%** here against **1%** in the other two, and the comparison rate is **12%** here against **14%** there. The arithmetic down to the ₹30,03,733 advance is **identical in all three**. ==The difference in bad debts changes the savings by ₹80,000 and so the effective cost from 16.09% to 13.42%, and the difference in the comparison rate flips the September 2026 decision to the same reject on a different margin. **Work the chain once and three official questions are answered.**==

**The annualisation step, which is where the ₹8,83,200 comes from and which candidates most often fumble.** The commission and the interest are both incurred **every 80 days**, that is **360 ÷ 80 = 4.5 times a year**. Annualising the per-cycle charges rather than applying the rates once to an annual figure is what ICAI's format means by **'Factoring Commission [Annual credit Sales × % of Commission (or calculated annually)]'** — the parenthesis is doing real work.
also_asked_as: MTP-M24-S1-FMCQ1 and RTP-S26-FQ8 run the identical chain with bad debts at 1%, giving 16.09%

official_questions.question: A firm has total annual sales of ₹200 lakhs, of which 80% are made on credit. The company offers credit terms of 2/40, net 120. Out of the total credit customers, 50% avail themselves of the cash discount, while the remaining customers settle their accounts after 120 days. Based on past experience, bad debt losses amount to approximately 1% of credit sales. In addition, the firm incurs ₹2,40,000 per annum in administering its credit sales. These costs can be avoided because a factor is willing to purchase the firm's receivables. The factor will charge a 2% commission and provide advances against receivables at an interest rate of 18%, while retaining 10% of the receivables as a reserve. Required: (i) Determine the effective cost of factoring. Assume a 360-day year. (ii) If bank finance for working capital is available at an interest rate of 14%, advise whether the firm should avail itself of the factoring service.
answer_points: **The working is identical to RTP September 2025 Q9 down to the advance**, because only the bad-debt percentage differs. **Credit sales ₹1,60,00,000; blended collection period 80 days; average receivables ₹35,55,556; commission ₹71,111; reserve ₹3,55,556; amount available for advance ₹31,28,889; advance after interest ₹30,03,733.**

==**A. Savings.** Administration cost saved **₹2,40,000**; **bad debts avoided 1% of ₹1,60,00,000 = ₹1,60,000.** **Total = ₹4,00,000** — ₹80,000 less than the September 2025 version, because bad debts are 1% rather than 1.5%.==
**B. Annual cost of factoring = ₹8,83,200**, unchanged.

==**ICAI's own footnote on the denominator, reproduced because it settles a recurring question:** **'If cost of factoring is calculated on the basis of total amount available for advance, then, it will be …'** — that is, ₹4,83,200 ÷ ₹31,28,889 = **15.44%** rather than 16.09%. ==**Both are acceptable; name the denominator you used.** This book takes the advance actually paid (₹30,03,733) as the primary basis, because that is the sum the firm actually receives and ICAI's main computation uses it.==

==**(ii) The advice: reject.** **16.09% exceeds the 14% at which bank finance is available**, so the firm should **not** avail the factoring service. ICAI's rule: do not avail factoring where the effective cost exceeds the existing cost of borrowing.==

==**The three-way comparison worth tabulating once, because it shows exactly what drives a factoring decision:**
**MTP Mar 2024 S1 (NV Industries):** bad debts 1%, bank 14% → **16.09%, reject**.
**RTP Sep 2025 Q9:** bad debts 1.5%, bank 12% → **13.42%, reject**.
**RTP Sep 2026 Q8:** bad debts 1%, bank 14% → **16.09%, reject**.
==All three reject, and in every case the decisive figure is the **₹8,83,200 of annual cost against savings of only ₹4,00,000 to ₹4,80,000.** The commission of 2% on an 80-day cycle — effectively 9% a year — plus 18% interest cannot be covered by administration savings and sub-2% bad debts. **A factoring proposal only wins when it also shortens the collection period**, as Bright Ltd's and Sukrut Limited's do.==

**One point on why the bad-debt difference matters so little.** Half a percentage point on ₹1.6 crores is ₹80,000, which moves the effective cost by 2.67 percentage points. The **commission and interest structure**, not the bad-debt rate, is what makes these proposals uneconomic — which is the substantive lesson behind the repetition.
keywords: 16.09% on the advance, 15.44% on the amount available
a factoring proposal wins only if it shortens collection
also_asked_as: MTP-M24-S1-FMCQ1 is this question as a five-MCQ Division A case; RTP-S25-FQ9 is it with bad debts at 1.5%

official_questions.question: NV Industries Ltd. manages its accounts receivables internally through its sales and credit department. Total sales ledger ₹200 lakhs of which 80% is credit sales. Credit policy 2/40, net 120. On average 50% of customers avail the discount and the balance of the receivables are collected on average in 120 days. Bad debt losses are around 1% of credit sales. The firm spends about ₹2,40,000 per annum to administer its credit sales, which are avoidable as a factoring firm is prepared to buy the firm's receivables. The proposal: (i) 2% commission; (ii) advance against receivables at 18% after withholding 10% as reserve. The company also has the option of a long-term loan at 15% interest or bank finance for working capital at 14%. Consider year as 360 days. I. What is the average level of receivables? II. How much advance will the factor pay against receivables? III. What is the annual cost of factoring to the company? IV. What is the net cost to the company on taking factoring service? V. What is the effective cost of factoring on advance received? (5 × 2 = 10 Marks)
answer_points: ==**ICAI's published keys: (b), (c), (a), (d), (a).**==

**I. Average level of receivables — (b) ₹35,55,556.**
**Total sales ₹200 lakhs → credit sales 80% = ₹160 lakhs.**
**Average collection period = (40 × 0.5) + (120 × 0.5) = 80 days.**
**Average level of receivables = ₹1,60,00,000 × 80 ÷ 360 = ==₹35,55,556==.**
==Option (a) ₹53,33,333 is the figure on a 120-day period; option (b)'s neighbours are built from 40 days and from 160 days. **The blended period is the whole of this mark.**==

**II. Advance the factor will pay — (c) ₹30,03,733.**
**Factoring commission** = ₹35,55,556 × 2/100 = ₹71,111.
**Factoring reserve** = ₹35,55,556 × 10/100 = ₹3,55,556.
**Amount available for advance** = ₹35,55,556 − (₹3,55,556 + ₹71,111) = **₹31,28,889**.
**The factor deducts its interest at 18% for 80 days**: ₹31,28,889 × 0.18 × 80/360 = ₹1,25,156.
**Advance = ₹31,28,889 − ₹1,25,156 = ==₹30,03,733==.**
==Option (a) ₹31,28,889 is the amount **available** for advance rather than the advance **paid** — the distinction ICAI draws in its own format, and the reason it offers two denominators for the effective cost.==

**III. Annual cost of factoring — (a) ₹8,83,200.**
The commission and the interest are both incurred every 80 days, that is **4.5 times a year**. Annualising: **commission ₹71,111 × 4.5 = ₹3,20,000** and **interest ₹1,25,156 × 4.5 = ₹5,63,200**, giving ==**₹8,83,200**==.
==**Equivalently and more quickly:** commission = 2% × ₹1,60,00,000 = ₹3,20,000, and interest = ₹31,28,889 × 18% = ₹5,63,200. **Both routes give ₹8,83,200, and the second is the one to use under time pressure.**==

**IV. Net cost to the company — (d) ₹4,83,200.**
**Savings:** administration ₹2,40,000 + bad debts avoided 1% × ₹1,60,00,000 = ₹1,60,000, **total ₹4,00,000**.
**Net cost = ₹8,83,200 − ₹4,00,000 = ==₹4,83,200==.**
==Option (a) ₹4,00,000 is the savings figure offered as the answer, and option (b) ₹4,26,667 is a near miss built from a different collection period. **Read whether the question wants the gross cost (III) or the net cost (IV); they are consecutive MCQs for exactly that reason.**==

**V. Effective cost of factoring on advance received — (a) 16.09%.**
**₹4,83,200 ÷ ₹30,03,733 × 100 = ==16.09%==.**
==The question says **'on advance received'**, which settles the denominator: the advance **paid**, ₹30,03,733, not the amount available, ₹31,28,889. On the latter it would be 15.44%, offered as a distractor. **ICAI tells you which denominator it wants in the stem of the MCQ.**==

==**The decision the case does not ask for but which every later version does.** Against a **long-term loan at 15%** or **bank finance for working capital at 14%**, an effective cost of **16.09% is dearer than both**, so the factoring proposal should be **rejected**. The question gives both rates precisely so that the candidate who reaches 16.09% can see it fails against either.==

==**Why this case is the single highest-value question in Chapter 9 to work through.** Its five steps are **exactly** the five steps of the factoring format, in order, each worth two marks: the blended period and receivables, the advance, the annual cost, the net cost, the effective cost. ==**It has since been republished twice as a descriptive question (RTP September 2025 Q9 and RTP September 2026 Q8) and once as a standalone MCQ on step II alone (MTP September 2025 Series I MCQ vii). Four official questions, one chain.**==
keywords: keys b, c, a, d, a
also_asked_as: RTP-S25-FQ9, RTP-S26-FQ8 and MTP-S25-S1-FMCQ7 all draw on this chain

official_questions.question: A company has annual credit sales of ₹6,00,00,000. The average collection period is 90 days. A factor offers to buy the receivables with a 2% commission. The factor will advance on receivables to the company at an interest rate of 18% per annum after withholding 10% as reserve. Calculate the amount of advance to be paid assuming 360 days in a year. (a) ₹1,32,00,000 (b) ₹1,28,92,500 (c) ₹1,40,38,500 (d) ₹1,26,06,000
answer_points: **Step 5 — deduct the factor's interest for the collection period.** ₹1,32,00,000 × 18% × 90 ÷ 360 = ₹1,32,00,000 × 0.045 = ==**₹5,94,000**==.
**Advance to be paid = ₹1,32,00,000 − ₹5,94,000 = ==₹1,26,06,000 — option (d)==**, which is ICAI's published key.

==**The distractor that catches most candidates is option (a) ₹1,32,00,000 — the amount *available* for advance, stopped one step early.** The question asks for the **'amount of advance to be paid'**, which is after the factor's interest has been withheld. ==**ICAI's own format distinguishes the two explicitly: 'Advances to be paid = (Amount available for advance − Interest deducted by factor)'. Step 4 is not the answer; step 5 is.**==

**Option (c) ₹1,40,38,500** omits the reserve, and **option (b) ₹1,28,92,500** applies the interest for a full year rather than for the 90-day collection period — the other two single-step errors available.

==**The interest shortcut worth memorising.** 18% for 90 days on a 360-day year is **exactly 4.5%**, so the deduction is 4.5% of the amount available. Any factoring question with a 90-day period and an 18% rate reduces to multiplying by 0.955.==

**Why this two-mark MCQ is worth more than two marks of study.** It is **step II of the MTP March 2024 Series I case** lifted out and asked on its own, with different figures. ==Three of the nine factoring questions test only part of the chain — the receivables, the advance, or the annual cost — so the chain should be practised as five separable steps, not as one long computation to be run end to end.==
keywords: option (a) is the amount available, not the advance
also_asked_as: MTP-M24-S1-FMCQ1 item II is the same step with an 80-day period

official_questions.question: Nirmoh Limited wants to avail a short-term loan from a bank, which grants short-term loans by keeping collateral in the form of accounts receivable. The bank is analysing the receivables to identify acceptable collateral. The company's current policy is 3/10 net 40. The bank will lend only to the extent of 90% of acceptable receivables at an interest rate of 12% only if both conditions are fulfilled, keeping a reserve of 5% for cash discount and returns: (a) customers are not currently overdue for more than 5 days to the net period; (b) average aging (payment period) of the customer should not exceed 15 days past the net period. If any condition is not fulfilled, the bank will lend 65% of the receivables subject to a reserve of 15% and interest at 15%. The corporate tax rate is 25%. The acceptable receivables are DR 01 ₹50,000 (37 days outstanding, 40 days aging); DR 02 ₹25,000 (25, 48); DR 03 ₹1,20,000 (47, 49); DR 04 ₹72,000 (10, 56); DR 05 ₹45,000 (30, 30); DR 06 ₹1,75,000 (39, 50); DR 07 ₹19,000 (55, 25); DR 08 ₹54,000 (44, 54); DR 09 ₹1,05,000 (15, 25); DR 10 ₹37,000 (22, 75). CALCULATE: (a) the total amount lent by the bank, and (b) the effective interest cost (%) to the company.
answer_points:
==**Translate the two conditions into day limits before looking at a single account — this is the whole question.**
**Condition (a):** the net period is **40 days**, and an account must not be **overdue by more than 5 days** to it, so **'Outstanding in Days since invoiced' must not exceed 45 days.**
**Condition (b):** **'Average aging (payment period) of the customer should not exceed 15 days past the net period'**, that is **40 + 15 = 55 days.** ICAI states it in its answer: **'it should not exceed 55 days'.**==

==**Screen all ten accounts against both tests.**
**Fails (a), outstanding over 45 days:** DR 03 (47), DR 07 (55), DR 08 (44 — within 45, so passes (a)).
**Fails (b), aging over 55 days:** DR 04 (56) and DR 10 (75).
**ICAI's result:** the accounts qualifying for **90% lending** are **DR 01, DR 02, DR 05, DR 06, DR 08 and DR 09**, totalling **₹4,54,000**; the accounts falling to **65% lending** are **DR 03, DR 04, DR 07 and DR 10**, totalling **₹2,48,000.**==

==**(a) The amount lent — and ICAI's order of operations is the examinable point.**
**90% tier:** acceptable ₹4,54,000, **less a 5% reserve of ₹22,700**, giving a net of **₹4,31,300**; **then 90% of that = ₹3,88,170.**
**65% tier:** acceptable ₹2,48,000, **less a 15% reserve of ₹37,200**, giving a net of **₹2,10,800**; **then 65% of that = ₹1,37,020.**
**Total short-term loan granted = ₹3,88,170 + ₹1,37,020 = ==₹5,25,190==.**==

==**Note the double haircut, and note that it is ICAI's own reading.** The reserve is deducted **first**, and the lending percentage is applied to the **balance** — not 90% of ₹4,54,000 (which would be ₹4,08,600). ICAI's table is explicit: **Total 4,54,000 → (−) Reserve 22,700 → Net 4,31,300 → Loan 3,88,170.** ==A literal reading of 'lend to the extent of 90% of acceptable receivables **subject to** a reserve of 5%' could support either order, and this book follows ICAI's. **It is recorded as an open item in the verification block.**==

==**The tax shield is the detail most candidates miss.** The question gives a corporate tax rate of 25% for one reason only: **interest is deductible**, so the cost to the company is the **post-tax** figure. A pre-tax answer of 12.78% is arithmetically correct and answers a different question. ==**Where a receivables-financing question gives a tax rate, the effective cost is post-tax.**==

==**Why this question belongs to §20 and not §22.** It looks like an ageing-schedule question — ten accounts, two day-columns — but the ageing is only the **screening mechanism**. The substance is **pledging of accounts receivable** under SM §20.1: **'The lender scrutinizes the quality of the account receivables, selects acceptable accounts, creates a lien on the collateral and fixes the percentage of financing receivables which ranges around 50 to 90%.'** ==Nirmoh's two tiers, 90% and 65%, sit squarely inside ICAI's own '50 to 90%' range, and the question is the only official illustration of pledging in the period reviewed.==

**One reading trap in the data.** The two day-columns measure different things: **'Outstanding in Days since invoiced'** is how long *this* invoice has been unpaid, and **'Average Aging (payment period) in Days'** is how slowly *that customer* generally pays. An account can pass one and fail the other — DR 07 is 55 days outstanding (fails (a)) but has a 25-day aging (passes (b)), while DR 04 is only 10 days outstanding (passes (a)) but has a 56-day aging (fails (b)). ==**Test every account against both columns separately; a single combined judgement gets several accounts wrong.**==
keywords: reserve deducted first, then the lending percentage
also_asked_as: MTP-M26-S1-FQ3 uses an ageing schedule for a different purpose — the cost of the collection policy itself

official_questions.question: EXPLAIN the difference between factoring and forfaiting. (4 Marks)
answer_points: **Open with what each one is.** **Factoring** is the **outright sale of accounts receivables to a factor or a financial agency**; the **factoring agency bears the risk of collection and services the accounts for a fee.** **Forfaiting** — from the French **'forfait', meaning 'relinquish a right'** — is **an arrangement of bill discounting in which a financial institution or bank buys the trade bills or trade receivables from exporters of goods or services, where the exporter relinquishes his right to receive payment from the importer.**

==**1. Nature of the receivable.** Factoring covers the firm's **sales ledger generally**, domestic or export. Forfaiting is confined to **export trade bills and receivables**, arising from the sale of goods or services to an **overseas buyer**.==

==**2. Recourse.** Factoring may be **with recourse** — where the factor cannot collect, **'factor can turn back the same to the organization for resolution'** — or **without recourse**, where **'the factor bears the ultimate risk of loss in case of default and hence in such cases they charge higher commission.'** Forfaiting is **always 'without recourse'**: **'risk and rewards related with the bills/receivables transferred to the financial institutions/banks.'**==

==**3. The instrument.** Factoring rests on the **invoices themselves** under a **factoring agreement** that **'lays down the conditions of the sale'**. Forfaiting rests on a **letter of credit or other negotiable instrument** opened by the importer through its bank in favour of the exporter.==

==**4. Services provided.** Factoring is **finance plus service**: the factor provides **'efficient record keepings and effective management of the collection process'**, and relieves the client of sales-ledger administration. Forfaiting is **finance alone** — a discounting transaction, with no ledger management.==

==**5. Duration and pattern.** Factoring is typically a **continuing arrangement** over the whole ledger, giving **'immediate conversion of receivables into cash and predicted pattern of cash flows.'** Forfaiting is **transaction by transaction**, and typically on **deferred payment terms**, so that **'an overseas buyer (importer) can import goods and services on deferred payment terms.'**==

**6. What each does for the client.** Factoring **'can help a company having liquidity without creating a net liability on its financial condition and hence no impact on debt equity ratio'** and **'allows the firm to use cash for the growth needs of business.'** Forfaiting **'motivates exporters to explore new geographies as payment is assured'**, gives the exporter **'reduced transaction costs and complexities of international trade transactions'**, and lets him **'compete in the international market and continue to put his working capital to good use to scale up operations.'**

**Close with ICAI's own example of forfaiting**, which shows the two apart in practice: **Exim Bank of India's 'Buyer's Credit'** programme **'facilitates exports for SMEs by providing credit to overseas buyer to import goods from India'** and **'provides non-recourse finance to Indian exporters by converting deferred credit contract into cash contract'**, extending **advance payments to Indian exporters on behalf of the overseas buyer.**

==**The one-line summary that earns the fourth mark:** **factoring is a domestic-or-export sales-ledger service bundled with finance and may carry recourse; forfaiting is export-only, non-recourse, instrument-based finance with no service attached.**==
keywords: with or without recourse against always without recourse
sales ledger against export trade bills
finance plus service against finance alone
continuing arrangement against transaction by transaction
no impact on debt equity ratio

mcqs.question: A firm's credit terms are 3/30, net 90, and 40% of customers take the discount while the rest pay on the net date. Its average collection period is:

options.A: 60 days
options.B: 90 days
options.C: 66 days
options.D: 54 days

mcqs.explanation: The weighted average is (30 × 0.40) + (90 × 0.60) = 12 + 54 = 66 days. Option A is the simple average of the two periods, ignoring the take-up weights; option B uses the net period alone and option D reverses the weights. Three official factoring questions turn on this step, all with a 50% take-up on 2/40 net 120, giving 80 days.

mcqs.question: Which of the following does the study material give as an advantage of factoring **over** pledging of accounts receivable?

options.A: The percentage of receivables financed is higher under factoring
options.B: Factoring carries no commission, only interest on the advance
options.C: Factoring is always on a non-recourse basis, so the client bears no credit risk
options.D: Factoring is a sale rather than a loan, so there is no net liability and no impact on the debt equity ratio

mcqs.explanation: SM §20.1 says factoring 'can help a company having liquidity without creating a net liability on its financial condition and hence no impact on debt equity ratio' and 'This is not considered as a loan.' Pledging, by contrast, 'being a loan, it leaves an impact on the debt equity ratio as well by increasing the amount of debt.' Option C is wrong because factoring may be with or without recourse — it is **forfaiting** that is always without recourse.

recap: Pledging is a secured loan on selected receivables, financing 50 to 90%, and it increases debt. Factoring is an outright sale, so there is no net liability and no effect on the debt-equity ratio.
Recourse lets the factor turn uncollected receivables back to the client; non-recourse leaves the loss with the factor, which charges a higher commission for it.
The format: savings (administration, bad debts, interest on a shorter collection period) less costs (commission, interest on the advance), then the effective cost on the advance.
Five steps to the advance: receivables, less commission, less reserve, equals amount available, less the factor's interest, equals the advance paid.
Compute the blended collection period first wherever a discount period and a net period are both given — 2/40 net 120 at a 50% take-up is 80 days.
Accept factoring only if the effective cost is below the existing cost of borrowing; a proposal that does not shorten the collection period rarely passes.
Forfaiting means relinquishing a right: export bills only, always without recourse, usually under a letter of credit, and finance without service.

concepts.title: 21–22 Innovations in Receivable Management, and the Monitoring of Receivables
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 1 (May 2026 Series I Q3, 10 marks)
understand: ==**§21 The five determinants of innovation in receivables management** (SM §21), and ICAI's framing: **'the nature of accounts receivables is such that decisions made elsewhere in the organization are likely to affect the level of resources that are expended on the management of accounts receivables.'**==

==**1. Re-engineering Receivable Process** — **'Re-engineering is a fundamental re-think and re-design of business processes by incorporating modern business approaches.'** Three aspects offer the opportunity:==

==**(a) Centralisation** — **'Centralisation of high nature transactions of accounts receivables and payable is one of the practices for better efficiency. This focuses attention on specialized groups for speedy recovery.'**==

==**(b) Alternative Payment Strategies** — **'It is observed that payment of accounts outstanding is likely to be quicker where a number of payment alternatives are made available to customers. Besides, this convenient payment method is a marketing tool that is of benefit in attracting and retaining customers.'** The five modes ICAI lists: **(i) Direct debit — 'authorization for the transfer of funds from the purchaser's bank account'; (ii) Integrated Voice Response (IVR) — 'uses human operators and a computer-based system to allow customers to make payment over phone', beneficial where a large number of payments are processed regularly; (iii) Collection by a third party — 'the payment can be collected by an authorized external firm', by cash, cheque, credit card or EFT, with banks also acting as collecting agents; (iv) Lock Box Processing — 'an outsourced partner captures cheques and invoice data and transmits the file to the client firm for processing in that firm's systems'; (v) Payments via Internet using fund transfer methods like RTGS, NEFT, IPMS UPIs, and app-based payment.**==

==**(c) Customer Orientation** — **'Where individual customers or a group of customers have some strategic importance to the firm a case study approach may be followed to develop good customer relations. A critical study of this group may lead to formation of a strategy for prompt settlement of debt.'**==

==**2. Evaluation of Risk** — **'Risk evaluation is a major component in the establishment of an effective control mechanism. Once risks have been properly assessed controls can be introduced to either contain the risk to an acceptable level or to eliminate them entirely.'** It also **'provides an opportunity for removing inefficient practices'** and **'involves a re-think of processes and questioning the way that tasks are performed.'**==

==**3. Use of Latest Technology** — the major innovations being **'the integration of systems used in the management of accounts receivables, the automation and the use of e-commerce.'**
**(a) E-commerce** — **'the use of computer and electronic telecommunication technologies, particularly on an inter-organisational level, to support trading in goods and services'**, using **Electronic Data Inter-change (EDI), Electronic Mail, Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT) and Electronic Catalogue Systems**, with **Amazon and Flipkart** as ICAI's examples.
**(b) Automated Accounts Receivable Management Systems** — **'Manual systems of recording the transactions and managing receivables are not only cumbersome but ultimately costly also. These integrated systems automatically update all the accounting records affected by a transaction.'** ICAI's example: a credit sale **'increases the amount the customer owes to the firm, reduces the inventory for the item purchased, and records the sale.'**==

==**4. Receivable Collection Practices** — **'The aim of debtors' collection should be to reduce, monitor and control the accounts receivable at the same time maintain customer goodwill.'** And the rule: **'The fundamental rule of sound receivable management should be to reduce the time lag between the sale and collection. Any delays that lengthen this span causes receivables to unnecessary build up and increase the risk of bad debts. This is equally true for the delays caused by billing and collection procedures as it is for delays caused by the customer.'**==

==**The eight collection procedures and practices** (SM §21.4): **(i) Issue of Invoice; (ii) Open account or open-end credit; (iii) Credit terms or time limits; (iv) Periodic statements and follow ups; (v) Use of payment incentives and penalties; (vi) Record keeping and Continuous Audit; (vii) Export Factoring — 'Factors provide comprehensive credit management, loss protection collection services and provision of working capital to the firms exporting internationally'; (viii) Business Process Outsourcing — 'a strategic business tool whereby an outside agency takes over the entire responsibility for managing a business process like collections in this case.'**==

==**5. Use of Financial tools/techniques**, of which ICAI develops **credit analysis** and **credit rating**: **'While determining the credit terms, the firm has to evaluate individual customers in respect of their credit worthiness and the possibility of bad debts. For this purpose, the firm has to ascertain credit rating of prospective customers.'** On rating: **'This involves decisions regarding individual parties so as to ascertain how much credit can be extended and for how long. In foreign countries specialized agencies are engaged in the task of providing rating information regarding individual parties. Dun and Broad street is one such source.'** And the test: **'The finance manager has to look into the credit-worthiness of a party and sanction credit limit only after he is convinced that the party is sound. This would involve an analysis of the financial status of the party, its reputation and previous record of meeting commitments.'**==

==**§22 Monitoring of Receivables — two steps, and the second is the examinable one.** **'Constant monitoring of the current status of receivables is very essential for any organization to make sure that its receivables management is as effective as it should be.'**==
==**(i) Computation of average age of receivables** — **'It involves computation of average collection period.'**==
==**(ii) Ageing Schedule** — **'When receivables are analysed according to their age, the process is known as preparing the ageing schedules of receivables.'**==

==**What the average collection period gives you, and what it does not.** It is **'a quick and effective method of comparing the liquidity of receivables with the liquidity of receivables in the past and also comparing liquidity of one firm with the liquidity of the other competitive firm'**, and it **'helps the firm to predict collection pattern of receivables in future.'** But the ageing schedule is needed because **'the purpose of classifying receivables by age groups is to have a closer control over the quality of individual accounts'** — it **'requires going back to the receivables' ledger where the dates of each customer's purchases and payments are available.'**==

==**Why the ageing schedule is the better tool, in ICAI's own words:** **'The ageing schedule, by indicating a tendency for old accounts to accumulate, provides a useful supplement to average collection period of receivables/sales analysis. Because an analysis of receivables in terms of associated dates of sales enables the firm to recognise the recent increases, and slumps in sales.'** And how to use it: **'To ascertain the condition of receivables for control purposes, it may be considered desirable to compare the current ageing schedule with an earlier ageing schedule in the same firm and also to compare this information with the experience of other firms.'**==

==**What that comparison actually shows, and it is the point of printing two dates.** In June, **53.4% of the book was 61–90 days old** and only 11.9% was current. By September, **79.5% is within 60 days** and the 61-day-and-over band has collapsed from 66.7% to 20.5%. ==**The total receivables have risen by ₹92,600 and the quality has improved sharply** — which is exactly the combination a single average collection period cannot reveal, because the average would merely have fallen without telling you whether that was better collection or lower sales.==
concepts.example: MTP May 2026 Series I's Shilpa Limited is the only official question on this section, and it is a ten-marker. The answer computes the effective cost of running that policy as a percentage of the operating cost of sales, and then asks for the three aspects of receivables management from §16.

official_questions.question: Being the financial controller of Shilpa Limited, you are provided with the debt collection policy and the debtors' ageing analysis as on the date of analysis. Ageing (₹): Customer A — Current 3,12,500, 31–60 days 1,05,000, total 4,17,500; Customer B — 61–90 days 3,11,200, total 3,11,200; Customer C — Current 6,81,600, total 6,81,600; Customer D — 91 or more 1,62,000, total 1,62,000; Customer E — 61–90 days 3,01,500, 91 or more 2,10,000 and 38,000, total 5,49,500. Column totals: Current 9,94,100; 31–60 days 4,06,500; 61–90 days 5,21,200; 91 or more 2,00,000; grand total 21,21,800. Collection Policy: (a) normal credit terms are for 30 days; (b) interest of 2% is charged on accounts overdue for 45 days; (c) interest of 4% is charged on accounts overdue for more than 75 days; (d) a cash discount of 2% is given to customers who make payment within 10 days of the invoice getting due. Additional information: (a) 40% of the invoice value after bad debt falling in the ageing criteria of 31–60 days pay after the 45th day but within the 60th day, with 1.5% of the total being uncollectible; (b) 25% of the invoice value after bad debt falling in the ageing criteria of 61–90 days pay after the 75th day but within the 90th day, with 3% of the total being uncollectible; (c) 15% of the total invoice value overdue for 91 days or more are uncollectible; (d) 50% of the customers (invoice value) avail the cash discount; (e) administration cost for managing the above customers would be ₹50,000. (i) CALCULATE the effective cost involved in the collection process assuming that the operating cost of sales ratio is 0.75. (ii) EXPLAIN three aspects of management of receivables. (10 Marks)
answer_points:
==**ICAI's answer to (i): Effective Cost of Debtors Policy = 6.50%, built as**
**(Bad debts + Cash discount + Administration Cost − Interest Charged Received) ÷ Operating Cost of Sales**
**= (₹51,734 + ₹9,941 + ₹50,000 − ₹8,259) ÷ ₹15,91,350 = 6.50%.**==
**The denominator first, because it is the easiest mark.** **Operating cost of sales = 0.75 × ₹21,21,800 = ==₹15,91,350==.**

==**Bad debts — ₹51,734, computed bucket by bucket.**
**31–60 days bucket:** 1.5% of the total in that bucket is uncollectible.
**61–90 days bucket:** 3% of the total is uncollectible.
**91 days and more:** **15% of the total invoice value** is uncollectible — the largest rate, on ₹2,00,000.
==The rates escalate with age (1.5% → 3% → 15%), which is the whole economic point of an ageing schedule: **'by indicating a tendency for old accounts to accumulate'**, it shows where the losses actually sit.==

==**Cash discount — ₹9,941.** A **2% discount** is given to customers who pay **within 10 days of the invoice becoming due**, and **50% of the customers by invoice value avail it.** The discount is therefore computed on **half of the eligible (current) invoice value, net of bad debt**, at 2%.==

==**Interest charged and received — ₹8,259, and note that it is a *deduction* from the cost.** The policy **charges** the customer interest: **2% on accounts overdue for 45 days** and **4% on accounts overdue for more than 75 days.** Applying those rates to the stated paying proportions — **40% of the 31–60 bucket paying after day 45**, and **25% of the 61–90 bucket paying after day 75** — gives ₹8,259 of interest income, which **reduces** the net cost of running the policy.==
**Administration cost — ₹50,000**, given directly.

==**ICAI's own note, which should be reproduced:** **'In absence of information on Opportunity Rate of return on Investment, Opportunity Cost of Investment in receivables is not calculated.'** ==That is an important omission to flag: the question gives no required rate of return, so the **largest cost in a normal credit-policy evaluation — the opportunity cost of funds tied up — is absent here.** The 6.50% is therefore the cost of the *collection process*, not the full cost of the credit policy.==
==**(ii) The three aspects of management of receivables** (SM §16) — four marks of pure recall at the end of a demanding computation:==

==**1. Credit Policy.** **'A balanced credit policy should be determined for effective management of receivables. Decision of Credit standards, Credit terms and collection efforts is included in Credit policy. It involves a trade-off between the profits on additional sales that arise due to credit being extended on the one hand and the cost of carrying those debtors and bad debt losses on the other. This seeks to decide credit period, cash discount and other relevant matters.'**==

==**2. Credit Analysis.** **'This requires the finance manager to determine as to how risky it is to advance credit to a particular party. This involves due diligence or reputation check of the customers with respect to their credit worthiness.'**==

==**3. Control of Receivable.** **'This requires finance manager to follow up debtors and decide about a suitable credit collection policy. It involves both laying down of credit policies and execution of such policies.'** Add the **four costs of maintaining receivables** — the interest or opportunity cost on funds blocked, administrative costs, collection costs and defaulting costs — all four of which appear by name in part (i).==

==**Why part (ii) is where the easy marks are, and a word of exam strategy.** Part (i) is a bucket-by-bucket computation with five interlocking assumptions and is easy to lose half-way through; part (ii) is four headings from §16 that can be written in three minutes. ==**In a ten-mark question structured like this, write part (ii) first.** Several official questions in this chapter pair a hard numerical with a short recall item, and the recall item is never worth fewer than three marks.==

**One structural observation about the question itself.** The ageing analysis is given **by customer and by bucket**, but every computation uses only the **column totals**. The customer names and the distribution across them are **not needed** — they are there to make the schedule look like a real ledger, and to test whether the candidate can see that the policy operates on age bands rather than on customers. ==Work from the row of column totals: ₹9,94,100 / ₹4,06,500 / ₹5,21,200 / ₹2,00,000.==

mcqs.explanation: SM §22: 'The purpose of classifying receivables by age groups is to have a closer control over the quality of individual accounts.' ICAI calls the ageing schedule a 'useful supplement' to the average collection period rather than a replacement for it — the average is step (i) of monitoring and the schedule step (ii). options.B: Integrated Voice Response

mcqs.explanation: SM §21.1(b)(ii): Integrated Voice Response (IVR) 'uses human operators and a computer-based system to allow customers to make payment over phone. This system has proved to be beneficial in the organisations processing a large number of payments regularly.' Direct debit is an authorisation to transfer funds from the purchaser's bank account; lock box processing has an outsourced partner capture cheques and invoice data; EDI is a technology used in e-commerce under §21.3.

recap: Five determinants of innovation: re-engineering the process, evaluation of risk, latest technology, collection practices, and financial tools.
Re-engineering has three aspects: centralisation, alternative payment strategies, and customer orientation.
Five payment modes: direct debit, Integrated Voice Response, collection by a third party, lock box processing, and internet transfers including RTGS, NEFT and UPI.
The fundamental rule: reduce the time lag between sale and collection, counting internal billing delays as much as customer delays.
Credit rating analyses a party's financial status, reputation and previous record of meeting commitments; Dun and Bradstreet is ICAI's example of a rating source.

Monitoring has two steps: the average age of receivables, and the ageing schedule — which gives closer control over the quality of individual accounts and should be compared with an earlier schedule and with other firms.

concepts.title: 23–25 Management of Payables (Unit V) — Introduction, the Cost and Benefits of Trade Credit, and the Computation of the Cost of Payables
concepts.evidence: PYQ 1 (May 2026 Q2(b)) · RTP 1 (Sep 2025 Q10(b)) · MTP 1 (Sep 2024 Series I Q4(a))
understand: ==**ICAI's opening, which is quotable and short** (SM §23): **'There is an old age saying in business that if you can buy well then you can sell well. Management of your creditors and suppliers is just as important as the management of your debtors.'**==

==**What trade credit is:** **'Trade creditor is a spontaneous / short term source of finance in the sense that it arises from ordinary business transaction.'** And the warning: **'it is also important to look after your creditors - slow payment by you may create ill-feeling and your supplies could be disrupted and also create a bad image for your company.'** **'Creditors are a vital part of effective cash management and should be managed carefully to enhance the cash position.'**==

==**§24(a) The cost of availing trade credit — four costs, and ICAI opens by conceding the usual assumption:** **'Normally it is considered that the trade credit does not carry any cost. However, it carries the following costs:'**==

==**(i) Price** — **'There is often a discount on the price that the firm undergoes when it uses trade credit, since it can take advantage of the discount only if it pays immediately. This discount can translate into a high implicit cost.'**==

==**(ii) Loss of goodwill** — **'If the credit is overstepped, suppliers may discriminate against delinquent customers if supplies become short. As with the effect of any loss of goodwill, it depends very much on the relative market strengths of the parties involved.'**==
==**(iii) Cost of managing** — **'Management of creditors involves administrative and accounting costs that would otherwise be incurred.'**==
==**(iv) Conditions** — **'Sometimes most of the suppliers insist that for availing the credit facility the order should be of some minimum size or even on regular basis.'**==

==**§24(b) The cost of NOT taking trade credit — three costs:**
**(i) Impact of Inflation** — **'If inflation persists then the borrowers are favored over the lenders as they were better off to pay the fixed outstanding amount later than sooner. Also, the subsequent transactions shall be at higher prices.'**
**(ii) Interest** — **'Trade credit is a type of interest free loan, therefore failure to avail this facility has an interest cost. This cost is further increased if interest rates are higher.'**
**(iii) Inconvenience** — **'Sometimes it may also cause inconvenience to the supplier if the supplier is geared to the deferred payment.'**==
==**§25 The two formulae, and both are needed.** **'By using the trade credit judiciously, a firm can reduce the effect of growth or burden on investments in Working Capital.'**==
==**The nominal annual cost of not taking the discount: **d ÷ (100 − d) × 365 ÷ t**==

==**But ICAI immediately adds: 'the above formula does not take into account the compounding effect and therefore, the cost of credit shall be even higher. The cost of lost cash discount can be estimated by the formula:'** **[100 ÷ (100 − d)]^(365 ÷ t) − 1**==

==**where d = the size of the discount (for a 6% discount, d = 6) and t = 'The reduction in the payment period in days, necessary to obtain the early discount, or Days Credit Outstanding − Discount Period.'**==

==**SM Illustration 17 — the compounded form in action.** ABC Ltd is offered **2/10, net 45**, so **'the company has the choice of paying ₹10 per ₹100 or to invest ₹98 for an additional 35 days and eventually pay the supplier ₹100 per ₹100.'** **t = 45 − 10 = 35 days**, and
**[100 ÷ 98]^(365/35) − 1 = ==23.5%==.**==

==**And then ICAI tests it against an actual opportunity rate**, which is the structure May 2026's past paper follows. If ABC can earn **25%** on cash and the invoice is **₹10,000**:
**Refuse discount:** payment to supplier ₹10,000, less the return from investing ₹9,800 between day 10 and day 45 = ₹9,800 × 25% × 35/365 = **₹(235)**, giving a **net cost of ₹9,765.**
**Accept discount:** payment of **₹9,800.**
**'Thus, it is better for the company to refuse the discount, as return on cash retained is more than the saving on account of discount.'**==

==**SM Illustration 18 — the Dolce Company, and the error it is built to expose.** Terms of **2/10, net 30**; payments are usually made **15 days** after purchase; the accountant says the funds cost only 2% whereas a bank loan would cost 12%.==

==**ICAI's answer:** **'Rohit's argument of comparing 2% discount with 12% bank loan rate is not rational as 2% discount can be earned by making payment 5 days in advance i.e. within 10 days rather 15 days as payments are made presently. Whereas 12% bank loan rate is for a year.'** Assuming a purchase value of ₹100, the discount earned by paying within 10 days is ₹2, so the net payment is ₹98, and the **annualised benefit = (₹2 ÷ ₹98) × (365 ÷ 5) × 100 = ==149%==.** **'This means cost of not taking cash discount is 149%.'**==

==**And part (b) of the same illustration, which is the practical punchline:** **'If the bank loan facility could not be available, then in this case the company should resort to utilise maximum credit period as possible. Therefore, payment should be made in 30 days to reduce the interest cost.'** ==If you cannot afford to take the discount, **do not pay on day 15 — pay on day 30.** Paying early without taking the discount is the worst of both worlds, and it is the single most useful piece of advice in Unit V.==

==**The t to use is a judgement, and the two illustrations differ.** Illustration 17 takes **t = net period − discount period = 35 days**, because the comparison is between paying on day 10 and paying on day 45. Illustration 18 takes **t = 5 days**, because the company is **currently paying on day 15** and would have to move to day 10. ==**t is the number of days actually given up, measured from what the company does now, not always from the net date.**==
concepts.example: May 2026's B Ltd is Illustration 17 rebuilt with tax: a 2% discount on a ₹75,000 invoice for paying in one month instead of three, financed by a 10% overdraft, tax at 30%. ICAI gives the cash comparison — net benefit ₹1,050 against after-tax interest of ₹857.50, a net saving of ₹192.50 — and then the annualised form, 2/98 × 12/2 = 12.245% before tax and 8.571% after, against a post-tax overdraft rate of 7%. Both routes accept the discount, and ICAI prints both.

official_questions.question: B Ltd. has received an offer to get a discount of 2% on an invoice value of ₹75,000, if payment is made within one month instead of normal credit terms of 3 months. If the company makes early payment, it will need to finance the payment through a bank overdraft of 10% p.a. Tax rate is 30%. Whether B Ltd. should accept the offer? Support your decision with calculations. (3 Marks)
answer_points: ==**ICAI's main route — the cash comparison.**==
**Discount on early payment** = 2% × ₹75,000 = **₹1,500**.
**Net Benefit (A)** = ₹1,500 less tax at 30% = ==**₹1,050**==. *The discount is a reduction in a deductible expense, so it is taxed.*
**The amount that must be borrowed.** The company pays the discounted invoice, so **₹75,000 − ₹1,500 = ₹73,500**, and it must borrow that for the **two months** by which payment is advanced.
**Bank overdraft interest for 2 months** = ₹73,500 × 10% × 2/12 = ==**₹1,225**==.
==**Decision:** **'Since the company gains a net benefit of ₹192.50 by making early payment, B Ltd. should accept the discount offer.'**==

==**ICAI's alternative route, printed immediately below, and worth giving as a cross-check.**
**Annualised benefit of discount** = [Discount % ÷ (100 − Discount %)] × [12 months ÷ (Credit period − Discount period)]
**= 2/98 × 12/2 × 100 = ==12.245%==**
**Post-tax benefit** = 12.245% × (1 − 0.3) = ==**8.571%**==
**Post-tax bank overdraft rate** = 10% × (1 − 0.3) = ==**7%**==
**'Benefit of discount is more than cost of OD. Hence, discount should be accepted.'**==

==**The two routes must agree, and checking that they do takes ten seconds.** 8.571% against 7% is a margin of 1.571% a year; on ₹73,500 for two months that is ₹73,500 × 0.01571 × 2/12 = ₹192.45 — the ₹192.50 of the cash route. ==**Giving both and noting that they reconcile is how a three-mark answer becomes a complete one.**==

==**Three technique points, each of which is a mark somewhere in this chapter.**
**(1) Tax both sides.** The discount is taxable income forgone on the expense side and the interest is deductible; applying 30% to only one of them is the commonest error and reverses the decision if applied to the interest alone.
**(2) Borrow the net figure, not the gross.** The company pays ₹73,500, not ₹75,000, so the overdraft is on ₹73,500. Using ₹75,000 overstates the interest by ₹25 before tax.
**(3) The period is two months, not one.** Payment moves from month 3 to month 1, so the financing is needed for the **two months saved** — which is also the t in the annualised formula.==

**And the shape of the answer.** This is SM Illustration 17 with the opposite conclusion: there the firm could earn **25%** on retained cash and so refused a discount worth 23.5%; here it can borrow at **7% post-tax** against a discount worth 8.571% post-tax, and so accepts. ==**The decision rule is the same in both — compare the annualised value of the discount with the rate at which the money can be had or placed — and only the rates differ.**==

official_questions.question: DISCUSS the Costs of Availing Trade Credit. (4 Marks)
answer_points: ==**Open with ICAI's own concession, because it frames the whole answer:** **'Normally it is considered that the trade credit does not carry any cost. However, it carries the following costs.'** And set the context from §23: **trade credit is a spontaneous, short-term source of finance in the sense that it arises from ordinary business transaction** — which is precisely why its cost is invisible.==

==**(i) Price.** **'There is often a discount on the price that the firm undergoes when it uses trade credit, since it can take advantage of the discount only if it pays immediately. This discount can translate into a high implicit cost.'** ==Quantify it to show what 'high implicit cost' means: on terms of **2/10, net 45**, forgoing the discount costs **23.5% a year** on ICAI's own compounded formula (Illustration 17); and where a firm is already paying on day 15 under **2/10, net 30**, the cost of not taking the discount reaches **149% a year** (Illustration 18). **A 2% discount is never a 2% cost.**==

==**(ii) Loss of goodwill.** **'If the credit is overstepped, suppliers may discriminate against delinquent customers if supplies become short. As with the effect of any loss of goodwill, it depends very much on the relative market strengths of the parties involved.'** The qualification is the examinable part: a dominant buyer bears little of this cost, a small buyer in a tight market bears most of it. §23 adds that **slow payment 'may create ill-feeling and your supplies could be disrupted and also create a bad image for your company.'**==

==**(iii) Cost of managing.** **'Management of creditors involves administrative and accounting costs that would otherwise be incurred.'** Running a creditors ledger, reconciling supplier statements, scheduling payments and tracking discount dates all consume resource that a cash-on-delivery business does not spend.==

==**(iv) Conditions.** **'Sometimes most of the suppliers insist that for availing the credit facility the order should be of some minimum size or even on regular basis.'** The cost here is a loss of flexibility: the buyer may have to order more than it needs, or more often than it would choose, to keep the facility — which pushes the cost back into inventory holding.==

==**Close by naming the other side of the ledger**, because it shows the four costs are not an argument against trade credit. SM §24(b) gives the **costs of *not* taking trade credit**: **the impact of inflation**, since **'borrowers are favored over lenders as they were better off to pay the fixed outstanding amount later than sooner'** and later transactions will be at higher prices; **interest**, because **'trade credit is a type of interest free loan, therefore failure to avail this facility has an interest cost'**; and **inconvenience** to a supplier **'geared to the deferred payment'.**==

==**The one-sentence conclusion that earns the fourth mark:** **trade credit is free only in the sense that no interest is charged for it; its real cost is the discount forgone, and that cost must be compared with the firm's own cost of funds before a payment policy can be called rational.** Where the discount is worth more than the cost of borrowing, take it; where it is not, SM Illustration 18 is explicit that the firm **'should resort to utilise maximum credit period as possible'** — pay on the last day, not in between.==

minimum order size or regular basis
costs of not taking: inflation, interest, inconvenience
if you cannot take the discount, pay on the last day

official_questions.question: Trade credit and bank overdraft are two commonly used short-term financing sources but each has distinct features. On the light of the statement SHOW the difference between trade credit and bank overdraft.
answer_points: ==**1. How it arises.** **Trade credit is a spontaneous source**: **'it arises from ordinary business transaction'** (SM §23) and needs no negotiation — **'If a buyer is able to get the credit without completing much formality, it is termed as open account trade credit'** (SM §27.1). A **bank overdraft is a negotiated source**: SM §26 classifies negotiated sources as **'those which have to be specifically negotiated with lenders say, commercial banks, financial institutions, general public etc.'**==
==**2. Who provides it.** Trade credit comes from the **supplier of goods or services**; an overdraft comes from a **commercial bank**.==

==**3. Explicit cost.** Trade credit carries **no interest** — **'Trade credit is a type of interest free loan'** (SM §24(b)) — but it has an **implicit cost**, the **discount forgone**, which **'can translate into a high implicit cost'** (SM §24(a)). An overdraft carries an **explicit rate of interest**, charged on the amount actually drawn.==

==**4. Security.** Trade credit is **unsecured**, resting on the trading relationship and the buyer's reputation. An overdraft is typically **secured**, and SM §29 notes that **'the banks will impose limits on the amount they can lend'**.==

==**5. Flexibility and repayment.** An overdraft is highly flexible: **'It is a short-term borrowing facility made available to the companies in case of urgent need of funds. … When the borrowed funds are no longer required they can quickly and easily be repaid'** — but **'the banks issue overdrafts with a right to call them in at short notice'** (SM §29). Trade credit is tied to the **purchase cycle**: it rises and falls with buying, cannot be drawn on demand, and is repaid on the invoice due date.==

==**6. Conditions attached.** Trade credit may require **a minimum order size or regular ordering** (SM §24(a)(iv)), and overstepping it risks **loss of goodwill and disrupted supplies**. An overdraft is subject to a **sanctioned limit** and to the bank's **right of recall**, but imposes no conditions on what the buyer purchases.==

==**7. Effect on the balance sheet and on relationships.** Trade credit appears among **trade payables** and is part of the **spontaneous** working-capital base, financing about **'one-third of the total short-term requirements'** by ICAI's estimate (SM §27.1). An overdraft is **bank borrowing**; SM §6.2 expressly excludes bank credit from the current liabilities deducted in computing the working-capital requirement, because it is the **financing** of that requirement rather than a spontaneous part of it.==

==**8. Availability to the small firm.** ICAI notes that trade credit is **'more helpful to small and medium enterprises'** because of **'its simplicity, easy availability and lesser explicit cost'** (SM §27.1), whereas an overdraft depends on the bank's assessment of the borrower.==

==**The closing judgement, which is what the question's 'each has distinct features' is inviting.** Trade credit is **cheap, automatic and limited in amount and timing**; an overdraft is **dearer, negotiated and flexible in amount and timing**. ==A firm therefore uses trade credit for the **predictable, purchase-linked** part of its short-term need and the overdraft for the **variable residue** — which is the matching approach of SM §26 applied inside the short-term layer itself.==

explicit interest on the amount drawn
unsecured against secured with a limit
tied to the purchase cycle against drawn on demand
right to call them in at short notice
bank credit excluded from current liabilities in §6.2

options.B: A benefit of a bank overdraft over trade credit
options.C: A reason suppliers impose minimum order sizes
options.D: A cost of **not** taking trade credit

t is the number of days actually given up: 35 days in Illustration 17, but only 5 in Illustration 18 where the firm already pays on day 15.
2/10 net 45 costs 23.5% a year to refuse; 2/10 net 30 refused by a firm paying on day 15 costs 149%.
If the discount cannot be taken, pay on the last day of the credit period — never in between.

concepts.title: 26–27.1 Financing of Working Capital — Introduction, Sources of Finance, and Spontaneous Sources
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 1 (May 2024 Q8(ii); RTP Jan 2026 Q11(b) on the same heading is placed in FM Ch 2 under F02.22) · MTP 1 (Jan 2025 Series I Q4(a), placed under F09.09)
understand: ==**The opening instruction, which is the whole logic of Unit VI** (SM §26): **'After determining the amount of working capital required, the next step to be taken by the finance manager is to arrange the funds. As discussed earlier, it is advisable that the finance manager bifurcate the working capital requirements between the permanent working capital and temporary working capital.'**==

==**And the rule that follows:** **'The permanent working capital is always needed irrespective of sales fluctuation; hence it should be financed by the long-term sources such as debt and equity. On the contrary the temporary working capital may be financed by the short-term sources of finance.'**==

==**The two broad categories** (SM §26):
**Spontaneous Sources** — **'those which naturally arise in the course of business operations. Trade credit, credit from employees, credit from suppliers of services, etc. are some of the examples which may be quoted in this respect.'**
**Negotiated Sources** — **'as the name implies, are those which have to be specifically negotiated with lenders say, commercial banks, financial institutions, general public etc.'**==

==**The six parameters guiding the choice of source** (SM §26) — the list to give for any 'what factors' question on financing:
**(i) Cost factor**
**(ii) Impact on credit rating**
**(iii) Feasibility**
**(iv) Reliability**
**(v) Restrictions**
**(vi) Hedging approach or matching approach i.e., Financing of assets with the same maturity as of assets.**==
==**§27.1 The three spontaneous sources, in ICAI's order:**==

==**(a) Trade Credit.** **'Trade credit is a spontaneous source of finance which is normally extended to the purchaser organization by the sellers or services providers.'** And the figure worth quoting: **'This source of financing working capital is more important since it contributes to about one-third of the total short-term requirements. The dependence on this source is higher due to lesser cost of finance as compared with other sources.'** **'Trade credit is guaranteed when a company acquires supplies, merchandise or materials and does not pay immediately. If a buyer is able to get the credit without completing much formality, it is termed as open account trade credit.'**==

==**(b) Bills Payable.** **'in the case of Bills Payable the purchaser will have to give a written promise to pay the amount of the bill/invoice either on demand or at a fixed future date to the seller or the bearer of the note.'** ICAI's gloss on both: **'Due to its simplicity, easy availability and lesser explicit cost, the dependence on this source is much more in all small or big organizations. Especially, for small enterprises this form of credit is more helpful to small and medium enterprises. The amount of such financing depends on the volume of purchases and the payment timing.'**==

==**(c) Accrued Expenses.** **'Another spontaneous source of short-term financing is the accrued expenses or the outstanding expenses liabilities. The accrued expenses refer to the services availed by the firm, but the payment for which has yet to be made. It is a built in and an automatic source of finance as most of the services like wages, salaries, taxes, duties etc., are paid at the end of the period.'** And the key sentence: **'The accrued expenses represent an interest free source of finance. There is no explicit or implicit cost associated with the accrued expenses and the firm can ensure liquidity by accruing these expenses.'**==

==**The distinction between trade credit and accrued expenses that is worth stating, because it is the answer to 'what is the cost of these sources'.** Trade credit has **no explicit cost but a real implicit cost** — the discount forgone, which SM §24(a) calls **'a high implicit cost'** and §25 values at 23.5% or more. **Accrued expenses have neither:** ICAI says expressly **'There is no explicit or implicit cost associated with the accrued expenses.'** ==**So of the three spontaneous sources, accruals are the only genuinely free finance in the whole syllabus**, and the limit on them is not cost but the fact that the firm cannot choose when wages and taxes fall due.==

==**Why 'spontaneous' matters for the arithmetic, not just the theory.** Spontaneous sources are the **current liabilities deducted in the working-capital statement** of §6.2 — trade payables, outstanding wages, outstanding overheads. **Negotiated sources are not deducted**, because SM §6.2 says working capital is lowered by current liabilities **'(other than bank credit)'**. ==**That single parenthesis is the link between Unit I and Unit VI: the statement computes what the negotiated sources must fund, after the spontaneous ones have done their work.**==

**A placement note.** RTP January 2026 Q11(b) — **'What do you understand by Spontaneous Sources of finance and explain its sources of finance?'** — is the most direct question on this heading in the period reviewed, and it is already placed in **FM Chapter 2 under F02.22 Short-term Sources of Finance**, which covers the same ground. It is cross-referenced here rather than moved.
concepts.example: RTP May 2024 Q8(ii) asks for 'the importance of trade credit and accruals as source of working capital' and then, pointedly, 'What is the cost of these sources?' The second half is the whole question: trade credit's cost is the discount forgone — an implicit cost that can exceed 20% a year — while accruals have no explicit or implicit cost at all. A candidate who answers 'both are free' has missed the distinction ICAI drew two sections earlier.
