differentiate.q: Gross working capital vs net working capital
differentiate.a: Both measure the same balance sheet from the value point of view. Gross working capital is the firm's investment in current assets; net working capital is current assets less current liabilities. A positive net figure indicates the ability to pay short-term liabilities, a negative one the inability — though a retail business collecting in cash and paying in arrear may run on negative net working capital quite soundly, as RTP January 2025's Samvar Ltd does at ₹(5.9396) lakh a store.

differentiate.q: Aggressive vs conservative working capital investment
differentiate.a: Aggressive keeps current assets at a minimum — lower inventory, a strict credit policy, less cash — so less funding is tied up and financial costs are lower, but there is stock-out risk and growth is forgone, leaving lower utilisation of fixed assets and long-term debt. Conservative invests high in current assets, winning higher sales volume, demand from liberal credit and supplier goodwill, but paying an increased cost of capital and risking inventory obsolescence, bad debts and a longer operating cycle. Conservative means greater liquidity and lower risk; aggressive means higher risk and poor liquidity.

differentiate.q: Baumol's model vs the Miller-Orr model
differentiate.a: Both determine how much cash to hold and both balance the cost of holding cash against the cost of converting securities. Baumol is an inventory-type model assuming cash needs are known with certainty and used uniformly; it gives a single optimum C = √(2UP ÷ S), and its stated limitation is that it does not allow cash flows to fluctuate. Miller-Orr is a stochastic control-limit model: the net cash flow is completely random, and it sets h, z and zero, investing h − z at the upper limit and selling securities at the lower. The current Study Material gives no formula for Miller-Orr's limits.

Both convert receivables into cash before due date. Factoring is 'invoice factoring' — a sort of management of book debts, between client, factor and debtor, continuous over the whole sales ledger, with credit control and ledger administration included, and no specific Act applies. Bills discounting is 'invoice discounting' — a sort of borrowing from commercial banks, between drawer, drawee and payee, transaction by transaction with no service attached, and the Negotiable Instruments Act applies.

Both are non-loan ways of turning receivables into cash. Factoring covers domestic or export receivables, may be with or without recourse, runs as a continuing arrangement over the ledger, and bundles finance with credit control and sales-ledger administration. Forfaiting applies only to export trade bills, is always without recourse, works transaction by transaction usually under a letter of credit or other negotiable instrument, and provides finance alone. Exim Bank of India's Buyer's Credit is ICAI's example of forfaiting.

Both are short-term sources. Trade credit is spontaneous — it arises from ordinary business transaction, comes from the supplier, is unsecured and informal where it is 'open account', carries no explicit interest but a high implicit cost in the discount forgone, and is tied to the purchase cycle. A bank overdraft is negotiated with a commercial bank, is usually secured and limited, carries explicit interest on the amount drawn, can be drawn and repaid quickly for an urgent need, and is issued with a right to call it in at short notice. Trade credit funds about one-third of short-term requirements; §6.2 excludes bank credit from the current liabilities deducted in sizing the requirement.

Both are running bank limits the borrower may not exceed, and both charge interest on the drawn amount. Cash credit is given 'on continuous basis' and is the standard working-capital facility, normally secured against inventory and receivables. A bank overdraft is 'made available to the companies in case of urgent need of funds', can be repaid 'quickly and easily' when no longer needed, and is issued with a right of recall at short notice — which is the operative distinction.

differentiate.q: Total Approach vs Incremental Approach to credit policy evaluation
differentiate.a: Both reach the same decision and both end in a net benefit compared across policies. The Total Approach states every policy in levels — credit sales, variable and fixed costs, bad debts, cash discount, tax, then the opportunity cost of receivables — and ICAI uses it in seven of its eight published answers. The Incremental Approach states only the differences from the present policy and the required return on the incremental investment; it is quicker where one proposal is on the table but unforgiving, because nothing in the statement reveals the level it started from.

steps: Read the requirement: a cycle, a statement, a cash budget, a policy choice, or a source
Fix the conventions in the first two lines: 360 or 365 days, and cost basis or sales basis
For an estimation question, build two working notes first — the cost per unit, and the annual cash cost of production and of sales

Value each current asset at the cost that has reached it: raw material on consumption, WIP on material plus the completed part of conversion, finished goods on cost of production, debtors on cash cost of sales
Add prepayments as current assets and the minimum cash balance; subtotal as Gross Working Capital
Deduct current liabilities — trade payables on credit purchases, wages and overheads on their lags — but never bank credit
Apply the margin last, and read whether it is a mark-up ('20% of working capital') or a gross-up ('inclusive of the margin')
For a cycle question instead, compute the five periods as labelled fractions, add as R + W + F + D − C, divide the year, then divide the annual operating cost
For a credit policy, build ICAI's Total Approach skeleton, hold fixed cost constant, convert turnover ratios to days, and keep the sign if the investment falls
For factoring, run the five steps to the advance, then three savings less two costs, then the effective cost against the cost of borrowing
Close with the decision in words, and state every assumption as a numbered note
flowchart.note: Steps 2 to 7 are the estimation route and steps 8 to 10 the decision routes; every official question in this chapter is one of the four, and the conventions fixed in step 2 decide whether the rest can be right.

five: Operating Cycle = R + W + F + D − C; cycles = 360 or 365 ÷ cycle; working capital = annual operating cost ÷ cycles.
Finished goods at the cash cost of production, debtors at the cash cost of sales; profit and depreciation fund nothing.
Baumol: C = √(2UP ÷ S), with U and S on the same time basis. Miller-Orr: h, z and zero, investing h − z at the top.
Credit policy: expected profit less the opportunity cost of receivables (on cost of sales, not sales value), and the highest net benefit wins — not the highest profit.
Factoring: receivables, less commission, less reserve, less the factor's interest; effective cost on the advance, accepted only if below the cost of borrowing.

Add the three approaches and the CA/FA ratio, with Illustration 1's 20% / 22.22% / 25% against 1.00 / 0.80 / 0.60.
Add the two margin forms: '20% of working capital' multiplies by 1.20, 'inclusive of the margin' divides by 0.80.
Add the four floats, concentration banking, the lock box, and the cost-benefit rule that governs both.
Add the four purposes of a cash budget and the three methods of cash flow budgeting, with receipts and payments the one commonly used.
Add the cost-of-payables formulae and the fact that t is the days actually given up.

sections.title: Unit I — the requirement
points: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities; gross is the investment in current assets, net the difference
Permanent working capital is the minimum carried at all times, financed long term; temporary meets sales fluctuation, financed short term
Too much means idle funds and over capitalization; too little means the risk of insolvency and lost sales
Current ratio 2 and quick ratio 1 are thumb rules only — optimum depends on the particular circumstances of the specific situation
Nine planning factors: cash · inventory · receivables · short-term financing · nature of business · market and demand · technology · operating efficiency · price levels and forex
Three Es: economy in financing, efficiency in utilisation, effectiveness in achieving objectives
Five components in the trade-off: inventory, receivables, pre-paid expenses, cash, payables — the payables row reads the opposite way
Investment asks 'how much' (effectiveness); financing asks 'where from' (economy)
Aggressive / moderate / conservative; a higher CA/FA ratio is conservative, and the ratio moves inversely to return on total assets
Illustration 1: ₹5L / ₹4L / ₹3L of current assets → 20% / 22.22% / 25% and 1.00 / 0.80 / 0.60
Minimise total costs — the cost of liquidity plus the cost of illiquidity

sections.title: Unit I — estimating it
points: Three methods: current assets holding period (the operating cycle, 'one of the most reliable'), ratio of sales, ratio of fixed investments
Operating Cycle = R + W + F + D − C, and C is the only subtraction
R ÷ consumption · W ÷ cost of production · F ÷ cost of goods sold · D ÷ credit sales · C ÷ credit purchases, each per day
Cycles = 360 or 365 ÷ cycle; working capital = annual operating cost ÷ cycles; more cycles is better
Each current asset = units per period × the cost that has reached it × the holding period
Debtors and finished goods at cash cost — profit and depreciation are excluded
Prepayments are current assets; bank credit is never deducted as a current liability
Split WIP into material and conversion and apply the two completion percentages separately
Cash cost of production = material + wages + cash manufacturing; cash cost of sales adds administrative and selling
Double shift: stocks rise less than proportionately, WIP is unchanged, fixed cost per unit halves — Samreen needs ₹94,800 more

sections.title: Unit II — treasury and cash
points: Treasury management: planning, organizing and controlling funds and working capital for best use, liquidity, lower cost and less risk
Five tasks: cash management · currency management · fund management · banking · corporate finance
Keynes's three motives: transaction, speculative, precautionary
Cash budget — the most significant device; four purposes; three methods, of which receipts and payments is commonly used
Accruals and depreciation never enter a receipts-and-payments budget
Four floats: billing · mail · cheque processing · banking processing
Concentration banking shortens the mail float; the lock box eliminates the cheque processing float
Decide either by comparing added cost with the marginal income from released funds
Baumol: C = √(2UP ÷ S); carrying cost is interest forgone, transaction cost is clerical, brokerage and registration
Miller-Orr: net cash flow completely stochastic; h, z and zero; invest h − z at the top; no formula in the SM
Seven recent developments, ending in virtual banking — popular for speed, convenience and round-the-clock access
Marketable securities: safety, maturity, marketability — mainly treasury bills, bank deposits and inter-corporate deposits
Cash cycle = debtors + inventory − creditors; minimum cash = annual outlay ÷ cash turnover

sections.title: Units III to V — inventory, receivables, payables
points: Inventory: objectives similar to cash management; detail is in Paper 4 Chapter 2
Receivables management is trade credit management, and the objective is to optimise the return on investment
Three aspects: credit policy · credit analysis · control of receivable
Four costs: interest or opportunity cost · administrative · collection · defaulting
'3/15 net 60' — 3% off by day 15, otherwise pay by day 60
Seven factors determining credit policy, and a rising trend in costs depresses the investment
Total Approach: credit sales − variable − fixed − bad debts − discount − tax, then the opportunity cost of receivables
Fixed cost from the present policy, held constant; opportunity cost on cost of credit sales
Net benefit peaks before profit does — AB Enterprises's Policy A, ABC Pvt Ltd's Policy 1, Banu Limited's Option I
Factoring: receivables − commission − reserve = available; − interest = advance; effective cost = net cost ÷ advance
Three savings (administration, bad debts, interest on a shorter cycle) against two costs (commission, interest)
Accept if the effective cost is below the cost of borrowing — Bright Ltd 7.504% yes, X Ltd 17.307% no
Pledging is a loan and raises debt; factoring is a sale and does not; forfaiting is export-only and always without recourse
Monitoring: the average age of receivables, then the ageing schedule for closer control over individual accounts
Payables: four costs of availing trade credit, three of not availing it
Lost discount: nominal d ÷ (100 − d) × 365 ÷ t; compounded [100 ÷ (100 − d)]^(365/t) − 1 — 23.5% on 2/10 net 45
If you cannot take the discount, pay on the last day of the credit period

sections.title: Unit VI — financing it
points: Bifurcate permanent and temporary, and match the maturity of the source to the asset
Six parameters: cost · credit rating · feasibility · reliability · restrictions · the hedging or matching approach
Spontaneous: trade credit (about one-third of short-term needs), bills payable, accrued expenses
Accrued expenses have no explicit or implicit cost; trade credit has no explicit cost but a high implicit one
Commercial paper: unsecured promissory note, highly rated issuers, 7 days to less than 1 year, ₹5 lakhs or multiples
Five CP advantages and two limitations — no early redemption and no extension
Funds from operations = profit + depreciation; public deposits suit well-established big companies
Bill Rediscounting Scheme: RBI, from 1 November 1970, all licensed scheduled banks eligible
Factoring against bills discounting: management of book debts against borrowing; no specific Act against the Negotiable Instruments Act
MPBF withdrawn by the RBI in April 1997; banks set their own methods with Board approval; Tandon and Chore Committees
Seven forms of bank credit — four fund-based, three (bills acceptance, letter of credit, bank guarantee) non-fund-based
